questions.stem: Who is the 1st registrar of the Nepal Engineering Council?
questions.solution:
**Er. Bindeshwar Yadav.**

The three founding office-holders of the Council, established under the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**:

| Post | First holder |
|---|---|
| **Chairman** | Er. Ram Babu Sharma |
| **Vice-chairman** | Er. Nirajan Prasad Chalise |
| **Registrar** | **Er. Bindeshwar Yadav** |

The **Registrar** is the Council's chief executive and serves as its **Member-Secretary**. The post is distinct from the nominated and elected memberships: the Registrar administers the register of engineers, runs the registration examination, and executes the Council's decisions.

The wider framework this sits in, which is the durable part worth learning:

| Post | Qualification | Experience |
|---|---|---|
| Chairman | Bachelor's degree in engineering | **15 years** |
| Vice-chairman | Bachelor's degree in engineering | **10 years** |
| Five members | Nominated by the Government | — |
| Five members | **Elected** by the Nepal Engineers' Association | — |
| Two members | Nominated by **the Council itself** | — |
| **Registrar** | — | **Member-Secretary** |

plus the President of the Nepal Engineers' Association, one Campus Chief, and one representative of the Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University.

Registration categories, the other reliably examined fact: **A — General Engineer, B — Professional Engineer, C — Foreign Engineer.**

Do not confuse the **Council (NEC)** with the **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)**. The Council is the **statutory regulator** — registration with it is a legal prerequisite to practise, and it can suspend or cancel that registration for misconduct. The Association is a voluntary professional membership body, though its President and five of its elected engineers sit on the Council.

examTip.trick: A pure recall question about the Council's institutional history — the sort that costs nothing to know and cannot be reasoned out.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the NEC facts as one block: Act 2055 BS (1998), Regulations 2057, chairman needs a bachelor's degree and 15 years, vice-chairman 10 years, and TWO members are nominated by the Council itself.** Institutional questions appear in every paper and are the cheapest marks on it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about a dummy activity?
options: It doesn't have head and tail event
It can be added anywhere in the network
questions.solution:
**It doesn't consume resources.**

A **dummy activity** is an artificial activity inserted into a network diagram purely to express **logic**. It consumes **neither time nor resources**, and is drawn as a **dashed arrow**.

Why the other options are wrong:
- **(b)** A dummy is an arrow like any other, so it **does** have a tail and a head event — that is precisely how it carries the dependency.
- **(c)** It cannot be added anywhere. A dummy is inserted only where it is logically required; adding a spurious one would impose a dependency that does not exist and could change the critical path.
- **(d)** It **complicates** the drawing rather than simplifying it. It is a necessary evil of activity-on-arrow notation, not a convenience.

**The two situations that force a dummy**, which is the real content of the topic:

| Purpose | Situation |
|---|---|
| **Grammatical (identity) dummy** | Two or more activities share the **same tail and head events**. Without a dummy they would be indistinguishable, since an activity is identified by its i-j node pair |
| **Logical dummy** | Some but not all of a group of activities depend on a predecessor — the dependency has to be routed selectively |

The classic logical case: if C depends on both A and B, but D depends on **A only**, the two cannot simply share a node. A dummy carries A's completion forward to C while leaving D free of B.

**A note on notation.** Dummies exist only in **activity-on-arrow (AOA)** networks. The **activity-on-node (AON)** or precedence diagram method needs none, because dependencies are drawn as links between boxes and can be routed freely. Modern planning software uses AON for exactly that reason, so dummies are largely an examination topic now.

One consequence worth remembering: because a dummy has zero duration, both its events share the same time, so it can still lie **on the critical path** — a dummy with zero float is critical even though no work happens along it.

examTip.trick: A dummy exists purely to show a **logical dependency** that the network's arrow geometry cannot otherwise express. It consumes **no time and no resources**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dummies are drawn as a DASHED ARROW and belong to activity-on-arrow (AoA) networks only.** Activity-on-node (precedence) diagrams need none, which is one reason they have largely replaced AoA in practice.

questions.stem: Farm pond is used for:
questions.solution:
**Water storage.**

A farm pond is a small tank or reservoir, usually excavated or formed by a low embankment, built to **store water collected from surface run-off**. Its purpose is to hold that water until it is needed, and it serves:

- **supplementary irrigation** during dry spells within the growing season;
- **livestock watering**;
- **fish production**;
- domestic and household use in remote areas;
- **groundwater recharge** as a secondary benefit.

The distinction from the other options is one of **primary function**. A farm pond does incidentally detain run-off, so it has some effect on erosion and peak flow — but those are side-effects of a structure whose reason for existing is storage. Erosion control is the job of **contour bunds, terraces, check dams and vegetative barriers**; flood control needs **detention basins, levees and reservoirs** on a quite different scale.

**Design points:**

| Aspect | Consideration |
|---|---|
| Capacity | From the **crop water requirement** during the critical dry spell, and the catchment's yield |
| Siting | A natural depression with an impervious base; away from trees and from contamination |
| **Seepage loss** | The main problem — controlled by a **clay or membrane lining**, or by soil compaction |
| **Evaporation loss** | Significant for a shallow pond; a **deeper, smaller-surface** pond loses less |
| Inlet and spillway | Silt trap at the inlet; an emergency spillway so the embankment cannot be overtopped |

Note the design tension in the last two rows: for a given volume, a **deep pond with a small surface area** loses far less to evaporation than a shallow wide one — which is why farm ponds are made as deep as the ground and the excavation cost allow.

**Why it matters in Nepal.** Most Nepali agriculture is rain-fed, and the monsoon delivers most of the year's rainfall in a few months. A farm pond lets a smallholder capture part of that surplus and carry it into the dry spell — turning a single rain-fed crop into a supplementary-irrigated one. It is a **water harvesting** structure, and the same logic scales down to rooftop harvesting and up to a storage reservoir.

examTip.trick: A farm pond captures and holds **runoff during the wet season** for use when the rain stops — storage, not conveyance and not treatment.
examTip.mnemonic: **In Nepal the water problem is SEASONAL, not annual** — about 80% of the rain falls June to September. Annual totals look ample; the **dry-season** balance is what limits everything. That is why **storage, not yield**, is usually the binding constraint on a scheme.

questions.stem: The ductility of a material …… with the increase in percentage reduction in area of a specimen under tensile test.
questions.solution:
**Increases.**

**Ductility** is a material's capacity to undergo **plastic deformation before fracture**, and it is measured in two equivalent ways from a tensile test:

> **Percentage elongation** = (increase in gauge length / original gauge length) × 100
> **Percentage reduction in area** = (reduction in cross-section at fracture / original area) × 100

Both are direct measures of how much the specimen deformed before it broke. A larger reduction in area means the material necked down further before parting — which is more plastic deformation, hence **greater ductility**. The relationship is straightforwardly proportional, so (a) is correct and (c) overstates it.

The conventional thresholds:

| Elongation | Classification |
|---|---|
| **> 15%** | **Ductile** |
| 5 – 15% | Moderately ductile |
| **< 5%** | **Brittle** |

**Why ductility is the property structural engineering cares most about**, beyond strength:

- It gives **warning** before failure — visible yielding, cracking and deflection rather than sudden fracture.
- It permits **redistribution of moments** in an indeterminate structure, so an overloaded section sheds load to its neighbours instead of failing.
- It absorbs **energy**, which is the entire basis of ductile seismic design.

That is why structural steel and reinforcement are kept to **low carbon** content, and why IS 1786 pairs a minimum elongation with each grade — **23% for Fe 250** falling to **12% for Fe 500** and 10% for Fe 550. Strength and ductility trade against each other, and seismic codes call for **Fe 500D**, with enhanced elongation, rather than plain Fe 500.

The same logic explains why an **over-reinforced** concrete section is prohibited (the concrete crushes while the steel is still elastic, forfeiting all warning), and why **plastic analysis** of steel frames is legitimate at all — it depends on the hinges being able to rotate without fracturing.

Related fracture appearance: a **ductile** specimen fails with a **cup-and-cone** fracture along planes of maximum shear at roughly 45°, whereas a **brittle** one breaks square across the bar on the plane of maximum normal stress.

examTip.trick: Both measures of ductility move together: **percentage elongation** and **percentage reduction in area** are two ways of measuring the same capacity to deform plastically before fracture.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reduction in area is the better measure for a very ductile material**, because it is not affected by the gauge length. Elongation must always be quoted with its gauge length (usually 5.65√A₀) or the number is meaningless.

questions.stem: Brick is soaked in water before use:
options: To prevent moisture loss from mortar
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — soaking serves all three purposes at once.

- **Preventing moisture loss from the mortar** is the most important. A dry brick is porous and acts like a **sponge**, drawing water out of the fresh mortar. That starves the cement of the water it needs for **hydration**, so the joint never gains its designed strength and the bond is weak. This is the reason soaking is specified.
- **Washing off dust** matters because dust and loose particles on the brick face prevent the mortar from adhering to it at all.
- **Even spreading of mortar** follows from the first two: a wet brick lets the mortar remain workable and be spread uniformly, instead of stiffening on contact.

A fourth benefit worth adding: soaking removes **soluble salts** from the brick, which would otherwise migrate to the surface and appear as **efflorescence** — white powdery deposits on the finished wall.

**How it is done in practice.** Bricks are immersed in water for **at least 1 to 2 hours** (or until saturated, commonly overnight) and then allowed to drain so the surface is damp but not streaming. The target is essentially the **saturated surface dry** condition — pores full, surface free of running water — the same idea as for concrete aggregate.

That qualification matters: a brick laid **dripping wet** is as bad as a dry one. Free surface water dilutes the mortar at the interface, weakens it, and lets the brick float and slip out of line under the next course.

Related masonry practice examined alongside:

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| Mortar joint thickness | **10 mm** |
| Bricks laid | **Frog upward**, so the frog fills with mortar and keys the course |
| Height of brickwork in a day | **1.5 m** maximum, to avoid overloading green mortar |
| **Curing** of finished brickwork | **7 to 10 days** |
| Bond | **English bond** is strongest; raking bond the weakest |

The **frog** — the indentation on the brick face, the subject of the next question — is what the mortar keys into, and it only works if the brick is laid the right way up.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — read every option. Soaking serves several purposes at once.
examTip.trick: A dry brick **sucks water out of the mortar**, which stops the cement hydrating properly at exactly the interface where the bond is formed. Soaking also removes surface dust and dissolves soluble salts that would later cause **efflorescence**.
examTip.mnemonic: **A dry brick steals the mortar's water and kills the bond.** But an over-soaked (dripping) brick is equally bad — it floats on the mortar bed and the joint squeezes out. Soak until bubbles stop, then let the surface dry.

questions.stem: Indentation on the surface of a brick is called:
questions.solution:
**Frog.**

The frog is the shallow **recess or indentation** formed in one or both bed faces of a brick during moulding. Its purposes:

- **Keys the mortar.** Laid frog upward, the recess fills with mortar and forms a mechanical key between courses, greatly improving the **shear bond** of the joint.
- **Reduces weight** without a material loss of strength.
- Carries the **manufacturer's mark**.
- Helps identify the correct laying orientation.

Standard dimensions for a modular brick: the frog is about **100 × 40 mm in plan and 10 to 20 mm deep**.

**The rule that follows, and is examined:** bricks must be laid **frog upward**. Laid frog down, the recess forms a **void** rather than a key — it fills with air instead of mortar, weakening the joint and creating a path for moisture. Note the exception: the **top course** and bricks in a **half-brick wall or thin partition** may be laid frog down where a level bed is needed.

Bricks without a frog are also made and used:

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Frogged brick** | One or two frogs; the ordinary building brick |
| Solid / no-frog brick | Extruded wire-cut bricks often have none; used where full bearing is wanted |
| Perforated brick | Vertical holes through the brick; lighter, better insulation |
| Hollow brick | Large cavities; lightweight partition work |

The distractors are not brick terminology at all: **striking** is the operation of removing formwork (or the act of finishing a mortar joint), and a **spike** is a fastener.

Related brick facts commonly asked together: **modular size 190 × 90 × 90 mm**, 200 × 100 × 100 mm including the 10 mm mortar joint, about **500 bricks per cubic metre** of brickwork, and the traditional non-modular size of 230 × 110 × 70 mm still widely made in Nepal.

examTip.trap: "Bat" and "closer" are also brick terms, but both are **cut** bricks, not a feature moulded into a whole one.
examTip.trick: The frog does two jobs: it **keys the mortar** for a stronger bond, and it carries the maker's mark.
examTip.mnemonic: **Frog goes UP when laid**, so the mortar fills it and locks the course. Laid frog-down it becomes a void — a real site error that weakens the wall and is invisible once built.

questions.stem: What is the formula for the active earth pressure coefficient?
questions.solution:
**K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ).**

Equivalently, **K_a = tan²(45° − φ/2)**.

**The check that fixes it in memory.** Active pressure is the **minimum** lateral pressure — it develops when the wall yields away from the soil and the soil expands laterally. So K_a must be **less than 1**. With φ = 30°:

> K_a = (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.5/1.5 = **1/3** ✓ (less than 1)

Option (a) is its **reciprocal**, the **passive** coefficient:
> K_p = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = 1.5/0.5 = **3**

So the pair for φ = 30° is **1/3 and 3**, worth memorising outright, together with **K_p = 1/K_a**.

Options (c) and (d) use sin²φ and are simply not earth-pressure formulae.

The three states, and the wall movement that produces each:

| State | Wall moves | Coefficient | At φ = 30° |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Active** | **Away from** the soil | **(1−sin φ)/(1+sin φ)** | **1/3** |
| At rest | Not at all | K_o = 1 − sin φ | 0.5 |
| **Passive** | **Into** the soil | (1+sin φ)/(1−sin φ) | 3 |

Always **K_a < K_o < K_p**.

**The resulting thrust** on a wall of height H in cohesionless backfill:
> P_a = ½ K_a γ H², acting at **H/3 above the base**

**A practical point.** Full active pressure develops after only **0.1 to 0.5% of the wall height** of movement, so active conditions arise in almost any real wall. Full **passive** resistance needs **2 to 5%** — often more movement than the structure can tolerate — so passive resistance is normally reduced by a factor of safety before being relied on.

**A note on the source explanation.** The circulating answer sheet keys (b), which is correct, but its accompanying note describes the formula as the coefficient of **passive** earth pressure and writes Kp = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ). That is a mislabelling: the keyed option (b) is the **active** coefficient, which is what the question asks for. The letter is right; the explanation has been rewritten.

verification.notes: The keyed option (b) is the correct ACTIVE coefficient, but the source's explanation labels it as the passive coefficient and prints the Kp formula. The letter is correct; the explanation was mislabelled and has been rewritten.

examTip.trick: Two instant checks: **K_a < 1 < K_p**, and **K_p = 1/K_a**. Any expression giving a value above 1 is the passive coefficient, not the active one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active has (1 − sin φ) on TOP. For φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3, K₀ = 1 − sin φ = 0.5.** Also **K_a = tan²(45 − φ/2)**. Note K₀ sits between the two — which is why a **restrained** basement wall carries about 50% more than an active one.

questions.stem: The bending moment in an arch is zero when:
options: The line of thrust is parallel to the line of axis
The line of thrust coincides with the line of axis
questions.solution:
**When the line of thrust coincides with the line of the axis.**

The bending moment at any section of an arch is the thrust multiplied by its **eccentricity** from the centroidal axis:

> **M = H × e**

where e is the perpendicular distance between the **line of thrust** (the locus of the resultant thrust) and the **arch axis** (the centre line of the section). If the two coincide, **e = 0 everywhere and M = 0 everywhere** — the arch carries its load in **pure axial compression**, with no bending at all.

That is the ideal an arch aspires to, and it is why arches can span far more efficiently than beams: masonry and concrete are strong in compression and weak in bending, so eliminating the bending exploits the material fully.

**Why option (a) fails:** a line of thrust *parallel* to the axis but offset from it has a **constant non-zero eccentricity**, hence a constant bending moment — not zero. Parallel is not the same as coincident. Options (c) and (d) describe **end conditions**, which affect the magnitude and distribution of the thrust but do not by themselves make the eccentricity vanish.

**The funicular shape.** For a given loading there is one arch profile along which the thrust line runs exactly — the **funicular** or ideal shape:

| Loading | Ideal arch axis |
|---|---|
| **UDL over the horizontal span** | **Parabola** |
| Load proportional to arch length (self-weight) | **Catenary** |
| Point load at the crown | Two straight segments |

A real arch carries several load cases, so no single profile can be funicular for all of them; the designer chooses the shape for the dominant load (usually dead load) and accepts modest bending under the others. This is exactly why a **parabolic** arch is used for a bridge deck carrying a roughly uniform load, and a **catenary** where self-weight dominates.

**Where the thrust line lies** determines safety in a masonry arch: it must stay **within the middle third** of the section, so that no tension develops — the same middle-third rule that governs gravity dams. If the thrust line reaches the extrados or intrados, a hinge forms there, and enough hinges make a collapse mechanism.

Recall from the two- and three-hinged arch questions that the thrust is **inversely proportional to the rise**, H = M_c/y_c for a three-hinged arch — so a shallow arch develops enormous thrust and needs massive abutments.

examTip.trick: An arch carries load by **axial compression along its axis**. If the thrust line strays from the axis, the eccentricity produces a **bending moment M = H × e**. Zero eccentricity means zero moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ideal arch shape is the one that makes the thrust line coincide with the axis for the given loading — a PARABOLA for a UDL, a CATENARY for self-weight.** Real arches are designed for varying load, so some bending is unavoidable and the section is proportioned for it.

questions.stem: A drainage structure provided parallel to a road to intercept rain in a hilly region is called:
questions.solution:
**Catch drain** (catch-water drain).

A catch drain is cut into the hillside **above the road cutting**, running roughly parallel to the alignment. Its job is to **intercept run-off descending the hill slope before it reaches the road**, and divert it to a natural watercourse.

The distinction from a **side drain** is where each sits and what each collects:

| Drain | Position | Collects |
|---|---|---|
| **Catch drain** | **Above the cut slope**, on the hillside | **Hill-slope run-off**, before it reaches the road |
| **Side drain** | **Alongside the carriageway**, at the toe of the cut | Water from the road surface and the cut face |
| **Cross drain** | **Across** the road — culvert, causeway, scupper | Carries water from the hill side to the valley side |
| Sloping / chute drain | Down the face of an embankment | Leads water down without eroding the slope |

So the catch drain is the **first line of defence** and the side drain the second; the cross drain then takes the collected water across the road and discharges it safely down-slope.

**Why this matters so much in Nepal.** Water is the principal enemy of a hill road. Uncontrolled run-off:
- **saturates the cut slope**, and as Set 2 Q45 showed, steady seepage roughly **halves** the factor of safety of a slope;
- **erodes** the formation and the shoulders;
- **softens the subgrade**, whose strength falls sharply on wetting, leading to rutting and pavement failure;
- **scours** the embankment toe.

The great majority of monsoon damage to Nepali hill roads traces back to drainage that was inadequate, blocked or never maintained. That is why the whole drainage system — catch drain, side drain, cross drains, chute drains, and **weep holes** through retaining and breast walls — must be designed as one connected system, and why **clearing the drains before the monsoon** is the single most valuable maintenance activity.

Design notes: catch drains are set well back from the crest of the cutting (so they do not themselves saturate and destabilise it), given a **lined** invert where the gradient or soil demands it, and provided with a gradient sufficient to be self-cleansing — otherwise they silt up and overflow, which is worse than having none at all.

examTip.trick: Hill road drainage by position: a **catch water (catch) drain** runs **above** the road on the hillside to intercept water before it reaches the formation; a **side drain** runs beside the carriageway.
examTip.mnemonic: **Catch it BEFORE it reaches the road — that is the whole principle of hill road drainage.** Water on a hill road causes more damage than traffic does: it saturates the cut slope, undermines the formation, and is the direct cause of most landslides along mountain alignments.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not prevent water logging?
questions.solution:
**Frequent irrigation** — it **causes** waterlogging rather than preventing it.

Waterlogging is the condition in which the **water table rises so close to the ground surface** that the root zone becomes saturated, air is driven out of the soil pores, and the crop suffocates. Applying water more often than the soil can transmit away raises the water table further, so option (a) works in exactly the wrong direction.

Why the other three **do** prevent it:

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Lining of canal** | Cuts **seepage** from the canal — often the single largest contributor to a rising water table in a command area |
| **Subsurface drainage** | Buried perforated pipe or tile drains **lower the water table** directly, below the root zone |
| **Reducing FSL** | A lower full supply level reduces the **head driving seepage** out of the canal into the surrounding ground |

So (b) and (d) attack the **cause** (canal seepage) and (c) treats the **effect** (a high water table). In practice both are needed.

**The full list of causes**, all of which raise the water table: over-irrigation with inadequate drainage; **seepage from unlined canals** and reservoirs; **obstruction of natural drainage** by roads, railway embankments and canal banks; flat topography; impervious subsoil; and heavy rainfall.

**The effects**, which explain why it is taken seriously:
- Poor aeration, so roots cannot respire — the immediate agronomic damage.
- **Salinity and alkalinity**: a shallow water table brings salts up by **capillary rise**, and evaporation at the surface leaves them behind and concentrates them year on year. Left long enough this produces a **sodic soil** with pH above 10, structureless and practically infertile.
- Difficulty of cultivation, weed growth, and falling yields.

That salinity consequence is the reason waterlogging and salinity are always taught together, and it dictates the remedy. A **saline** soil is reclaimed by **leaching** with adequate drainage; a **sodic** soil needs **gypsum first** to replace the exchangeable sodium and restore permeability, and only then can it be leached — amend first, leach second.

**Remedies in summary:** line the canals, provide surface and sub-surface drains, lower the water table by tube wells (vertical drainage), regulate the supply rather than over-applying, and grow crops of high water requirement to draw the table down.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Frequent irrigation is a **CAUSE** of waterlogging, not a cure for it.
examTip.trick: Waterlogging means the water table has risen **into the root zone**, so its causes all involve water arriving faster than it drains: over-irrigation, canal seepage, poor drainage, impervious subsoil.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging and SALINITY travel together** — capillary rise brings salts up and evaporation concentrates them at the surface. The remedy for both is **DRAINAGE**, and for sodic soil, gypsum before leaching.

questions.stem: In the process of finding fixed inorganic solids in a sludge sample, the temperature is:
questions.solution:
**550° ± 5°C for 15 minutes**, in a muffle furnace.

The solids analysis of a sludge or wastewater sample proceeds in **two stages at two temperatures**, and the question turns on keeping them apart:

| Stage | Temperature | Time | What is measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Drying** | **103–105°C** | ~1 hour to constant weight | **Total solids** — drives off water only |
| **Ignition** | **550 ± 50°C** | **15 minutes** | Burns off organic matter; residue is the **fixed (inorganic) solids** |

So the **105°C** figures in options (c) and (d) belong to the *drying* step that determines total solids, and only **550°C** ignites the organic fraction.

**What the two weighings give you:**

> **Total solids (TS)** = residue after drying at 105°C
> **Fixed solids (FS)** = residue remaining after ignition at 550°C — the **inorganic, non-combustible** fraction
> **Volatile solids (VS)** = TS − FS = the fraction burnt off — an estimate of the **organic** content

**Why volatile solids matter more than the fixed fraction in practice.** VS is the standard proxy for the **biodegradable organic load**, so it is the parameter used to:

- size and control an **anaerobic digester** — loading is expressed as kg VS per m³ per day;
- measure **digester performance**, since digestion destroys 40 to 60% of the volatile solids;
- assess how **stabilised** a sludge is: a well-digested sludge has a low VS/TS ratio and no longer putrefies.

Raw primary sludge typically runs about **60 to 80% volatile**, falling to roughly 50% after digestion.

The wider solids classification, examined alongside:

| Solids | Determination |
|---|---|
| **Total solids** | Evaporate at 105°C |
| **Suspended solids** | Retained on a filter (0.45 μm) |
| **Dissolved solids** | TS − SS, i.e. passing the filter |
| **Settleable solids** | Imhoff cone, 1 hour, mL/L |
| Volatile / fixed | Ignition at 550°C, as above |

Each of those can be split into volatile and fixed by the same 550°C ignition — hence **VSS** and **FSS** for the suspended fraction, and **MLVSS** in an activated sludge plant, which is the measure of the *living* biomass rather than total MLSS.

examTip.trick: The solids analysis is a sequence of **temperatures**: dry at **103–105 °C** to get total solids, then ignite at **550 °C** to burn off the **volatile (organic)** fraction, leaving the **fixed (inorganic)** residue.
examTip.mnemonic: **105 °C removes WATER; 550 °C removes ORGANICS.** Volatile solids are the biodegradable part, so **VSS is the measure of the active biomass** in an activated sludge plant — which is why MLVSS rather than MLSS is the parameter that matters operationally.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not have the same unit as the modulus of elasticity?
questions.solution:
**Section modulus** — its unit is **m³**, not N/m².

The modulus of elasticity is a **stress** divided by a dimensionless strain, so it carries the units of stress: **N/m² (Pa)**. Checking each option:

| Quantity | Definition | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **Modulus of elasticity, E** | σ/ε (strain is dimensionless) | **N/m²** |
| **Modulus of rigidity, G** | τ/γ (shear strain dimensionless) | **N/m²** ✓ same |
| **Shear stress, τ** | Force / area | **N/m²** ✓ same |
| **Pressure, p** | Force / area | **N/m²** ✓ same |
| **Section modulus, Z** | **I / y** = m⁴ / m | **m³** ✗ different |

So three of the four are stresses or moduli of stress type, and only the section modulus is a **purely geometric** property of the cross-section — it contains no material information at all.

**That distinction is the real content of the question.** The section properties and the material properties are different families:

| Geometric (section) properties | Material properties |
|---|---|
| Area A (m²) | E, G, K (N/m²) |
| Moment of inertia I (m⁴) | Poisson's ratio μ (dimensionless) |
| **Section modulus Z (m³)** | Yield and ultimate stress (N/m²) |
| Radius of gyration k (m) | Density (kg/m³) |

**Where Z is used.** It converts a bending moment directly into the extreme-fibre stress:

> σ = M·y/I = **M/Z**

so the moment capacity of a section is simply **M = σ_permissible × Z**. For a rectangle, Z = bd²/6; for a solid circle, Z = πd³/32.

Note the useful contrast with **plastic** section modulus Z_p, which uses the fully plastic stress distribution. Their ratio is the **shape factor**: 1.5 for a rectangle, 1.7 for a circle, and only 1.10 to 1.20 for a rolled I-beam.

**A dimensional habit worth carrying into the exam.** Checking units eliminates wrong options faster than recalling formulae — the same test that disposes of WL⁴/EI as a deflection when W is a total load, or of T/d⁴ as a torsional shear stress.

The other elastic constants for completeness, all in N/m²: **E = 2G(1 + μ) = 3K(1 − 2μ)**.

examTip.trick: Check the units. **E, G and K are all stresses (N/mm²)**; the **section modulus Z = I/y is a volume (mm³)**. Odd one out on dimensions alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dimensional analysis settles more multiple-choice questions than any formula.** Here: I is mm⁴, y is mm, so Z is mm³ — nothing like a stress. Z governs **strength** (σ = M/Z) while I governs **stiffness** (δ ∝ 1/I).

questions.stem: DO value of fresh pond water at 20°C temperature, 760 mm of Hg pressure and zero salinity is:
questions.solution:
**About 9.08 mg/L** (commonly tabulated as 9.1 mg/L).

This is the **saturation** concentration of dissolved oxygen — the most water can hold at that temperature, pressure and salinity.

The saturation values at 760 mm Hg and zero salinity, worth knowing as a shape rather than a list:

| Temperature (°C) | DO saturation (mg/L) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 14.6 |
| 5 | 12.8 |
| 10 | 11.3 |
| 15 | 10.1 |
| **20** | **9.1** |
| 25 | 8.3 |
| 30 | 7.6 |

**The three factors that reduce DO**, all examined:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Temperature ↑** | DO **falls** — gas solubility decreases as water warms |
| **Salinity ↑** | DO **falls** — dissolved salts displace dissolved gas |
| **Altitude ↑** (pressure ↓) | DO **falls** — less partial pressure of oxygen above the water |

That last one matters in Nepal: at Kathmandu's altitude the atmospheric pressure is roughly 85% of sea level, so saturation DO is correspondingly lower than the table value, and lower still at hill stations.

**Why DO is the central parameter in stream pollution.** Aquatic life needs a minimum of about **4 to 5 mg/L**; below that fish die. When organic waste enters a river, bacteria consume oxygen to oxidise it, and the DO falls. The competition between that **deoxygenation** and **reaeration** from the atmosphere produces the classic **oxygen sag curve**, described by the **Streeter–Phelps** equation:

> D_t = [k_d L_0/(k_r − k_d)](10^{−k_d t} − 10^{−k_r t}) + D_0 10^{−k_r t}

where D is the oxygen deficit, L_0 the initial BOD, k_d the deoxygenation constant and k_r the reaeration constant. The **critical point** of the curve — the lowest DO, furthest downstream — is what determines whether the river can assimilate the discharge.

This is why **temperature makes thermal pollution doubly damaging**: warm water holds less oxygen *and* speeds up the bacterial oxidation that consumes it.

Measurement is by the **Winkler (azide modification) titration** or by a DO probe, and the same Winkler method underlies the **BOD** test, which measures DO depletion over 5 days at 20°C.

examTip.trick: **DO saturation falls as temperature rises** and as altitude rises (lower partial pressure). At **20 °C and sea level, saturation is about 9.1 mg/l**.
examTip.mnemonic: **DO saturation: ~14.6 at 0 °C, ~9.1 at 20 °C, ~7.5 at 30 °C.** That temperature dependence is why **thermal pollution** matters — warm discharge water holds less oxygen exactly when the increased biological activity demands more. A DO below about 4 mg/l is stressful to fish.

questions.stem: Which premix is used in base course?
questions.solution:
**Bituminous bound macadam** (bituminous penetration macadam).

It consists of **coarse aggregate, a bitumen spray and key aggregate**, and it is used as a **base course** — either over a stretch of a larger project or in small works where a hot-mix plant is not available. That last point is its practical advantage: it can be laid without the plant that a properly graded premix requires.

Why the others belong elsewhere in the pavement:

| Material | Layer | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Bituminous bound / penetration macadam** | **Base course** | Coarse aggregate + bitumen spray + key aggregate; no hot-mix plant needed |
| **Bituminous concrete (BC)** | **Wearing course** | Dense, well-graded **premix**; the highest-quality bituminous layer |
| **Otta seal** | Surface treatment | Graded gravel + soft bitumen; a **low-cost** surfacing for low-volume roads |
| **Surface dressing** | Surface treatment | Bitumen spray + single stone chip layer; **seals and waterproofs**, adds no strength |

The key distinction the question is testing: **bituminous concrete is a wearing course**, not a base course. It is the top layer, laid 25 to 50 mm thick, designed for riding quality, skid resistance and waterproofing — the most expensive bituminous material and never used where a cheaper base-course material would do.

**The layers of a flexible pavement**, so the roles are clear:

| Layer | Thickness | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wearing (surface) course | 25 – 50 mm | Wear, weather, riding quality |
| Binder course | 50 – 100 mm | Transfers load to the base |
| **Base course** | **100 – 300 mm** | **Main load-spreading layer** |
| Sub-base | 100 – 300 mm | Further spreading; drainage |
| Subgrade | 150 – 300 mm compacted | Prepared natural ground |

The bituminous coats between them: a **prime coat** on a granular base to seal and bond it, a **tack coat** between successive bituminous layers, and a **seal coat** on top.

**The aggregate quality required falls with depth**, which is the underlying economy: the **Los Angeles abrasion** limit is 30% for a bituminous concrete surface course but 50% for bituminous bound macadam, because wear and polishing only matter at the surface. That is the same table used in Q70 of this paper to decide which layer a 37.6% aggregate is fit for.

examTip.trick: Bituminous layers by position and grading: **BM/BUSG** for the base, **DBM** for the binder, and **BC or SDBC** for the wearing course. The base course uses a coarser, more open mix.
examTip.mnemonic: **Coarser and more open at the bottom, finer and denser at the top.** The wearing course must be dense and impermeable to shed water; the base course only has to carry load and drain.

questions.stem: The assessment done by the implementing agency to check the eligibility of a firm to carry out a contract is:
questions.solution:
**Pre-qualification.**

Pre-qualification assesses potential contractors **before** they submit tenders, to establish that they are capable of doing the work at all. Only firms that pass are invited to bid.

The stages of procurement, in order — which is what the question is really testing:

| Stage | When | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-qualification** | **Before** tenders | Screen firms for **capability**: experience, technical staff, plant, financial standing, past performance |
| **Tender assessment** | After tenders are opened | Evaluate the **bids** on price and compliance with the specified criteria |
| **Post-qualification** | After selecting the lowest evaluated bid | **Verify** the selected bidder's claimed qualifications before award |
| **Contract assessment** | During execution | Monitor **compliance** with the contract terms and performance standards |

So the distinction between pre- and post-qualification is one of **timing and population**: pre-qualification screens **all interested firms in advance**, whereas post-qualification checks **only the successful bidder afterwards**.

**Why pre-qualification is used at all.** For large, complex or high-risk works it saves everyone effort: the employer does not have to evaluate bids from firms that could never deliver, and unqualified firms do not spend money preparing tenders they cannot win. It also protects the employer from being contractually bound to accept a low bid from an incapable contractor.

Its cost is that it **reduces competition** and takes time, so for straightforward works the modern preference — and the default under Nepal's **Public Procurement Act 2063** — is **open bidding with post-qualification**, which keeps the field wide and checks only the winner.

**Typical pre-qualification criteria:**
- **Experience**: similar works completed, of comparable value and nature.
- **Financial capacity**: annual turnover, liquid assets or credit line; the **acid test ratio** and current ratio are examined here.
- **Personnel**: qualified engineers, with the required registration.
- **Plant and equipment** available or committed.
- **Litigation history** and record of terminated contracts.

The financial instruments that accompany the process, and are routinely confused: **bid security** (2–3%, guarantees the bid), **performance security** (5–10%, guarantees performance of the contract), **retention money** (withheld from each bill against defects), and the **mobilisation advance** (paid to start work, against a bank guarantee).

examTip.trick: **Pre-qualification** screens bidders **before** they tender, so that only capable firms are invited. **Post-qualification** checks the same things **after** bids are opened, on the lowest bidder only.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pre-qualification saves everyone's time on large complex works; post-qualification suits smaller straightforward ones.** Both assess the same criteria: financial capacity, similar past experience, plant and key personnel.

questions.stem: Moment of inertia of a semicircle about its base is:
questions.solution:
**πD⁴/128.**

The derivation is one line if you see it as half a circle. A **full circle** has, about a diameter,

> I = **πD⁴/64**

A semicircle is exactly half that area, symmetric about the same axis, and its **base is that diameter** — so its moment of inertia about the base is simply half:

> I_base = ½ × πD⁴/64 = **πD⁴/128** ✓

Note that option (c), πD⁴/64, is the **full circle** value — the intended trap.

The moments of inertia worth carrying as a set:

| Section | About | I |
|---|---|---|
| Circle | Centroidal diameter | **πD⁴/64** |
| **Semicircle** | **Base (diameter)** | **πD⁴/128** |
| Semicircle | Own centroidal axis | ≈ 0.11 r⁴ |
| Hollow circle | Centroidal | π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 |
| Rectangle | Centroidal, parallel to b | bd³/12 |
| Rectangle | Base | bd³/3 |
| Triangle | Centroidal | bh³/36 |
| Triangle | Base | bh³/12 |

**Why the semicircle's two values differ so much**, and why the question specifies the axis. The centroid of a semicircular area lies at **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r** from the base, not at the base. So the base value and the centroidal value are related by the **parallel axis theorem**:

> I_base = I_G + A·ȳ²
> πr⁴/8 = I_G + (πr²/2)(4r/3π)²

which gives I_G ≈ 0.11 r⁴ — appreciably less than the base value, because material concentrated near the base contributes heavily to I about the base.

That is the general lesson: **a moment of inertia is meaningless without naming the axis**, and the parallel axis theorem is what moves between them. It is the same relation that turns the rectangle's centroidal bd³/12 into bd³/3 about its base.

**Where semicircular sections arise** in practice: half-round channels and drains, the plan of a semicircular arch or apse, and — most often in the examination — as a component when finding the centroid and I of a **composite section** built from rectangles, triangles and part-circles.

examTip.trick: A semicircle is **half** a full circle, and the base is a diameter — so take the circle's diametral value and halve it: **(πD⁴/64)/2 = πD⁴/128** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Semicircle about its base = πD⁴/128 = πR⁴/8.** But be careful: about its **CENTROIDAL** axis it is NOT simply half, because the centroid is at **4r/3π**, not on the base — the parallel axis theorem must be applied.

questions.stem: Pressure at inlet and outlet of a draft tube shouldn't be:
options: Greater than one third of atmospheric pressure
Less than one third of atmospheric pressure
questions.solution:
**Less than one third of atmospheric pressure.**

If the pressure anywhere in the turbine falls below about **one third of atmospheric**, the water approaches its **vapour pressure** and **cavitation** begins: vapour bubbles form, are carried into a higher-pressure region, and **collapse violently**. The implosions pit and erode the runner blades and the draft tube liner, cause noise and vibration, and cut efficiency and output.

The draft tube outlet region is where the danger is greatest, because it is the **lowest-pressure point** in a reaction turbine — pressure has fallen continuously through the guide vanes and the runner, converting into work.

**The governing parameter** is **Thoma's cavitation factor**:

> **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s)/H**

where H_a is atmospheric head, H_v the vapour pressure head, **H_s the suction head** (height of the runner above tailwater) and H the net head. Cavitation is avoided by keeping σ above the critical value σ_c for that turbine's specific speed — and σ_c **rises with specific speed**, so Kaplan turbines are more cavitation-prone than Francis.

**The remedies follow directly from the formula:**
- **Lower the runner setting** — reduce H_s, even setting the runner *below* tailwater so H_s is negative. This is the principal control.
- Note that **H_a falls with altitude**, so a turbine high in the Nepali hills has less margin and must be set lower than the same machine in the Terai.
- Use **cavitation-resistant materials** — stainless steel runners or overlays.
- Proportion the **draft tube** to recover pressure gradually rather than abruptly.
- Avoid prolonged operation far from the design point, where flow separation lowers local pressures.

**What the draft tube is for**, since the question presupposes it. It is a gradually expanding conduit from runner exit to tailrace which:
1. lets the runner be set **above** tailwater while still recovering the head down to it, and
2. converts the **residual kinetic energy** at runner exit into pressure by gradual expansion, recovering much of what would otherwise be wasted.

Hence it is required for **reaction** turbines (Francis, Kaplan) and **not** for an impulse **Pelton**, which discharges freely to atmosphere and is essentially free of cavitation — one of the practical advantages of impulse machines at very high heads.

examTip.trick: A draft tube's purpose is to **recover the exit kinetic energy** of a reaction turbine by creating **sub-atmospheric pressure** at the runner outlet — which is what lets the runner sit above tailwater without losing that head.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit is CAVITATION** — the pressure must never reach vapour pressure. That is what **Thoma's parameter σ** checks, and it is why the **setting level** (runner height above tailwater) is limited. **At altitude the atmospheric pressure is lower, so the permitted setting is lower** — a genuine constraint in Nepal.

questions.stem: Binding wire quantity in 1 quintal of reinforcement is:
questions.solution:
**About 1 kg** per quintal (100 kg) of reinforcement — the usual allowance is **0.9 to 1.3 kg**.

Binding wire is the soft annealed mild steel wire, typically **18 gauge (about 1.2 mm)**, used to tie reinforcing bars together at their intersections so the cage holds its shape and position during concreting.

Expressed the other way round, that is roughly **1% of the weight of steel** — a convenient figure to carry, and it is why estimates commonly add 1% of the reinforcement weight for binding wire.

**Why it matters in an estimate.** Binding wire is a small item, but it is a **separate material** that must be quantified and priced, and omitting it is a common gap in a bill of quantities. It sits alongside the other allowances that are easy to forget:

| Item | Allowance |
|---|---|
| **Binding wire** | **1 kg per quintal (≈ 1%) of reinforcement** |
| Wastage of reinforcement | 3 – 5% |
| Wastage of bricks | 5% |
| Wastage of cement | 2 – 3% |
| Water charges | 1.5% of the cost of work |
| Tools and plant | 1 – 2% of labour cost |
| **Contractor's profit** | **10%** |

**How reinforcement itself is measured**, since the two go together. IS 1200 requires steel to be measured by **weight**, computed from the standard unit weight:

> **w = d²/162 kg/m**, with d in mm

so a 12 mm bar weighs 0.89 kg/m and a 16 mm bar 1.58 kg/m. **Laps, hooks and bends are included** in the measured length, and — importantly — **no deduction is made from the concrete volume** for the space the reinforcement occupies.

The binding wire's structural job is worth a word: it holds the cage together but carries **no design load**. It must not be confused with reinforcement, and it must not be left projecting into the **cover** zone, where it would rust and stain or spall the surface. That is also why **cover blocks** — not binding wire — are what maintain the cover to the steel.

examTip.trick: A practical site-quantity figure: binding wire is taken as about **1% of the reinforcement weight** — so 1 kg per quintal (100 kg).
examTip.mnemonic: **Binding wire ≈ 1% of steel weight; steel weight = d²/162 kg per metre.** Both are estimator's numbers that never appear in a textbook derivation but are needed for every bar bending schedule and every rate analysis.

questions.stem: How many satellites are used for GPS by the US Department of Defense?
questions.solution:
**24.**

The United States commits to maintaining at least **24 operational GPS satellites, available 95% of the time**. In practice more are flown — 31 or so — to provide redundancy and improve coverage, but **24 is the design constellation** and the figure quoted in surveying texts.

The constellation is arranged in **6 orbital planes** of 4 satellites each, inclined at 55° to the equator, at an altitude of about **20,200 km** with a 12-hour period. That geometry guarantees that at least **four satellites** are visible from anywhere on Earth at any time.

**Why four is the magic number**, which is the part worth understanding rather than memorising. A GPS receiver measures the travel time of a signal to compute its distance from each satellite. There are **four unknowns**:

> **x, y, z** (position) **and Δt** (the receiver's clock error)

The receiver's cheap quartz clock cannot be trusted against the satellites' atomic clocks, so the clock error must be solved for as a fourth unknown. Four unknowns need **four equations, hence four satellites**. Three would fix position only if the receiver's clock were perfect.

The distances are called **pseudo-ranges** precisely because they contain that clock error before it is solved out.

**The error sources**, examined alongside:

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ionospheric and tropospheric delay** | The largest; reduced by dual-frequency receivers and models |
| Satellite clock and ephemeris error | Corrected by broadcast data |
| **Multipath** | Signal reflected off buildings or ground |
| Receiver noise | — |
| **Satellite geometry (GDOP)** | Well-spread satellites give a better fix than clustered ones |

**Accuracy and how it is improved.** A standalone receiver gives metre-level accuracy — adequate for reconnaissance but not for control survey. Survey work therefore uses:
- **DGPS**, with a base station at a known point broadcasting corrections;
- **RTK** (real-time kinematic), giving **centimetre** accuracy;
- **static post-processing**, for millimetre-level geodetic control.

GPS is one of several GNSS constellations — **GLONASS** (Russia), **Galileo** (EU), **BeiDou** (China) — and modern receivers use several together, which improves both accuracy and availability in the deep valleys and steep terrain where Nepali surveying so often has to work.

examTip.trick: The GPS constellation is designed so that **at least four satellites** are visible from anywhere on earth at any time — which needs about **24 operational satellites** in six orbital planes.
examTip.mnemonic: **24 in the constellation, but only FOUR needed for a fix — three for position and a fourth for the receiver's CLOCK error.** The clock is the fourth unknown, and it is why a cheap quartz receiver can still achieve metre accuracy.

questions.stem: What is EIA?
options: A method for promoting rapid project development without considering its potential impact on the environment
Economic Investment Appraisal, focusing on financial considerations rather than environmental effects
A process that intentionally overlooks potential negative effects of a project on the surrounding ecosystem
A systematic process used to evaluate the environmental consequences of a proposed project or development, aiming to identify and mitigate potential adverse effects on the environment
questions.solution:
**A systematic process to evaluate the environmental consequences of a proposed project, so that adverse effects can be identified and mitigated.**

Options (a) and (c) describe the **opposite** of an EIA — promoting development *without* regard to impact, and *overlooking* negative effects. Option (b) misreads the acronym as an economic appraisal. Only (d) states what an **Environmental Impact Assessment** actually is.

Two features of the definition are worth emphasising because they are the whole point of the instrument:

1. It happens **before** the decision, so it can still change it. An assessment produced after commitment is worthless.
2. It aims not merely to *predict* impacts but to **mitigate** them — the mitigation plan and the environmental management plan are outputs, not afterthoughts.

**The standard EIA sequence:**

> **Screening** (is an EIA needed?) → **Scoping** and Terms of Reference → **baseline** data collection → **impact prediction and evaluation** → **mitigation measures** → **Environmental Management Plan** → **monitoring and auditing**

with **public consultation** running throughout, including a public hearing.

**The tiers under Nepal's Environment Protection Act 2076 and Rules 2077**, which decide which study a project needs:

| Level | Projects | Scoping? | ToR? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BES** — Brief Environmental Study | Small, minor impacts | No | No |
| **IEE** — Initial Environmental Examination | Moderate impacts | **No** | **Yes** |
| **EIA** | Major, significant impacts | **Yes** | **Yes** |

Note that **scoping is a defining requirement of EIA** and is not required for IEE or BES — a distinction the circulating key for Set 3 Q58 gets wrong.

**What an EIA covers**, beyond the purely physical: air, water, soil, noise, flora and fauna and biodiversity; plus the **social** dimensions — resettlement and compensation, cultural and religious sites, occupational health and safety, and effects on livelihoods.

**Why it matters for Nepali infrastructure.** Hydropower, roads and transmission lines all cross steep, seismically active, biodiverse and often culturally significant terrain, and land acquisition and resettlement are frequently the critical path of a project. An EIA that is treated as a formality to be completed rather than a study to be acted on is a recurrent source of delay, cost and litigation — which is why the mitigation and monitoring commitments it contains are legally binding conditions of approval.

examTip.trick: The key words are **systematic**, **evaluate consequences**, and **proposed** — an EIA is done **before** a decision, so that the decision can be informed by it.
examTip.mnemonic: **EIA sequence: screening → SCOPING → terms of reference → study → report → review → approval → MONITORING.** The last step is the one most often neglected: an EIA that is not followed by monitoring and enforcement is a document, not a safeguard.

questions.stem: Bearing capacity formula for cohesionless soil from a plate load test is:
questions.solution:
**q_f = q_p (B_f/B_p)** — the bearing capacity scales in direct proportion to the width.

A plate load test loads a small plate of width B_p and measures its behaviour; the result must then be extrapolated to a foundation of width B_f. **How it extrapolates depends entirely on the soil type**, and keeping the four relations apart is the whole content of this question:

| Soil | **Bearing capacity** | **Settlement** |
|---|---|---|
| **Sand (cohesionless)** | **q_f = q_p (B_f/B_p)** | S_f = S_p [B_f(B_p+0.3)/B_p(B_f+0.3)]² |
| **Clay (cohesive)** | **q_f = q_p** — independent of width | S_f = S_p (B_f/B_p) |

So the two answers swap between the columns, and options (a) and (c) are the *settlement* relations — (a) being the sand case, which is asked separately as Q64 of this same paper.

**Why sand and clay behave oppositely**, which makes the table memorable rather than arbitrary:

- In **sand**, strength comes from **friction**, which grows with confining stress. A wider footing mobilises friction over a deeper zone, so its bearing capacity **rises with width** — the 0.5γBN_γ term in Terzaghi's equation dominates.
- In **clay** loaded undrained, φ = 0 and the capacity is q_u = **5.7 c_u**, which contains no B at all. The strength is cohesion, and cohesion does not care how wide the footing is.

The settlement behaviour then follows in reverse: a wider footing on **clay** stresses a deeper layer of compressible soil and settles **more** in proportion to width, whereas on **sand** the settlement grows far more slowly than the width — hence the awkward-looking squared bracket, which tends to a limit rather than growing linearly.

**The test itself** (IS 1888): a square or circular plate of **300 to 750 mm**, loaded in increments to about 1.5 times the expected working pressure, with settlement read until it stabilises at each stage.

**Its limitations**, which matter more than the formulae:
- The plate influences only a shallow zone — roughly **twice its width** — so a weak stratum below that depth is **completely missed**. This is the test's fundamental weakness.
- It gives **immediate** settlement only, so for clay it says nothing about the long-term **consolidation** settlement that usually governs.
- It is unsuitable for layered or non-uniform ground.

For those reasons a plate load test is used alongside borehole data and SPT results, never on its own — a point Q25 of this paper makes from the other direction.

examTip.trick: For **cohesionless** soil the bearing capacity scales with **width**, because the N_γ term contains B. So the plate result must be **scaled up by the width ratio**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cohesionless: q scales with B (linear). CLAY: q is INDEPENDENT of B** (N_γ = 0), so no scaling at all. Settlement scales differently again: **S_f/S_p = [2B_f/(B_f + B_p)]².** Three different scaling rules — check which quantity and which soil.

questions.stem: What is the function of a surge tank?
options: To reduce the effects of pressure
questions.solution:
**To reduce the effects of pressure** — specifically, the **water-hammer** pressure surge.

When the turbine gates close suddenly the momentum of the water column in a long conduit cannot vanish instantly, and a pressure wave races back up the pipe. Unrelieved it can burst the penstock or wreck the runner and spiral casing. A surge tank is an open-topped shaft at the junction of the low-pressure headrace tunnel and the high-pressure penstock, and it works in **both** directions:

- **On sudden closure** it accepts the rejected water; the level rises and the pressure surge becomes a harmless change of water level. Crucially, this **confines the water-hammer pressure to the short penstock below the tank** instead of the whole tunnel.
- **On sudden opening** it supplies water immediately from its own storage while the flow in the long tunnel accelerates, preventing negative pressure and cavitation.

Option (a) is the near miss and worth addressing: a surge tank **does** hold water, and the source's own note lists "storing water when the load is decreased" among its functions. But storage is the *mechanism*, not the purpose — the tank exists to **control pressure**, and its volume is sized from the surge calculation rather than from any demand for storage. Storage for its own sake is the job of a **forebay** or **pondage**.

**The quantitative reason it works.** The pressure rise depends on the conduit length:

> Closure time **< 2L/c** → sudden; Δh = **cV/g** — very large
> Closure time **> 2L/c** → gradual; Δh = **VL/(gt)** — much smaller

The surge tank effectively **shortens the L that matters**, which is precisely how it reduces the surge. With c ≈ 1449 m/s in a rigid pipe (or ~1025 m/s in an elastic steel penstock), 2L/c is a second or two for a kilometre of conduit — so any realistic valve movement is "gradual" only if the tank has cut the effective length.

**Types**, in order of damping effectiveness: simple, **restricted orifice**, **differential (Johnson)**, and inclined. The restricted-orifice and differential types throttle flow into the shaft and damp the oscillation faster.

Where a surge tank is impractical — a very long conduit, or difficult topography — a **pressure relief valve** serves instead. And the surge tank is one of a family of protections: it is why penstock velocities are optimised at 5 to 8 m/s rather than pushed higher, since the water-hammer rise is proportional to V.

examTip.trick: The surge tank gives the decelerating water column a **free surface** to rise into, turning a destructive pressure wave into a slow rise and fall of level.
examTip.mnemonic: **It protects only what is UPSTREAM of it** — the long low-pressure tunnel. The short penstock below still takes the full water hammer and is designed for it. It also **supplies water instantly on load acceptance**, before the tunnel column can accelerate.

questions.stem: Turbidity of water is expressed:
options: In numbers in an arbitrary scale
questions.solution:
**In ppm** (equivalently mg/L), on the **silica scale**.

Turbidity is the loss of transparency caused by **suspended matter** — clay, silt, finely divided organic and inorganic material, and micro-organisms such as bacteria, algae and protozoa. Two conventions for reporting it exist, and the question is testing the older one:

| Convention | Unit | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Silica scale** (older) | **ppm or mg/L** | Turbidity equivalent to that produced by 1 mg of **finely divided silica** in 1 litre of distilled water |
| **Nephelometric** (modern) | **NTU** | Intensity of light **scattered at 90°** by the sample, against a formazin standard |

So turbidity expressed "in ppm" means *silica-equivalent* ppm — it is not a direct measure of the mass of suspended solids, but a comparison against a reference suspension. Numerically 1 ppm on the silica scale is roughly 1 NTU, which is why the two are often used interchangeably in older texts.

Modern practice and the Nepali standard use **NTU**, measured with a **nephelometer**:

| Standard | Limit |
|---|---|
| Nepal drinking water — desirable | **5 NTU** |
| WHO, for effective disinfection | **< 1 NTU** |
| Rapid sand filter influent | up to 100 NTU |
| Slow sand filter influent | < 30 NTU |

The historical instruments are worth knowing since they explain the units: the **Jackson candle turbidimeter** (JTU) measured the depth of water that just extinguished a candle flame, and **Baylis** and **Hellige** turbidimeters compared scattered light visually.

**Why turbidity matters beyond appearance** — this is the engineering point:
- Suspended particles **shield pathogens** from disinfectant, so chlorination is unreliable in turbid water. That is why water is filtered to below 1 NTU **before** disinfection, and why turbidity is treated as a health parameter and not merely an aesthetic one.
- It indicates the **suspended solids load** the treatment plant must remove, and hence the coagulant dose.
- Consumers reject visibly turbid water and return to unsafe sources.

Distinguish it carefully from **colour**, which is caused by **dissolved** substances (humic acids, iron, manganese), measured in **TCU** on the platinum–cobalt scale by a tintometer, and determined *after* filtering out the suspended matter. Turbidity is suspended; colour is dissolved.

examTip.trick: Turbidity is measured by **light scattering** and expressed in **NTU** (nephelometric turbidity units), historically calibrated in **ppm of silica** — which is why the ppm form persists in older references and codes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Turbidity ≤ 5 NTU (ideally 1) for drinking water; colour ≤ 5 TCU.** They measure different things: **turbidity is SUSPENDED matter, colour is DISSOLVED matter** — which is why a sample is filtered before a true colour reading.

questions.stem: The direction of seepage water is:
questions.solution:
**Perpendicular to the equipotential line.**

An **equipotential line** joins points of equal total head. Water flows down the **steepest hydraulic gradient**, and the steepest gradient from any point on a line of constant head is **normal to that line** — exactly as heat flows perpendicular to an isotherm, or a ball rolls perpendicular to a contour.

So seepage travels along **flow lines (streamlines)**, which are everywhere **perpendicular to the equipotentials**. That orthogonality is the defining geometric property of a **flow net**, and it follows from the fact that both families are solutions of Laplace's equation:

> ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂z² = 0

Why the others fail:
- **(b)** Water flows **along** streamlines, not across them — perpendicular to a streamline is precisely the direction in which no flow occurs.
- **(a)** Parallel to an equipotential means along a line of constant head, i.e. **zero gradient**, so no flow at all.
- **(d)** Gravity alone does not decide it. Seepage follows the **total head** gradient, which combines elevation and pressure. That is why water can and does seep **upward** — the very condition that causes **quick sand** and **piping** at the downstream toe of a dam.

That last point is worth dwelling on, because it is the practical heart of the topic. Upward seepage reduces effective stress, and when the gradient reaches the **critical** value

> i_cr = (G_s − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ **1.0**

the effective stress falls to zero, the soil loses all shear strength, and it boils.

**Properties of a correctly drawn flow net:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| Flow lines ⟂ equipotentials | **90°** everywhere |
| Figures formed | **Curvilinear squares** |
| Between adjacent flow lines | **Equal discharge** Δq |
| Between adjacent equipotentials | **Equal head drop** H/N_d |
| Impervious boundary | Is itself a **flow line** |
| Permeable surface | Is an **equipotential** |

And the three quantities it yields, which are why it is drawn:

> **Seepage** q = k·H·(N_f/N_d)
> **Pore pressure** at any point, from the drops passed
> **Exit gradient** i_E — compared against i_cr with a factor of safety of 4 to 5

In **anisotropic** soil the section is first transformed by scaling one coordinate by √(k_z/k_x), the net drawn orthogonal in that transformed section, and the equivalent permeability taken as √(k_x k_z).

examTip.trick: Water flows down the **steepest hydraulic gradient**, and the steepest direction from any equipotential line is **perpendicular** to it. That is why flow lines and equipotentials cross at right angles.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flow net: streamlines and equipotentials ORTHOGONAL, forming curvilinear SQUARES. q = kH(N_f/N_d), and COUNT THE SPACES, NOT THE LINES.** The net's safety-critical output is the **exit gradient**, checked against i_c ≈ 1 with a factor of 4 to 7.

questions.stem: Bearing capacity is calculated from:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — each is a legitimate route to bearing capacity, and good practice uses more than one.

| Method | How it gives bearing capacity | Best suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **SPT N-value** | Empirical correlations to φ and to allowable pressure; also to relative density | **Sands** — where undisturbed sampling is impractical |
| **Pile / plate load test** | Loads the ground directly and measures its response | **In-situ** verification; the most direct evidence |
| **Shear strength parameters** (c, φ) | Theoretically, via **Terzaghi, Meyerhof, Hansen or Vesic**: q_u = cN_c + γD_f N_q + 0.5γBN_γ | **Clays** and any case needing analysis rather than correlation |

Because they have complementary weaknesses, they are used together:

- **SPT** is quick and cheap but crude — the blow count is sensitive to hammer energy, borehole condition and operator, and needs corrections for overburden, dilatancy and rod length before use.
- **Plate load tests** are direct but influence only a shallow zone, roughly **twice the plate width**, so a weak stratum below that depth is missed entirely. They also give immediate settlement only.
- **Theoretical formulae** are only as good as the c and φ fed into them, which depend on sampling quality and on choosing the right drainage condition (undrained for end-of-construction, drained for long-term).

So the correct answer is not merely a formality of "all of the above" — it reflects genuine engineering practice, in which a bearing capacity is **cross-checked** rather than taken from a single source.

**The two criteria that must both be satisfied**, which is the point candidates most often miss:

> **Safe bearing capacity** — from strength: q_safe = q_nu/FoS + γD_f, with FoS of 2.5 to 3
> **Allowable bearing pressure** — the **lesser** of q_safe and the pressure that keeps settlement within permissible limits

In **clay**, settlement almost always governs, because consolidation is large and slow; in **dense sand**, strength usually governs. IS 1904 permissible settlements are typically 50 mm for isolated footings on sand and 75 mm on clay, with tighter limits on **differential** settlement.

Other methods in the same family: the **static cone penetration test (CPT)**, which gives a continuous profile rather than point values; the **pressuremeter**; and **presumptive values** from IS 1904 — 50 kPa for soft clay up to 3000–4000 kPa for hard rock — useful only for preliminary sizing.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — read every option. Bearing capacity can be obtained by analysis, by field testing and from codes.
examTip.trick: The methods rank by reliability: **analytical (Terzaghi/IS 6403) from measured c and φ**, **plate load test**, **SPT and CPT correlations**, and **presumptive values** last.
examTip.mnemonic: **Presumptive values are for PRELIMINARY sizing and sanity checks only.** And the **plate load test** has its own blind spot — its small pressure bulb cannot see a soft layer that a full-size footing would stress.

questions.stem: In defining the Froude number, which depth parameter is used?
questions.solution:
**Hydraulic mean depth**, D = A/T.

> **Fr = V / √(g·D)**,  where **D = A/T** (area ÷ **top width**)

The distinction from the hydraulic radius is the whole point of the question, and the two are easily confused because both are area divided by a length:

| Quantity | Formula | Divided by | Used in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hydraulic mean depth, D** | **A / T** | **Top width** (free surface) | **Froude number** |
| **Hydraulic radius, R** | **A / P** | **Wetted perimeter** | **Manning's / Chezy's equation** |

So D concerns the **free surface** — appropriate for the Froude number, which measures the ratio of inertia to **gravity** and therefore governs surface-wave behaviour. R concerns the **wetted boundary** — appropriate for friction, which acts at the boundary.

**Values for the common sections:**

| Section | Hydraulic mean depth D = A/T |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular** (width b) | A = by, T = b → **D = y** |
| **Triangular** | A = zy², T = 2zy → **D = y/2** (whatever the side slope) |
| Trapezoidal | D = (by + zy²)/(b + 2zy) |
| Wide shallow channel | D → y |

Note the neat result for the triangle: **D = y/2 regardless of side slope**, since the slope cancels between area and top width. That is what makes Set 2 Q4 (Froude number of a triangular channel with 2H:1V sides) come out as V/√(g·y/2).

For a **rectangular** channel D = y exactly, which is why textbooks often write Fr = V/√(gy) — correct for a rectangle, and the source of option (a) as a distractor.

**What Fr tells you:**

| Fr | Regime | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **< 1** | **Subcritical** | Deep, slow; gravity dominant; disturbances travel upstream |
| **= 1** | **Critical** | Minimum specific energy; the depth is y_c |
| **> 1** | **Supercritical** | Shallow, fast; inertia dominant; disturbances cannot travel upstream |

The physical meaning of Fr = 1 is that the flow velocity equals the **celerity of a shallow-water wave**, √(gD) — so at critical flow a disturbance can just hold its position. That is also why a **hydraulic jump** can only occur when the upstream flow is supercritical, and why option (c), critical depth, is a *consequence* of Fr = 1 rather than a parameter inside its definition.

examTip.trick: The general Froude number is **V/√(gD)** with **D = A/T**, the **hydraulic depth** — area over top width, not the maximum depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr uses A/T.** For a **wide rectangular** channel A/T = y, which is why the simple V/√(gy) form works there — and why it FAILS for a triangle (D = y/2) or a trapezoid. Also note the **hydraulic RADIUS R = A/P** is a different quantity again, used in Manning.

questions.stem: Bulk modulus of a liquid:
options: Is independent of pressure and viscosity
Is larger when the fluid is more compressible
questions.solution:
**Increases with pressure.**

The bulk modulus measures a fluid's **resistance to volume change**:

> **K = −dp/(dV/V)** = pressure ÷ volumetric strain

As a liquid is compressed its molecules are forced closer together, and each further increment of compression becomes **harder to achieve**. So K rises with pressure — the liquid becomes progressively stiffer. For water, K rises from about 2.1 GPa at atmospheric pressure to appreciably more at high pressure.

Why the others are wrong:
- **(a)** K **does** depend on temperature. For water it peaks near 50°C and falls either side.
- **(c)** It depends on pressure, as above. (It is indeed independent of **viscosity** — those are unrelated properties — but the statement fails on the pressure half.)
- **(d)** This has the definition **inverted**. Compressibility is **1/K**, so a *more* compressible fluid has a **smaller** bulk modulus.

That last relation is worth stating plainly:

> **Compressibility = 1/K**

| Fluid | K | Compressibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **≈ 2.1 × 10⁹ Pa** | Very low |
| Air (isothermal, atmospheric) | ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa | ~20,000 × greater |

**Why water's slight compressibility matters at all**, given that hydrostatics and most pipe and channel flow treat it as incompressible. It is exactly what makes **water hammer** possible. The pressure wave speed in a rigid pipe is

> **c = √(K/ρ) = √(2.1 × 10⁹/1000) = 1449 m/s**

which is the speed of sound in water. Were water truly incompressible, K would be infinite, c infinite, and a valve closure would transmit an infinite pressure instantaneously. The finite bulk modulus gives the finite wave speed, and hence the **pipe period 2L/c** that decides whether a closure counts as sudden or gradual.

In an **elastic** pipe the wall stretches too, and both compliances add:

> C = √{1/[ρ(1/K + D/(E·e))]}

giving a **lower** wave speed than the rigid case — about 1025 m/s for a typical steel penstock, which is why a thin-walled pipe suffers a smaller water-hammer rise than a rigid one.

For a **gas** the bulk modulus depends on the process: **K = p** for isothermal and **K = γp** for adiabatic compression, which is why gas compressibility must always be quoted with the process specified.

examTip.trick: Compressing a liquid pushes its molecules closer, which makes further compression **harder** — so K rises with pressure. It **falls** with temperature.
examTip.mnemonic: **K_water = 2.1 GPa at ordinary conditions — high enough to treat water as incompressible EXCEPT for water hammer.** There the finite value gives **c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s**; assume true incompressibility and the wave speed is infinite and the analysis collapses.

questions.stem: Rational method is applicable for:
options: Duration of rainfall < time of concentration
Duration of rainfall > time of concentration
Duration of rainfall = time of concentration
Duration doesn't depend on the time of concentration
questions.solution:
**Duration of rainfall = time of concentration.**

The rational formula

> **Q = C·I·A**  (Q = 0.278 C I A with Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in km²)

assumes that the **entire catchment is contributing simultaneously** at the moment of peak flow. That happens only when the rain has lasted at least as long as the **time of concentration t_c** — the time for run-off to travel from the remotest point of the catchment to the outlet.

**Why the peak occurs at exactly t_c**, which is the reasoning the question is testing:

| Rainfall duration | What happens |
|---|---|
| **< t_c** | The whole catchment never contributes at once — only a part of the area is delivering run-off to the outlet, so the peak is **lower** |
| **= t_c** | **The whole area contributes, at the highest intensity that can be sustained for that duration → maximum peak** |
| **> t_c** | The whole area still contributes, but from the IDF curve the **intensity is lower** for a longer duration, so the peak is again **lower** |

The two effects pull against each other — more contributing area versus falling intensity — and their product peaks precisely at **duration = t_c**. That is why the design intensity I is read from the **intensity–duration–frequency curve at a duration equal to t_c**, for the chosen return period.

Since IDF curves fall steeply with duration, a **small catchment (short t_c) takes a much higher intensity** than a large one — which is why a small urban catchment can produce a surprisingly severe peak.

**The runoff coefficient C** is the dimensionless fraction of rainfall appearing as run-off, and land use dominates it:

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Paved, roofs** | **0.70 – 0.95** |
| Bare compacted soil | 0.50 – 0.70 |
| Cultivated land | 0.20 – 0.40 |
| **Lawns, sandy soil** | **0.05 – 0.20** |

For a mixed catchment a weighted value is used, C = Σ(C_i A_i)/ΣA. Hence **urbanisation raises the peak flow dramatically** for the same storm — the central fact of urban drainage, and why Kathmandu's flooding has worsened as the valley has been built over.

**Limits of the method:** rainfall assumed uniform over the area and constant for the duration; C constant, taking no account of antecedent wetness or storage; and the return period of the run-off assumed equal to that of the rainfall. These hold reasonably for **catchments up to about 50 km²**, so the method is standard for **storm sewers, culverts and side drains** but not for a river basin, where unit hydrograph or regional methods are used instead.

examTip.trick: Only when the storm lasts as long as the **time of concentration** is the **whole catchment contributing simultaneously** — which is the condition for the peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **Read I from the IDF curve AT t_c** — not the one-hour or 24-hour intensity. That substitution is the commonest misuse of the rational method. Respect the other limit too: **small catchments only**, under about 25–50 km².

questions.stem: Which canal is not considered to be used for irrigation?
questions.solution:
**Main canal.**

The main canal takes water directly from the river headworks or reservoir and **carries** it to the distribution network. Because its discharge is large and its banks are high, water is **never drawn from it directly onto fields** — doing so would risk breaching the bank and would make regulation impossible. Its function is conveyance, not delivery.

The canal hierarchy, in descending order of discharge:

| Canal | Function | Direct irrigation? |
|---|---|---|
| **Main canal** | Conveys water from the headworks to the branches | **No — conveyance only** |
| Branch canal | Carries water to distributaries; may irrigate | Occasionally |
| **Major distributary** | Distributes to minors and watercourses | **Yes** |
| **Minor distributary** | Feeds watercourses | **Yes** |
| **Watercourse (field channel)** | Delivers to individual fields | **Yes** — the final link |

So the answer follows from position in the chain: everything below the main canal delivers water somewhere useful; the main canal only moves it.
