The **outlet** (or module) is the structure at the head of a watercourse that draws the cultivator's sanctioned share from the distributary. Its three classes are examined constantly:

| Outlet | Discharge depends on | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| **Rigid / modular** | Nothing — fixed | **0** |
| Semi-modular (flexible) | Distributary level only | ~1 for a proportional outlet |
| Non-modular | **Both** distributary and watercourse levels | Variable |

**Other canal classifications**, since the examination mixes them:

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| **Function** | Main, branch, distributary, minor, watercourse, **feeder**, carrier |
| **Source / supply** | **Perennial** (permanent river or reservoir), non-perennial (inundation) |
| **Soil** | **Alluvial**, non-alluvial |
| **Alignment** | **Ridge (watershed)**, contour, side-slope |
| Discharge | Main, branch, distributary, minor |

A **ridge canal** is the preferred alignment because it can irrigate on **both sides** by gravity and needs few cross-drainage works; a **contour canal** irrigates on one side only and must cross every drainage line, so it needs aqueducts and syphons.

examTip.trick: The canal hierarchy runs **main → branch → distributary → minor → watercourse → field channel**. The **main canal** is a **carrier**: it conveys water from the headworks but does not offtake directly to fields.
examTip.mnemonic: **Main canal carries; distributaries and minors deliver.** Offtaking directly from a main canal would disturb the flow regime and make regulation impossible — which is why the hierarchy exists at all.

questions.stem: Water available for plants is:
questions.solution:
**FC − PWP** — field capacity minus the permanent wilting point.

This is the **available moisture**, the band of soil water the plant can actually use, and it is bounded at both ends:

| Limit | Meaning | Suction |
|---|---|---|
| **Field capacity (FC)** | Water retained after **free drainage has ceased** — the wet limit | ≈ **⅓ bar** |
| **Permanent wilting point (PWP)** | Plant can no longer extract water and **does not recover** even if watered — the dry limit | ≈ **15 bar** |

> **Available moisture = FC − PWP**

Above FC the excess is **gravitational water**, which drains away within a day or two and is unavailable. Below PWP the remaining water is held as **hygroscopic** films too tightly adsorbed for roots to overcome. Only the **capillary water** between the two limits is usable.

**Why irrigation is not scheduled all the way down to PWP.** As the soil dries towards PWP, the suction the plant must overcome rises steeply, and growth suffers long before wilting. So irrigation is applied when a permitted fraction of the available moisture has been depleted — the **readily available moisture**, commonly **50 to 75%** of the total. That is the RWW term option (a) alludes to, but RWW − PWP is not the definition of available moisture.

**The depth of water to apply** at each irrigation follows directly:

> **d = γ_d × D × (FC − OMC_before irrigation)**

where D is the root-zone depth and γ_d the dry unit weight — so a deeper-rooted crop draws on a larger reservoir and can go longer between waterings.

Available moisture varies strongly with texture, which is why soil type governs irrigation frequency:

| Soil | Available moisture |
|---|---|
| Sandy | **Low** — irrigate little and often |
| Loam | Moderate |
| Clay | **High** — irrigate more heavily, less often |

**Where this leads in design.** The available-moisture calculation gives the net depth per irrigation; aggregated over the season and divided by the irrigation efficiency it becomes the **gross irrigation requirement**, which is what the canal is sized for:

> C_u (consumptive use) → subtract effective rainfall → **NIR** → ÷ efficiency → **GIR** → canal capacity

The classification of soil water — gravitational, capillary, hygroscopic and chemically combined — is asked directly in Set 3 Q15, where **capillary water** is the only form available to plants.

examTip.trick: **Available water = field capacity − permanent wilting point.** Above FC, water drains away by gravity; below PWP, it is held too tightly for roots to extract.
examTip.mnemonic: **FC − PWP is the whole basis of irrigation scheduling.** Loams hold the most available water; sands hold little (so need frequent light irrigation); clays hold much total water but a surprising amount of it below the wilting point.

questions.stem: Tile drain is suitable for:
questions.solution:
**Wet soil.**

A tile drain is a **buried perforated pipe** — traditionally short lengths of unglazed clay tile butted together, now perforated PVC — laid below the root zone to **lower the water table**. It is therefore a remedy for ground that is **too wet**: soils that hold water for long periods, flat land that cannot shed water, and fields with patches prone to saturation.

Applying it to dry soil would serve no purpose at all, which disposes of option (a). Options (b) and (d) name soils by **colour**, which is not the relevant property — what matters is the **moisture regime and the permeability**.

Indeed **black cotton soil** is a poor candidate for tile drainage on its own account: it is a highly plastic expansive clay of very low permeability, so water cannot percolate to the drain fast enough for it to work. Sub-surface drainage needs at least moderate permeability; for heavy impermeable clays a **surface** method is used instead — the **bedding method** with dead furrows, as asked in Set 3 Q46.

**Design parameters:**

| Parameter | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Depth** | **1.0 – 2.0 m**, below the root zone |
| **Spacing** | 15 – 50 m, from soil permeability and the target water-table depth |
| Gradient | 0.1 – 0.5%, enough to be self-cleansing |
| **Envelope** | **Graded gravel or synthetic filter** around the pipe |
| Outfall | To an open collector drain or a sump |

The **filter envelope is essential**, not optional: without it fine soil migrates into the perforations and the drain silts up permanently. The filter must be graded so water passes freely while soil particles do not — the same inverted-filter principle used at the downstream toe of an earth dam.

The spacing follows from drainage theory: closer spacing for lower permeability, computed by relations such as **Hooghoudt's equation**, which links spacing to permeability, drain depth, and the permissible water-table height midway between drains.

**Where it sits among the drainage methods:**

| Method | Type | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| Bedding, open ditch, surface inlet | **Surface** | **Ponded water** from the ground surface |
| **Tile drain**, French drain | **Sub-surface** | **Lowers the water table** |
| Tube wells (vertical drainage) | Sub-surface | Pumps the water table down |

The purpose in every case is to prevent **waterlogging** — and with it the **capillary rise of salts** that turns a waterlogged field saline and then sodic. Drainage treats the effect; **canal lining** removes the usual cause.

examTip.trick: Tile (subsurface) drains **lower the water table** by intercepting groundwater — so they suit land that is wet from a high water table, not merely wet at the surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Surface drainage (bedding, open ditches) removes PONDED water; SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage lowers the WATER TABLE.** Waterlogging and salinity are water-table problems, so they need the second — which is why they are so much more expensive to fix than surface ponding.

questions.stem: If two point loads act directly above the two supports of a simply supported beam:
options: Bending moment is maximum at midspan
questions.solution:
**No internal force develops.**

Each load is transmitted **straight down into the support beneath it**, with no lever arm and no span to cross. Taking a section anywhere between the supports and summing the forces to one side:

> Reaction at that support = the load directly above it, so **V = 0**
> The two are collinear, so their moment about any section is **M = 0**

So both the shear force and the bending moment are **zero throughout the span**. The beam is, structurally speaking, doing nothing — the loads never enter it.

Why the others fail:
- **(a)** is too narrow — *all* internal forces are zero, not merely the axial force.
- **(c)** is wrong: the bending moment is zero at mid-span, not maximum. Compare a load at mid-span, which gives M = WL/4 there.
- **(d)** is plainly wrong: the **reactions do develop**, and each equals the load above it. Equilibrium requires them.

**The general principle** worth extracting: a bending moment requires a **lever arm** between the load and the reaction. Move a load onto the support and the lever arm vanishes, and with it the moment.

That leads to a useful contrast:

| Load position on a simply supported span L | Maximum bending moment |
|---|---|
| **Directly over a support** | **0** |
| At distance a from A (b = L − a) | **Wab/L** |
| At **mid-span** | **WL/4** — the maximum |

The expression Wab/L confirms both ends of the range: it goes to zero as a → 0 (load over the support) and to WL/4 when a = b = L/2.

**Where this matters in practice.** Loads are deliberately brought onto supports wherever possible, because it eliminates bending:

- **Purlins are placed at panel points** of a roof truss, directly over the joints, so members carry pure axial force and no bending. A purlin landing mid-panel would induce bending in the rafter.
- Column loads are aligned to bear directly on the wall or footing below.
- Bearing stiffeners in a plate girder are placed under concentrated loads to carry them straight into the web.

The converse case is instructive too: a couple applied at a section transmits its **full moment** to everything beyond it undiminished, because a couple has no lever arm to grow — which is why Q74 of this paper, with a 1 kN·m couple at mid-span, produces support reactions of 1 kN up and 1 kN down.

examTip.trick: A load applied **directly over a support** transfers straight into the reaction — there is no lever arm and no span between them, so no shear or moment develops in the beam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load over a support goes straight down the support.** The same idea is why IS 456 lets you take the **critical shear section at d from the support face**: load applied within d of the support arches directly into it rather than passing through the web.

questions.stem: Buoyancy force is:
options: Force exerted by the surrounding fluid
Force acting in the opposite direction to the weight of an object submerged in a fluid
Force experienced by an object due to its weight in the absence of any fluid
questions.solution:
**A force acting opposite to the weight of a submerged object** — that is, vertically **upward**.

Option (c) is the only one that states the defining feature: **direction**. Options (a) and (b) are true but far too vague — a submerged body experiences many forces from the surrounding fluid, including horizontal pressures that cancel. Option (d) describes weight in a vacuum, which is the opposite of buoyancy.

**Where it comes from.** Pressure increases with depth, so the pressure on the **bottom** of a submerged body exceeds that on its **top**. The horizontal pressures cancel all round, but that vertical imbalance leaves a **net upward force** — the buoyant force. It is a genuine contact force from the fluid, not a separate kind of force.

**Archimedes' principle** quantifies it:

> **F_B = γ · V_displaced** = weight of the fluid displaced

and it acts through the **centre of buoyancy B**, which is the **centroid of the displaced volume** — not the centroid of the body. That distinction is what makes floating-body stability a subject at all.

The three outcomes for a body placed in a fluid:

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **F_B > W** | Rises, then **floats** with part of its volume above the surface |
| **F_B = W** | **Neutrally buoyant** — floats fully submerged at any depth |
| **F_B < W** | **Sinks** |

A floating body displaces a volume of fluid whose weight equals **its own whole weight** — which is why a steel ship floats: its overall density, hull plus enclosed air, is less than water's.

**Stability**, which is where the topic leads. For a **floating** body, tilting shifts B sideways and the **metacentre M** appears. Stability then requires

> **GM = I/V − BG > 0**, i.e. **M above G**

A positive GM produces a **righting** couple; a negative one capsizes the body. For a **fully submerged** body the displaced shape does not change on tilting, so no metacentre arises and stability simply requires **B above G**.

A note on the practical consequence: **apparent weight** in a fluid is W − F_B, which is why a submerged concrete block weighs less and why the **submerged (buoyant) unit weight γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w** is the value used in soil mechanics below the water table. That same buoyancy is what reduces effective stress and halves the factor of safety of a saturated slope.

examTip.trick: Buoyancy is simply the **net vertical pressure force**: the bottom of the body is deeper and feels more pressure than the top, and the difference integrates to the weight of the displaced fluid.
examTip.mnemonic: **F_B = γ × displaced volume, acting UP through the CENTROID of the DISPLACED VOLUME — not of the body.** The civil engineering application that matters: an **empty basement or tank below the water table will FLOAT**. Check uplift with the structure complete but unloaded.

questions.stem: Momentum principle is not applicable to:
questions.solution:
**Venturimeter.**

A venturimeter works on **continuity and Bernoulli's equation** — that is, on **conservation of mass and energy**. The throat constricts the flow, the velocity rises, the pressure falls, and the measured pressure difference yields the discharge:

> Q = C_d · A₁A₂ · √(2gh) / √(A₁² − A₂²)

No external force is being computed, and no change of momentum is being resisted by a boundary, so the momentum principle is not the governing tool.

The other three **are** momentum problems, because in each case a **fluid changes its momentum and a solid surface supplies the force**:

| Case | Momentum change | Force |
|---|---|---|
| **Jet on a stationary plate** | Velocity brought to zero normal to the plate | F = **ρQV** (flat plate, normal impact) |
| **Force on a pipe bend** | **Direction** of momentum changes | Resultant from ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁), resisted by **anchor blocks** |
| **Jet on a moving plate** | Relative velocity (V − u) changes | F = ρA(V − u)², work done = F·u |

So the distinction the question tests is between the **three conservation laws** and what each is used for:

| Law | Gives | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuity** (mass) | A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ | Velocities from areas |
| **Energy** (Bernoulli) | p/γ + V²/2g + z = const | **Venturimeter, orifice, pitot tube**, pipe flow with losses |
| **Momentum** | ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁) | **Forces on plates, bends, nozzles, gates; the hydraulic jump** |

**The rule of thumb worth carrying:** if the question asks for a **force or a thrust**, use momentum. If it asks for a **discharge, velocity or pressure**, use energy. If it asks for a relation between two sections' areas and velocities, use continuity.

One important case needs momentum precisely *because* energy fails: the **hydraulic jump**. Energy is dissipated in the turbulence of the jump by an amount not known in advance, so Bernoulli cannot be applied across it. Momentum is conserved regardless, which is why the sequent-depth relation

> y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)

comes from the momentum equation, and the energy loss E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂) is computed **afterwards** as a result rather than used as an input.

Note also that a venturimeter's **C_d ≈ 0.98** is high precisely because its gradual convergence and divergence keep losses small — it is an energy device designed to lose as little energy as possible.

examTip.trick: A venturimeter is analysed by **continuity plus Bernoulli** — an **energy** approach — because the losses through a well-shaped venturi are small and known. Momentum gives forces, which is not what a flowmeter needs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use ENERGY where losses are small or known (venturi, orifice, nozzle); use MOMENTUM where they are large or unknown but the FORCES are wanted (pipe bends, hydraulic jump, sudden expansion).** Momentum's advantage is that it does not require the losses to be quantified at all.

questions.stem: Minimum bitumen ductility value to use in road is:
questions.solution:
**50** — and the unit is **centimetres**, not millimetres.

The **ductility test** (IS 1208) measures the distance a standard briquette of bitumen stretches before the thread breaks, pulled at **50 mm/minute at 27°C**. The result is reported in **cm**.

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum for road construction** | **50 cm** |
| Recommended for heavily trafficked roads | **100 cm or more** |

**A note on the printed options.** The original paper gives the choices as "50 mm, 40 mm, 30 mm, 60 mm". The unit is wrong: the standard is quoted in **centimetres**, and a ductility of 50 mm would indicate a brittle, unusable binder. The numeral 50 is correct and option (a) is the intended answer — read it as **50 cm**. The unit has been dropped from the options here so the item is not actively misleading.

**Why ductility matters.** A pavement flexes under every axle and expands and contracts with temperature. A binder that cannot stretch **cracks** instead of deforming, and a cracked surface admits water — which then attacks the layers beneath and the subgrade. Ductility is therefore a measure of the binder's ability to accommodate movement without fracturing, and it is especially important where **temperature swings are large**, as they are across Nepal's range of altitudes.

The standard bitumen tests, distinguished by the property each measures:

| Test | Measures | Standard condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Penetration** | **Consistency / hardness** | 25°C, 100 g, 5 s; result in **0.1 mm** units |
| **Ductility** | **Ability to stretch** | **27°C, 50 mm/min; result in cm** |
| Softening point (ring and ball) | Temperature at which it flows | 35 – 70°C typical |
| Viscosity | Flow resistance | 60°C and 135°C |
| Flash and fire point | Safety in heating | Minimum 175°C |
| Specific gravity | Identity / mix design | 0.97 – 1.02 |

Note the **penetration** test's units, since the two are easily confused: a grade of 62 means a penetration of 62 × 0.1 mm = **6.2 mm**, whereas ductility of 50 means **50 cm**. One is reported in tenths of a millimetre, the other in centimetres.

Indian and Nepali practice has largely moved from penetration grading to **viscosity grading (VG)** under IS 73:2013, because viscosity at 60°C correlates better with in-service performance — but the ductility requirement remains, since no viscosity measurement captures the ability to stretch without breaking.

verification.notes: The printed options give the values in mm, but the ductility standard is expressed in centimetres — 50 cm minimum, 100 cm for heavy traffic. A 50 mm ductility would indicate a brittle, unusable binder. The numeral 50 (option a) is correct; the unit has been omitted from the options here rather than reproducing the incorrect mm.

examTip.trick: **Ductility** measures how far a bitumen sample stretches before breaking, and it indicates the binder's ability to **deform without cracking** under traffic and temperature movement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ductility ≥ 50 cm minimum for paving bitumen.** A bitumen that is hard and brittle may pass a penetration test and still crack in service — which is why the specification includes **penetration, softening point, ductility, flash point and viscosity** rather than any one of them.

questions.stem: Shear strength of cohesionless soil doesn't depend on:
questions.solution:
**Force** — which is not a soil property at all, and is the odd one out among the options.

The shear strength of a cohesionless soil is

> **τ = σ′ tan φ′**  (c′ = 0)

so it depends on the **effective normal stress** on the plane and on the **angle of internal friction**. "Force" names neither: strength is a **stress**, and until a force is divided by the area it acts on and referred to a particular plane, it says nothing about strength. The other three options are all genuine influences on φ′ or on the measured strength, which is what makes (d) the answer.

How the others do matter:

| Factor | Effect on a cohesionless soil |
|---|---|
| **Confining pressure** | The dominant one — τ rises directly with σ′. It also suppresses **dilation**, so φ′ measured at high confinement is slightly lower |
| **Stress history** | An over-consolidated or pre-strained sand is denser and interlocks better, raising φ′ |
| **Rate of loading** | Matters through **drainage**: sand is so permeable that normal loading is drained, but very rapid or cyclic loading can generate excess pore pressure and trigger **liquefaction** |

That last row is the practically important one in Nepal. Loose saturated sand under **earthquake shaking** cannot drain fast enough; pore pressure builds, effective stress collapses towards zero, and with it the strength — the mechanism of **liquefaction**, observed in the Kathmandu Valley in 2015.

**What actually governs φ′:**

| Factor | Effect on φ′ |
|---|---|
| **Relative density** | The strongest influence — dense sand interlocks and dilates |
| Particle **shape** | Angular grains give higher φ′ than rounded |
| **Gradation** | Well-graded packs denser than uniform |
| Particle size | Minor |
| Mineralogy, surface roughness | Minor |

Typical values: **28–32° for loose sand**, **32–36° medium**, **36–45° dense** and higher for angular gravel. Note that the **critical dry slope angle of a cohesionless soil equals φ′** — the angle of repose — which is the result behind Set 4 Q68.

**A note on the source explanation.** The answer sheet keys (d), which is correct, but argues that "confining pressure also does not have much effect on the shear strength of cohesionless soil". That is wrong — confining pressure is the *principal* determinant, since τ = σ′ tan φ′ is directly proportional to it. The keyed letter stands because "force" is not a property; the reasoning has been rewritten.

verification.notes: The keyed answer (d) is correct — 'force' is not a soil property. But the source's explanation claims confining pressure has little effect on the shear strength of cohesionless soil, which is wrong: strength is directly proportional to effective confining stress. The reasoning has been rewritten.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Shear **strength** is a stress, not a force — and it depends on the **normal stress**, not on the applied load in isolation.
examTip.trick: For cohesionless soil **τ = σ′ tan φ**, so the strength depends on the **effective normal stress** and the **friction angle** — which in turn depends on density, grain shape, grading and mineralogy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sand has NO strength at zero normal stress** (c = 0, so the envelope passes through the origin). That is why dry sand cannot stand in a vertical cut and why a submerged sand slope is so much weaker: σ′ is halved.

questions.stem: The head loss formula h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵) is given by:
questions.solution:
**Darcy–Weisbach** — this is the same equation rewritten in terms of discharge instead of velocity.

**The derivation**, which is worth following because it shows why the odd constant 12.1 appears:

Start from the familiar form:
> h_f = **fLV²/(2gD)**

Substitute V = Q/A with A = πD²/4:
> h_f = fL/(2gD) × [Q/(πD²/4)]²
> h_f = fLQ² × 16/(2gD · π²D⁴)
> h_f = **fLQ²/(2gπ²D⁵/16)**

Evaluate the constant:
> 2gπ²/16 = 2 × 9.81 × 9.8696/16 = **12.1**

> **h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)** ✓

So 12.1 is simply **2gπ²/16**, and the two forms are identical. The D⁵ in the denominator absorbed one power of D from the original formula and four more from A².

**The consequence of that fifth power is the practically important part.** For a fixed discharge:

> **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵**

So increasing the diameter by just **15%** roughly **halves** the friction loss. That is why a modest enlargement of a main or a penstock pays for itself in saved pumping energy or recovered head, and it is the basis of the **economic diameter** calculation that balances the capital cost of a larger pipe against the lifetime value of the head lost in a smaller one.

**Distinguishing the four formulae named:**

| Formula | Expression | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Darcy–Weisbach** | **h_f = fLV²/2gD** | **Dimensionally rational**; f from the Moody diagram; valid for any fluid and any regime |
| Hazen–Williams | V = 0.849 C R^{0.63} S^{0.54} | **Empirical**, for water only, turbulent flow; common in water supply |
| Chezy | V = C√(RS) | Empirical; C has dimensions |
| **Manning** | V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2} | Empirical; standard for **open channels** |

Darcy–Weisbach is the only one of the four that is **dimensionally homogeneous**, which is why it is preferred wherever rigour matters. Its price is that f is not a constant: it depends on **Reynolds number and relative roughness**, read from the Moody diagram, with **f = 64/Re** in the laminar range.

In turbulent flow f varies only weakly, so h_f ∝ V² approximately — the square law tested in Set 4 Q51.

examTip.trick: **h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)** is Darcy–Weisbach expressed in terms of discharge. Check: 12.1 = 2g × (π/4)²/... — it is the same equation with the velocity substituted as Q/A.
examTip.mnemonic: **Same equation, two forms: h_f = fLV²/(2gD) from velocity, and h_f = 0.0826 fLQ²/D⁵ (= fLQ²/12.1D⁵) from discharge.** The **D⁵** is the dominant fact of pipeline economics — doubling the diameter cuts the loss **32-fold**.

questions.stem: In the water-supply distribution network, the dead-end system is not favoured because:
options: It is cumbersome in terms of design
The pressure at the dead ends becomes undesirably low in the case of additional extensions
It is difficult to maintain residual chlorine levels at the dead ends
At the time of repairs, service connections beyond the point of repair are deprived of water
questions.solution:
**Option (c) is the primary reason, and the keyed answer (a) is the one option that is false.**

**Why (a) cannot be right.** A dead-end (tree or branching) system is the **simplest layout to design**, not the most cumbersome. Flow in every pipe is determinate — it can be computed directly by working back from the far ends, with no iteration. It is the **grid iron** system that is hard to analyse, because the loops make the flow distribution indeterminate and require iterative solution by the **Hardy Cross** method or network software.

The source's own note concedes as much, observing that the dead-end system is "widely used in haphazardly developed and old cities like Kathmandu valley" — precisely because it is simple and fits an irregular street pattern.

**The genuine drawbacks**, all three of which the remaining options name correctly:

| Drawback | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Water quality (c)** | Water **stagnates** at a dead end. The chlorine residual decays, sediment accumulates with no through-flow to scour it, and bacterial regrowth follows. This is the most serious objection, because it is a **health** issue and it is present continuously |
| **Pressure (b)** | Each dead end is fed from one direction only, so head loss accumulates along a single path. Extending the network drops the pressure at the tip further |
| **Interruption (d)** | With no alternative path, a burst or a repair **cuts off every connection beyond it** |

**Why (c) rather than (b) or (d).** All three are real, but (b) and (d) are intermittent and can be managed — pressure by resizing, interruption by scheduling. Stagnation is **permanent and unavoidable** in the layout itself, and loss of disinfectant residual in a distribution main is the failure mode that actually endangers consumers. Hence dead-end mains require **scour valves at each end and periodic flushing** as a standing maintenance obligation.

**Flagged for review.** As printed the question has **three defensible answers** and its keyed option is the only false one, so it cannot be resolved to a single choice with confidence. The answer here is set to (c) as the primary and most commonly cited reason, but the owner should reword the item — for example as "which of the following is **not** a reason…", which would make (a) the correct answer and the question sound.

The layouts compared, for completeness:

| Layout | Reliability | Dead ends | Design | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dead end (tree)** | **Poor** | **Many** | **Simplest** | **Lowest** |
| **Grid iron** | **Best** | **None** | Hardy Cross iteration | Highest |
| Circular (ring) | Good | Few | Moderate | Moderate |
| Radial | Good; best pressure | Few | Moderate | Moderate |

verification.notes: The key answers (a), but a dead-end system is the SIMPLEST to design — flow is determinate, needing no iteration, unlike the grid iron which requires Hardy Cross. The source's own note concedes it is used because it suits haphazard old cities. Options (b), (c) and (d) are all genuine drawbacks, so as printed the question has three correct answers and its keyed option is false. Answer set to (c), stagnation and loss of chlorine residual, as the primary and continuously-present objection. Owner should reword the item (e.g. 'which is NOT a reason') before use in a paid set.

examTip.trick: Water sits in a dead end for a long time, so the **chlorine residual decays** and there is no through-flow to replenish it. That is the practical objection, above and beyond the reliability problem.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead ends: stagnation, loss of residual, sediment accumulation, and one break cuts off everything beyond.** The **GRID IRON** layout eliminates them and gives multiple paths — the best reliability and water quality, at the cost of more pipe and a Hardy Cross analysis.

questions.stem: A road inside a city is called:
questions.solution:
**Street.**

A street is a road **within an urban area**, whose defining characteristic is that **access dominates over mobility**: it connects buildings and provides entry to individual properties, carries local traffic at low speed, and normally has **footpaths, kerbs and frequent intersections**.

Contrast the others, each of which is defined by a different feature:

| Term | Defining feature |
|---|---|
| **Street** | **Inside a city**; access to properties; low speed; footpaths |
| **Ring road** | Encircles a city, so through traffic can **bypass** the centre |
| **Highway** | Long-distance route between towns; **mobility** dominant, access restricted |
| **Trunk road** | A major arterial route carrying long-distance traffic |

So a **ring road** is named for its *geometry and purpose* (bypassing) rather than for being inside the city — Kathmandu's Ring Road is the obvious local example, and it sits at the city's edge precisely to keep through traffic out of the streets.

**The functional classification** underlying all this is the durable idea, and it is a spectrum between two competing objectives:

| Class | Mobility | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Expressway / arterial** | **Highest** | Strictly limited |
| Sub-arterial | High | Limited |
| Collector | Moderate | Moderate |
| **Local street** | **Lowest** | **Highest** |

Mobility and access are **inherently in conflict**: every driveway and side junction that improves access interrupts through movement. Good network design therefore separates the functions into a hierarchy rather than trying to make one road do both — which is exactly what a ring road achieves for a city.

**Nepal's own classifications**, which the examination draws on:

| Standard | Classes |
|---|---|
| **Nepal Road Standard** (national network) | **National Highway (H), Feeder Road (F), District Road (D), Urban Road (U)** |
| By terrain | **Plain** (<10% cross slope), Rolling (10–25%), **Mountainous** (25–60%), Steep (>60%) |
| By surface | Earthen, gravelled, blacktopped |

The terrain classification matters as much as the functional one in Nepal, because it governs the geometric standards applied: the same National Highway is designed for 120 km/h in the Terai but as little as 40 km/h in steep terrain, with hairpin bends down to a 15 m radius.

examTip.trick: The functional hierarchy — **arterial, sub-arterial, collector, local street** — runs from maximum **mobility** to maximum **access**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arterials move traffic; streets serve property.** A road asked to do both at once becomes congested and dangerous, which is the standard diagnosis for a ribbon-developed highway through a bazaar.

questions.stem: Which of the following causes greasing in flocculation?
questions.solution:
**Surfactant.**

A **surfactant** (surface-active agent — the active ingredient of detergents) lowers the **surface tension** between two liquids or between a liquid and a solid. In a flocculation basin that is exactly the wrong property to have present: surfactants

- **coat the suspended particles**, so their surface charge is no longer neutralised by the coagulant and they will not adhere to one another;
- cause **greasing and foaming**, producing a scum layer on the basin surface;
- **disrupt floc formation**, so the flocs that do form are small, light and will not settle.

The net effect is that coagulation fails and turbidity carries through to the filters.

The other three chemicals all have legitimate roles in treatment, which is why they are offered as distractors:

| Chemical | Role |
|---|---|
| **Alum** — aluminium sulphate | The **coagulant**: hydrolyses to Al(OH)₃ floc, neutralising the negative charge on colloidal clay so particles can agglomerate |
| **Ammonia** | pH adjustment; forms **chloramines** in chlorination |
| **Chlorine** | **Disinfectant**; also oxidises iron, manganese and sulphide |

**Why coagulation is needed at all.** Colloidal clay particles of about 0.001 mm carry a **negative surface charge** and repel one another, so they remain in suspension indefinitely — Stokes' law gives them a settling velocity so low that they would take months to fall. Alum's gelatinous Al(OH)₃ floc neutralises that charge and binds the particles into flocs large enough to settle in hours.

**The process sequence** and its conditions:

> **Rapid mixing (flash mix, 30–60 s)** → **flocculation (slow stirring, 20–40 min)** → **sedimentation** → filtration → disinfection

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Alum dose | **10 – 40 mg/L**, fixed by a laboratory **jar test** |
| Effective pH | **6.5 – 8.5**, optimum ≈ 7 |
| Alkalinity consumed | ~0.5 mg/L as CaCO₃ per mg/L of alum |

The **slow** stirring in flocculation is deliberate: enough to bring particles into contact, gentle enough not to shear the fragile flocs apart. Over-mixing breaks them up as surely as a surfactant prevents them forming.

Where surfactants come from in practice: **domestic detergent** in the raw water, which is why a source receiving sewage or greywater is difficult to treat, and why detergent-laden industrial effluent must be pre-treated before discharge.

examTip.trick: Surfactants (from detergents) **lower surface tension** and stabilise foam, producing greasy scum on the surface of flocculation and sedimentation tanks and interfering with floc formation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Surfactants also cause FOAMING in aeration tanks and rivers below a discharge.** Their other significance: **phosphates** in detergents drive **EUTROPHICATION**, which is why phosphate-free formulations and phosphorus removal exist.

questions.stem: What is the value of coefficient of uniformity for well graded sand?
questions.solution:
**Greater than 6.**

The **coefficient of uniformity** measures the spread of particle sizes:

> **C_u = D₆₀ / D₁₀**

where D₆₀ and D₁₀ are the sizes below which 60% and 10% of the soil by weight is finer, read from the particle-size distribution curve.

The two thresholds must be kept apart, and the question is testing which is which:

| Soil | Well graded requires |
|---|---|
| **Sand** | **C_u > 6** |
| **Gravel** | **C_u > 4** |

and in **both** cases the coefficient of curvature must also satisfy

> **C_c = D₃₀²/(D₆₀ × D₁₀)**, with **1 ≤ C_c ≤ 3**

So option (a), C_u > 4, is the **gravel** criterion — the intended trap — and option (c), 1 to 3, is the range for **C_c**, not C_u.

**What the numbers mean physically.** A large C_u means a **wide range** of sizes present, so small grains fill the voids between large ones and the soil packs densely. A C_u near 1 means all the particles are much the same size — **uniform** or poorly graded — leaving large voids that cannot be filled.

| C_u | Description |
|---|---|
| **≈ 1** | **Uniform** (poorly graded); a beach sand or a filter sand |
| 6 – 15 | Well graded |
| Very large, with a missing size band | **Gap graded** — C_u is large but C_c falls outside 1–3 |

That is why C_c is needed alongside C_u: a soil missing an intermediate size range can have a wide overall spread yet still pack badly, and only C_c detects it.

**Why well-graded soil is wanted in construction:** it reaches a **higher maximum dry density** for the same compactive effort, has a **higher shear strength** and lower compressibility, and forms a stable, interlocked mass. That is what specifications for **sub-base and base course** material are enforcing when they set gradation limits.

**Where uniform soil is wanted instead:** a **filter** or drainage layer, where the object is high permeability rather than density — so a uniform coarse sand is chosen deliberately. Its gradation must still satisfy the **filter criteria** relative to the soil it protects, so that water passes but particles do not.

How the curve is obtained: **sieve analysis** for particles coarser than 75 μm, and **hydrometer (sedimentation) analysis** for the finer fraction, per IS 2720 Part 4. The resulting D-values then feed the **USCS classification** — SW or SP for a clean sand depending on whether these criteria are met.

examTip.trick: Two criteria must be satisfied **together** for well-graded soil, and forgetting the second is the usual error: **C_c between 1 and 3**, **and C_u > 6 for sand** (> 4 for gravel).
examTip.mnemonic: **C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀ measures the SPREAD; C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀ × D₆₀) measures the SHAPE of the curve.** Well graded means the small grains fill the voids between the large — which is why it compacts to a high density and drains predictably.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is constructed to separate the under sluices from the main weir?
questions.solution:
**Divide wall.**

A divide wall is built **at right angles to the weir axis**, separating the **under-sluice bays** next to the canal head regulator from the **main weir** section. It creates a quiet pocket in front of the intake and lets the two parts of the barrage be operated independently.

**What it achieves:**

| Function | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Creates a still pocket** | Water in front of the canal intake is calmed, so suspended **sediment settles** rather than entering the canal |
| **Separates the flows** | The under-sluices can be operated to scour that pocket without disturbing flow over the main weir crest |
| Prevents cross-currents | Keeps oblique flow and eddies away from the head regulator |
| Controls approach flow | Guides water squarely towards the regulator |

**Why the divide wall and under-sluices must be understood as a pair.** The divide wall creates the pocket in which silt deposits; the **under-sluices** — low-crested bays with gates — then **flush that deposit** back into the river downstream. Without the sluices the pocket would silt up solid and the wall would become useless; without the wall the sluices would have no quiet pocket to scour.

That is the same principle as the **silt excluder**, which goes a step further: horizontal tunnels in the pocket floor skim the **bottom, silt-laden layer** away through the under-sluices while the cleaner upper water passes over the tunnel roofs into the canal. All three devices exploit the fact that **sediment concentration is greatest near the bed**.

Why the other options are wrong:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Marginal bund** | An earthen embankment **along the river bank** upstream, confining the afflux and protecting adjoining land from flooding |
| **Head regulator** | The gated structure at the **head of the canal**, controlling the discharge entering it |
| **Guide bank** | Guides the river axially through the waterway (Set 4 Q47) |
| **Fish ladder** | Lets fish migrate upstream past the barrier |

So a marginal bund runs **parallel** to the flow and a divide wall **across** it — a useful way to keep them apart.

This matters particularly in Nepal's Terai, where Himalayan rivers carry very high sediment loads: without effective silt control at the headworks the canal silts up, its capacity falls, and the command area at the tail goes short of water.

examTip.trick: The **divide wall** separates the **under-sluice pocket** in front of the head regulator from the rest of the weir, creating a still pocket where silt settles out before the water enters the canal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Headworks components: weir/barrage, DIVIDE WALL, under-sluices, head regulator, SILT EXCLUDER, fish ladder, guide banks.** The divide wall and the silt excluder work together — the wall creates the pocket, the excluder draws the clear upper water into the canal and passes the silty bottom water down the sluices.

questions.stem: In pure bending, stress distribution in a beam is:
questions.solution:
**Linear** — varying directly with distance from the neutral axis.

From the flexure formula:

> **σ = M·y/I**

with M and I constant at a given section, **σ ∝ y**. So the bending stress is:
- **zero at the neutral axis**,
- **maximum at the extreme fibres**, tension on one face and compression on the other,
- varying **linearly** in between.

**Where the linearity comes from.** It rests on the fundamental assumption of simple bending theory — that **plane sections remain plane**. If a section stays flat as the beam curves, the strain at any fibre is proportional to its distance from the neutral axis:

> ε = y/R

and for a **linearly elastic** material, σ = Eε = Ey/R, which is linear in y. Note that the linearity therefore requires *both* plane sections **and** elastic behaviour.

The assumptions in full: the material is homogeneous, isotropic and elastic; the beam is initially straight with a constant cross-section; the load acts in a plane of symmetry; plane sections remain plane; and E is the same in tension and compression.

**Do not confuse bending stress with shear stress**, which is the classic pairing:

| Quantity | Distribution over the depth | At neutral axis | At extreme fibres |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bending stress** | **Linear** | **Zero** | **Maximum** |
| **Shear stress** | **Parabolic** (rectangle) | **Maximum** | **Zero** |

They are exact opposites, which is why option (a) is offered — parabolic belongs to shear. For a rectangle, τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg at the neutral axis.

**Where the linear distribution breaks down**, which is worth knowing:

| Case | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **Curved beam** (crane hook, chain link) | **Hyperbolic** — the neutral axis shifts towards the centre of curvature |
| Beyond the elastic limit | Stress block flattens; fully plastic at M_p |
| **RCC section** | Concrete's parabolic-rectangular block in compression, steel in tension |

The plastic case is the basis of **plastic analysis**: as the section yields, the linear distribution gives way to a rectangular one, and the ratio of the two moment capacities is the **shape factor** — 1.5 for a rectangle, 1.7 for a circle, only 1.10–1.20 for a rolled I-beam.

**Pure bending** itself means **constant moment and zero shear** — the condition in the middle third of a beam under two symmetric point loads, which is exactly why that arrangement is used in the standard flexure test.

examTip.trick: **σ = My/I** — stress is **directly proportional to the distance y** from the neutral axis. So the distribution is **linear**, zero at the neutral axis and maximum at the extreme fibres.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bending stress LINEAR (maximum at the extremes, zero at the NA); SHEAR stress PARABOLIC (maximum at the NA, zero at the extremes).** They are exact opposites — which is precisely why an **I-section** is efficient: **flanges take the moment, web takes the shear.**

questions.stem: Demography is the study of:
questions.solution:
**Population.**

Demography is the statistical study of populations — their **size, structure, distribution** and the processes that change them: births, deaths and migration.

The distractors each name a different discipline:

| Study of | Discipline |
|---|---|
| **Population** | **Demography** |
| Culture | Cultural anthropology |
| Heritage | Archaeology |
| Environmental change | Environmental science / ecology |

**Why a civil engineer needs it.** Every public utility is sized for a **future** population, not today's. The design period of a water supply or sewerage scheme is 15 to 30 years, so the first step in design is a **population forecast** — and the whole demand calculation rests on it:

> **Design population × per capita demand = design demand**

Get the forecast wrong and the scheme is either starved within a few years or grossly over-built and uneconomic.

**The forecasting methods**, which are the examinable content:

| Method | Assumption | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Arithmetical increase** | Constant **absolute** increase per decade | Large, **old, saturated** cities |
| **Geometrical increase** | Constant **percentage** growth | **Young, rapidly growing** towns; tends to over-estimate |
| **Incremental increase** | Average increase **plus** the average of the increments | A **compromise** — generally the most reliable |
| Decreasing rate of growth | Growth rate falls as saturation approaches | Cities nearing their limit |
| **Graphical / comparison** | Extrapolate the curve, or follow a similar city's history | Where records are good |
| **Logistic (S-curve)** | Growth follows an S-curve to a saturation value | Long-term projection |

The **incremental increase** method is usually preferred because arithmetic under-estimates a growing town and geometric over-estimates it; the incremental method sits between them.

**Design demands then follow from the forecast population:**

| Demand | Multiplier on average daily |
|---|---|
| Average daily | 1.0 |
| **Maximum daily** | **1.8** |
| **Peak hourly** | **2.7** |

with **fire demand** added on top for mains sizing.

A practical caution for Nepal: **migration** dominates, and it is the component demography handles worst. Kathmandu Valley's growth has been driven overwhelmingly by in-migration rather than natural increase, so a projection extrapolated from natural growth rates would badly under-predict it — which is part of why the Valley's water supply has lagged its population for decades.

examTip.trick: Demography is the study of **population** — its size, structure, distribution and how it changes through births, deaths and migration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Population forecasting is the first step in every water supply and sewerage design**, and the method matters: **arithmetic increase** for a stable old town, **geometric** for a rapidly growing one, **incremental increase** for a maturing one, and **logistic** where a saturation limit applies. Choosing the wrong one over a 30-year design period gives wildly different works.

questions.stem: The difference between the total head line and the hydraulic grade line represents the:
questions.solution:
**Velocity head, v²/2g.**

The two lines plot different parts of the same Bernoulli sum:

| Line | Plots | Equals |
|---|---|---|
| **Total head line (EGL)** | Total head | z + p/γ + **v²/2g** |
| **Hydraulic grade line (HGL)** | **Piezometric** head | z + p/γ |

Subtracting leaves exactly the term that distinguishes them:

> **EGL − HGL = v²/2g = velocity head**

Note that option (a), piezometric head, is what the **HGL itself** represents — not the gap between the lines.

**What the two lines tell you at a glance**, which is why they are drawn:

- The **EGL always lies above the HGL** by the velocity head, and the gap **widens where the flow accelerates** — through a contraction, for instance.
- In a pipe of **constant diameter** the velocity is constant, so the two run **parallel**.
- The **EGL always falls** in the direction of flow (except across a pump), because friction and minor losses continuously destroy total head. Its slope is the **energy slope** S_f = h_f/L.
- The **HGL may rise or fall**: at an enlargement the velocity drops, pressure recovers, and the HGL **climbs** even while the EGL continues to fall.
- Where the **HGL falls below the pipe axis**, the pressure is **sub-atmospheric** — the condition that admits air and invites **cavitation**, and the reason a summit in a pipeline or a long siphon must be checked against the vapour pressure limit.
- For a reservoir at rest v = 0, so the **EGL and HGL coincide** at the free surface.

**A useful check on any pipeline sketch:** at the exit into a reservoir the HGL meets the water surface, and the gap that existed just inside the pipe — the velocity head — is precisely the **exit loss**, k = 1.0. At entry the loss is only k = 0.5, because the flow contracts and re-expands rather than dissipating the whole velocity head.

The pieces of the sum, for completeness:

| Term | Name | Represents |
|---|---|---|
| **z** | Elevation (datum) head | Position |
| **p/γ** | Pressure head | Pressure energy |
| **v²/2g** | **Velocity head** | Kinetic energy |
| z + p/γ | **Piezometric head** | What a piezometer reads |

And for a **static** fluid the velocity head is zero, so the piezometric head is constant throughout — which is why every piezometer tapped into a still tank rises to the same level whatever its depth.

examTip.trick: **EGL = p/γ + z + V²/2g** and **HGL = p/γ + z**. The gap between them is the **velocity head**, by definition.
examTip.mnemonic: **The EGL always FALLS in the direction of flow (friction); the HGL may RISE where the pipe expands.** And **HGL below the pipe means NEGATIVE pressure** — which risks air being drawn in and, in a water main, **contamination being sucked through joints**. That is why codes require a minimum positive residual head everywhere.

questions.stem: Minimum weaving angle in a rotary section is:
questions.solution:
**15°.**

**Weaving** is the crossing of two traffic streams moving in the same general direction, achieved by successive merging and diverging rather than by direct crossing — which is exactly how a rotary (roundabout) eliminates crossing conflicts.

The **weaving angle** is the angle at which the entering and exiting streams cross one another's path. The design rule is that it should be kept **small, but not less than 15°**:

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Small angle** | Merging and diverging are gentler, so speeds need not drop as much and capacity is higher |
| **Not below 15°** | Below this the weaving length becomes excessively long and the geometry unworkable |

So the answer is the lower bound on a quantity the designer otherwise wants to minimise — which is what makes it worth asking.

**The other rotary design parameters**, which are examined alongside:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Weaving angle** | **≥ 15°** |
| Weaving length | **≥ 4 × the width** of the weaving section |
| Entry radius | 20 – 35 m |
| Exit radius | 1.5 – 2 × the entry radius |
| Radius of the central island | ≈ 1.33 × the entry radius |
| **Design speed** | **30 – 40 km/h** (urban), 40 km/h rural |
| Entry width | 6 – 7 m |

The **exit radius is deliberately larger** than the entry radius, so that vehicles leave the rotary faster than they enter it and do not queue back into the circulating carriageway.

**How a rotary works, and its limits.** All traffic circulates **one way** around a central island, so every conflict becomes a merge or a diverge and there are **no crossing conflicts** at all. That makes it safer and self-regulating with no signals. But:

- capacity is limited by the **weaving sections**, not by the entries, and it saturates at around **3000 PCU/hour** total;
- it needs a **large area**, which is often unavailable in a built-up centre;
- it is unsuitable where **pedestrian volumes are high** or where one approach dominates the flow;
- above its capacity it locks up, and a **signalised intersection** performs better.

Hence the general hierarchy of intersection treatment by volume: **uncontrolled → channelised → rotary → signalised → grade-separated interchange**. A **clover leaf** interchange achieves complete separation of traffic but requires a very large area and creates weaving sections of its own.

examTip.trick: The **weaving angle** is the angle at which merging and diverging streams cross. A small angle means a **gradual** merge, which is safer and allows higher speeds.
examTip.mnemonic: **Weaving angle 15–40°, and SMALLER is better.** The other rotary criteria: **weaving length at least 4 times the entry width**, and entry and exit radii large enough to keep speeds up — because a rotary works by converting **crossing** conflicts into **weaving** ones, and only if the weaving section is long enough to do it in.

questions.stem: The maximum limit of weight of fibreboards is:
questions.solution:
**960 kg/m³.**

Fibreboard — also called **reconstructed wood** — is a rigid board manufactured by breaking timber or plant residue down into fibres and re-forming them under **heat and pressure**, with or without a binder. Its density depends on the pressure applied during manufacture, and **960 kg/m³** is the upper limit.

A useful sanity check on the options: natural timber runs about **400 to 900 kg/m³**, and water is 1000 kg/m³. A wood-based board denser than about 1000 kg/m³ would be implausible, which rules out (b), (c) and (d) on inspection.

The board products, distinguished by how the wood is broken down:

| Product | Made from | Density |
|---|---|---|
| **Fibreboard** | **Wood fibres**, pressed | up to **960 kg/m³** |
| **Hardboard** | Fibres at high pressure | 800 – 1000 kg/m³ |
| **MDF** (medium density fibreboard) | Fibres + resin | 600 – 800 kg/m³ |
| **Particle board / chipboard** | Wood **chips** + resin | 500 – 800 kg/m³ |
| **Plywood** | **Veneers** glued in odd-numbered layers, grain crossed | 500 – 700 kg/m³ |
| Insulating board | Fibres, low pressure | < 400 kg/m³ |

**Why these products exist at all**, which is the more useful point than the number. They overcome the inherent defects of natural timber:

- **No knots, shakes, wane or twisted fibres** — the defects are dispersed rather than concentrated;
- **Dimensionally stable**, so much less shrinkage and warping than solid timber;
- **Uniform properties** in the plane of the board, whereas timber is strongly anisotropic;
- Available in **large sheets**, unconstrained by tree size;
- Made from **residue and small-diameter wood**, so they use the resource efficiently.

The trade-off is their weakness in the presence of **moisture**: most fibre and particle boards swell and lose strength when wet, so they are interior materials unless specially treated. **Plywood** — particularly BWP (boiling water proof) grade — is the one to use where dampness is expected.

Uses in building: partitions, false ceilings, panelling, door shutters, furniture, formwork facing (plywood), and insulating board for thermal and acoustic linings.

examTip.trick: Board products are classified by **density**, which determines their strength and use: **softboard** (low density, insulation), **medium board**, **hardboard** (high density, up to about 960 kg/m³).
examTip.mnemonic: **Higher density means higher strength and lower insulation value — the two trade off directly.** That is a general rule for all cellular and fibrous materials: whatever traps air insulates, and whatever traps air is weak.

questions.stem: Before plastering, the surface has to be:
questions.solution:
**Rough.**

Plaster adheres to a background by **mechanical key** as much as by adhesion, so the surface must be roughened to give it something to grip. The standard preparation:

- **Rake out the mortar joints** to a depth of about **10 to 20 mm**, so the plaster keys into them;
- **Scrape or hack** the brick or concrete surface to remove smoothness and any laitance;
- Brush off all dust and loose material;
- **Wet the surface** thoroughly before applying the plaster.

On a smooth surface — dense concrete, or a wall built with flush joints — the plaster has no key at all and will eventually **debond and fall away in sheets**. Where the background cannot be roughened, the remedy is a **bonding agent** or a spatterdash / key coat, not a hope that adhesion alone will hold.

**Note that option (a), watering, is also genuinely required** — but as a *separate* step, and it is not what the question asks for. Wetting stops the porous background sucking water out of the fresh plaster, which would starve the cement of the water it needs to hydrate. Rough is the answer because the question asks what the surface must **be**; watering is what is done to it.

That is the same reasoning as soaking bricks before laying them (Q5 of this paper): a dry porous background acts as a sponge and destroys the bond.

**Typical specification:**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Internal plaster | **12 mm**, single coat, 1:4 or 1:6 cement–sand |
| External plaster | **20 mm**, two coats (base 12 mm + finishing 8 mm) |
| Ceiling plaster | 6 mm |
| **Curing** | **7 to 10 days**, kept continuously damp |
| Mortar mix | 1:3 (rich) to 1:6 (lean) |

**Why plaster fails**, since the causes trace back to preparation:

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Debonding / peeling** | **Smooth or dusty background**; no key |
| **Crazing** — fine hairline cracks | Too rich a mix, or **rapid drying** from poor curing |
| Blistering | Unslaked lime particles expanding |
| **Efflorescence** | Soluble salts migrating out of the masonry |
| Popping | Contaminant particles in the mortar |

The **crazing** row is the subject of Q60 of this paper, and it points to the other half of good practice: preparation earns the bond, and **curing** earns the strength. Both are cheap, and both are the first things omitted under time pressure.

examTip.trick: Plaster needs a **mechanical key** to grip. On concrete the surface is **hacked**; on smooth brickwork the mortar joints are **raked out** to about 10 mm.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hack concrete, rake brickwork joints, and wet the surface before plastering** — the last because a dry substrate sucks water out of the plaster and stops it hydrating, exactly as a dry brick does to mortar. Three-coat work then goes **render (12 mm) → float (9 mm) → finish (3 mm)**, rough to smooth.

questions.stem: For reversal of stresses, the most suitable bolt is:
questions.solution:
**Friction grip bolt** — a high-strength friction grip (HSFG) bolt.

An HSFG bolt is tightened to a **controlled high tension**, which clamps the plates together so hard that the load is transferred by **friction between the faying surfaces**, not by shear on the bolt shank or bearing on the hole.

That is exactly what a **reversal of stress** demands. Because the connection carries load by friction:

- there is **no slip** in either direction, so the joint does not rattle back and forth as the load reverses;
- the bolt shank sees no alternating shear, so **fatigue** performance is far better;
- the clamping force is unaffected by the direction of loading.

By contrast an ordinary **bearing-type** bolt sits in a hole 1 to 3 mm larger than itself. Under reversing load it **slips one way, then the other**, hammering against opposite sides of the hole each cycle. The joint slackens, the hole elongates, and fatigue cracks initiate. That is why bearing bolts are unsuitable wherever the load reverses.

| Bolt | Load transfer | Hole clearance | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Black (unfinished) bolt** | **Shear and bearing** | Loose, 1.5 – 3 mm | Light, static, secondary members |
| **Turned bolt** | Shear and bearing | Close-fitting, turned to size | Better fit, but still bearing-type |
| **HSFG bolt** | **Friction** from **pre-tension** | Normal clearance | **Reversal of stress, dynamic and fatigue loading**, no-slip joints |

**Where HSFG bolts are specified:** bridge girders and gantry girders (moving loads), crane structures, members subject to **wind reversal** or **seismic** action, and any connection where slip cannot be tolerated — for instance where deflection or alignment must be maintained.

**Design consequences worth knowing:**
- Capacity depends on the **pre-tension** and the **slip factor** μ of the faying surfaces, so those surfaces must be **clean, unpainted and free of oil and mill scale**.
- Tightening must be **controlled** — by calibrated torque wrench, turn-of-nut method, or load-indicating washers — because the whole capacity rests on achieving the specified tension.
- IS 800 gives the slip resistance as V_dsf = μ_f n_e K_h F_o/γ_mf, with γ_mf = 1.10 for slip at the serviceability limit state and 1.25 at ultimate.
- **Welding** is the other good answer for stress reversal, since a properly executed weld has no slip path at all — but bolts are preferred for site connections.

Related bolt rules: **minimum pitch 2.5d**, maximum pitch the lesser of 32t or 300 mm, and minimum edge distance 1.7 × hole diameter for a sheared edge.

examTip.trick: A **friction grip (HSFG) bolt** is tensioned so hard that the load is carried by **friction between the plates**, with **no slip at all** — so a reversal of load cannot cause the joint to rattle loose or work back and forth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bearing bolts slip into bearing; HSFG bolts never slip.** That makes HSFG the choice wherever there is **stress reversal, fatigue loading or a need for a rigid joint** — bridges, crane girders, wind bracing. The price is careful surface preparation and controlled tightening (torque or turn-of-nut).

questions.stem: Minimum percentage of reinforcement required for a footing for Fe 415 grade steel is:
questions.solution:
**0.12%** of the gross cross-sectional area.

IS 456 sets the minimum reinforcement for a slab — and a footing is designed as a slab — according to the steel grade:

| Steel | Minimum reinforcement |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** (mild steel) | **0.15%** of gross area |
| **Fe 415 / Fe 500** (HYSD) | **0.12%** of gross area |
| Welded wire fabric | 0.12% |

So option (b), 0.15%, is the **mild steel** figure — the intended trap. The requirement is lower for high-strength steel simply because less area is needed to provide the same tensile force.

**Why a minimum exists at all**, which is the part worth understanding. It is not about flexural strength but about **controlling cracking from restrained volume change**:

- **Shrinkage and temperature** movements are resisted by the surrounding structure and the ground, which puts the concrete into tension.
- When the concrete cracks, the steel must be able to carry the released tensile force **without itself yielding** — otherwise the section fails suddenly at first cracking.
- Adequate distributed steel spreads that movement over **many fine cracks** rather than a few wide ones, which is what preserves durability.

Hence the minimum applies **in both directions**, and in a footing the reinforcement runs both ways as a mat.

**The companion limits for slabs and footings:**

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Minimum reinforcement** | **0.12% (HYSD) / 0.15% (mild steel)** of gross area |
| **Minimum thickness of footing** | **150 mm** on soil; **300 mm** over piles |
| Minimum depth below ground | **500 mm** (IS 1080) |
| Nominal cover in a footing | **50 mm** — larger than for a beam, being cast against soil |
| Maximum bar spacing | 3d or 300 mm (main), 5d or 450 mm (distribution) |
| Maximum tension steel | 4% of bD |

The **50 mm cover** deserves emphasis: a footing is in permanent contact with damp soil, often with sulphates and chlorides present, so the cover is the reinforcement's only protection. Blinding concrete is placed beneath so the steel is not laid on bare earth.

**The checks a footing must satisfy**, in the order they usually govern:
1. **Bearing pressure** on the soil ≤ allowable (this fixes the plan area);
2. **One-way shear** at a distance d from the face;
3. **Two-way (punching) shear** on the perimeter at d/2 from the column — this most often decides the thickness;
4. **Bending moment** at the column face, giving the steel area;
5. **Development length** available for the bars from the point of maximum moment.

Note from Set 2 Q92 that minimum tension steel in a **beam** follows a different rule — A_st/bd = 0.85/f_y — so the beam and slab minima must not be interchanged.

examTip.trick: A footing is designed as a slab, so it takes the **slab** minimum reinforcement: **0.12% of the gross area for Fe415/Fe500**, and 0.15% for Fe250.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slab minimum 0.12% (HYSD) / 0.15% (mild steel); BEAM minimum 0.85/f_y** (about 0.205% for Fe415). Different members, different minima — and the reason is the same in both cases: prevent a **sudden brittle failure on first cracking**, and control shrinkage and temperature cracking.

questions.stem: Length required for full transfer of bar stress to concrete is called:
questions.solution:
**Development length.**

It is the minimum embedded length of a bar needed for **bond** to transfer the bar's full force into the surrounding concrete. Derive it by equating the two:

> Force in the bar = (πφ²/4) × σ_s
> Bond resistance = (πφ · L_d) × τ_bd

Equating and cancelling:

> **L_d = φσ_s / (4τ_bd)**

The **4** comes from the ratio of the bar's cross-sectional area to its perimeter, which is why it cannot be anything else.

**Worked value** — Fe 415 in M20, deformed bars:
> τ_bd = 1.2 × 1.6 (the 60% increase for deformed bars) = 1.92 N/mm²
> L_d = φ × 0.87 × 415/(4 × 1.92) = **47φ**

Hence the familiar rules of thumb: about **47 diameters** for Fe 415 in M20, and **56φ** for Fe 500 in M20. Higher concrete grades shorten it; higher steel grades lengthen it.

**Distinguishing the terms in the options**, which is what the question tests:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Development length** | The **calculated** length needed to develop the bar's full design stress — the code term |
| **Bond length** | Loose synonym for the same idea; not the code term |
| **Anchorage length** | Length provided **at a bar end**, where bends and hooks may contribute |
| Equivalent length | Not a reinforcement term at all — it belongs to **column buckling** |

So (a) and (d) are near-synonyms in casual use, but **development length** is the defined quantity in IS 456, and option (c) belongs to a different topic entirely.

**Why it matters.** If a bar is not developed, it **pulls out of the concrete** and the member fails at a load far below its flexural capacity — a **bond failure**, brittle and sudden. Development length therefore governs:

- where bars may be **curtailed** — a bar must extend at least L_d beyond the point where it is no longer needed;
- the **anchorage into supports**;
- **lap lengths** in tension: the greater of L_d or 30φ, staggered and kept away from sections of maximum moment;
- the size of the **bend or hook** at a bar end.

IS 456 permits a standard bend or hook to count towards the anchorage: a **90° bend is worth 8φ** and a standard **U-hook 16φ**, which is how the full L_d is achieved in a shallow support where the straight length is insufficient.

The design bond stresses τ_bd (cl. 26.2.1.1) are **1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7 and 1.9 N/mm²** for M20 to M40, increased **60% for deformed bars** and a further 25% for bars in **compression** — the latter because a compressed bar bears on the concrete at its end as well as bonding along its length.

examTip.trick: Derive it from equilibrium: the bar's **tensile force** (πφ²/4)σ_s must be resisted by the **bond force** around its surface, πφL_d τ_bd. Equating gives **L_d = φσ_s/(4τ_bd)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Force in the bar equals bond around its surface — that IS the derivation.** τ_bd is increased **60% for deformed bars** and a further 25% in compression. Insufficient development length at supports and laps is a real and common detailing failure.

questions.stem: Power available continuously is:
questions.solution:
**Firm power** — also called **primary** or **dependable** power.

Firm power is the output a hydropower plant can guarantee **at all times**, and it is therefore governed by the **minimum flow** the river can be relied upon to provide:

> **Firm power = ηγQ_min H**

where Q_min is read from the **flow duration curve** at a high exceedance — commonly **Q₉₀ or Q₉₅**, the flow available 90 or 95% of the time.

The contrast with secondary power is the whole point:

| | **Firm (primary) power** | **Secondary power** |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | **Always** | **Only when surplus flow exists** |
| Based on | **Minimum dependable flow** (Q₉₀ / Q₉₅) | Flow above that minimum |
| Season in Nepal | Guaranteed even in the **dry season** | Abundant in the **monsoon** |
| Commercial value | **High** — can be contracted and relied on | Low — sold opportunistically or spilled |

**Why the distinction dominates Nepali hydropower economics.** A **run-of-river** scheme generates whatever the river carries at that moment, and Himalayan dry-season flows are a small fraction of monsoon flows. So its **firm power may be only 20 to 30% of installed capacity**, even though it produces abundantly for four months a year. The plant's nameplate rating therefore overstates what the system can depend on.

That gap is why:
- **storage** projects are valuable out of proportion to their capacity — they convert monsoon surplus into dry-season firm power;
- **pondage** is added wherever topography allows, to firm up at least the daily peak;
- Nepal exports surplus energy in the monsoon and has historically imported in the winter — a seasonal, not a total, deficit.

**How firm power is read off the flow duration curve.** The curve plots discharge against the percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded. At a fixed head each discharge converts to a power ordinate via P = ηγQH, turning it into a **power duration curve** — from which the firm power is read at the chosen reliability. A **steep** curve means a flashy river with little dependable flow; a **flat** one, well-sustained by snowmelt or baseflow, gives far more firm power for the same mean discharge.

Why the other options fail: **plant power** and **water power** are not standard terms in this classification. The related quantities are **installed capacity** (the nameplate rating), **average power** (energy ÷ time), and the factors linking them — **load factor** = average/peak and **capacity factor** = average/installed.

examTip.trick: **Firm (primary) power** is the power a plant can guarantee **at all times**, even in the driest year. **Secondary power** is the surplus available only when flows are good.
examTip.mnemonic: **Firm power is set by the DRIEST period, not the average** — which for a Nepali run-of-river plant means the dry-season low flow, often a small fraction of the installed capacity. That gap between firm and installed capacity is exactly what **storage or pondage** is built to close.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is wrong with respect to the strain energy method for finding deflection?
options: Deflection can be found only in the direction of load
Deflection can be found at any point in the desired direction
Deflection can be found only at the loaded point
Structure should be subjected to a single concentrated load
questions.solution:
**"Deflection can be found at any point in the desired direction" is the wrong statement.**

That is precisely what the strain energy method **cannot** do. By **Castigliano's second theorem**:

> **δ = ∂U/∂P**

The deflection obtained is the displacement **at the point where P is applied and in the direction of P**. The method differentiates the strain energy with respect to an *existing* load, so it can only report the movement of that load's point of application, along that load's line of action.

So the statements in options (a), (c) and (d) are all **true** of the method as stated, and (b) claims a freedom it does not have.

**How the limitation is overcome**, which is the useful part. To find a deflection where **no load acts**, or in a direction in which none acts, apply a **fictitious (dummy) load Q** there, carry it through the analysis, differentiate, and then set Q = 0:

> δ = [∂U/∂Q]_{Q→0}

That device — a dummy load applied purely to interrogate a displacement — is exactly the idea formalised in the **unit load method**, which is the practical tool:

> **δ = ∫ (Mm/EI) dx** for bending,  **δ = Σ(P·u·L/AE)** for trusses

where M and P are the real internal actions and m and u those caused by a **unit virtual load** placed at the point and in the direction whose displacement is wanted.

| Method | Unknown found | Restriction |
|---|---|---|
| **Castigliano (strain energy)** | δ = ∂U/∂P | **Only at, and along, an applied load** |
| **Unit load / virtual work** | δ = ∫Mm/EI dx | **Any point, any direction** |
| Moment area | δ, θ from the M/EI diagram | Best for simple beams |
| Conjugate beam | δ, θ as shear and moment of a fictitious beam | Simple beams |
| Macaulay's method | δ(x) by double integration | Beams with discontinuous loading |

So the honest summary is that Castigliano's theorem is elegant and quick where a load happens to sit at the point of interest, and the **virtual work method is the general one** — which is why the source's own note says that to find deflection in any direction, the virtual work method is used.

Note also **Castigliano's first theorem**, the converse: ∂U/∂δ = P, used to find a force from a known displacement, and the basis of the stiffness method.

A related restriction on both: they assume **linear elastic** behaviour and small deflections, so the principle of superposition holds. Neither applies once a member yields.

examTip.trick: The **unit load (virtual work) method** finds the deflection **at any chosen point, in any chosen direction** — you simply apply the virtual unit load there and in that direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **δ = Σ(PkL/AE) for a truss, ∫(Mm/EI)dx for a beam** — where k and m come from the **unit load** case. Compare **Castigliano (δ = ∂U/∂P)**, which gives the deflection only **where a real load acts**; for any other point you must add a dummy load first.

questions.stem: Stiffness for the free end if the far end is fixed is:
questions.solution:
**4EI/L.**

**Rotational stiffness** is the moment required to produce a **unit rotation** at an end, and it depends on how the **far** end is held:

| Far end | Stiffness at the near end |
|---|---|
| **Fixed** | **4EI/L** |
| **Hinged (pinned)** | **3EI/L** |

So a member whose far end is fixed is **4/3 times stiffer** than one whose far end is pinned — because the fixed far end resists the rotation that would otherwise be shed there.

**Why the two differ, and where the carry-over goes.** Apply a unit rotation at end A:
- With B **fixed**, a moment of 4EI/L is needed at A, and **half of it — 2EI/L — is carried over to B**. The **carry-over factor is ½**.
- With B **hinged**, B can rotate freely, so no moment develops there. The stiffness at A falls to 3EI/L, and the carry-over factor is **zero**.

Those two facts — **stiffness 4EI/L and carry-over ½** — are the entire arithmetic basis of the **moment distribution method**:

> **Distribution factor** at a joint = k_member / Σk at that joint

where k = 4EI/L for members fixed at the far end and 3EI/L for those pinned. The unbalanced moment at a joint is shared among the members in proportion to their stiffnesses, half of each share is carried over to the far end, and the process is repeated until the residuals are negligible.

Using the **modified stiffness of 3EI/L** for a member pinned at its far end is the standard shortcut that avoids having to carry moments over to a support that cannot resist them.

**The same coefficients appear in slope-deflection:**

> M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB

with the 2EI/L × 2θ_A term being the 4EI/L stiffness and the 2EI/L × θ_B term the carry-over.

**A note on the source explanation.** The answer sheet keys (a), which is correct, but its worked note discusses the **hinged** far-end case and quotes 3EI/L before adding the fixed case. The question asks for the far end **fixed**, so 4EI/L is right; the explanation buries it.

Related fixed-end moments, needed alongside the stiffnesses in any distribution: **wL²/12** for a UDL on a fixed-fixed span, **WL/8** for a central point load, and **wL²/8** or 3WL/16 respectively when the far end is pinned.

examTip.trick: Stiffness is the moment needed for **unit rotation**. **Far end FIXED: 4EI/L. Far end HINGED: 3EI/L.** The fixed case is stiffer because the far end resists.
examTip.mnemonic: **4EI/L fixed, 3EI/L hinged — and the CARRY-OVER factor is ½ for a fixed far end, ZERO for a hinged one.** Those four numbers are the whole basis of **moment distribution**: distribute in proportion to stiffness, then carry over half.

questions.stem: The size of a letter means the …… of the letter.
questions.solution:
**Height.**

In technical lettering the **size** of a letter is defined by its **height** — specifically the height of a **capital** letter, denoted **h**. Every other dimension of the character is then derived from h, which is what makes a lettering system consistent at any scale.

The standard proportions (IS 9609):

| Feature | Relation to h |
|---|---|
| **Capital height** | **h** — the nominal size |
| Lower-case height (x-height) | 0.7 h |
| **Line thickness** | **0.1 h** |
| Spacing between characters | 0.2 h |
| Minimum spacing between words | 0.6 h |
| Minimum spacing between baselines | 1.4 h |

The conventional **height-to-width ratio of a letter is about 7 : 5**, and the recommended nominal sizes follow a √2 progression to match the paper sizes: **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14 and 20 mm**.

**Why standardised lettering matters** — it is not a matter of neatness but of legibility after reproduction. A drawing is photocopied, scanned, faxed, reduced and printed, and lettering that is too fine or too tightly spaced becomes unreadable at each step. Hence the **minimum size** rule: characters must not be smaller than **2.5 mm** on the finished drawing, and dimensions and notes are usually 3.5 mm or larger.

That same √2 logic runs through the drawing standards, which is worth seeing as one system:

| Element | Progression |
|---|---|
| **Sheet sizes** | A0 → A4, each halved, ratio 1 : √2 |
| **Lettering heights** | 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm |
| **Line thicknesses** | Thin : thick ≈ 1 : 2, e.g. 0.35 and 0.7 mm |

So a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its proportions, and its lettering steps down to the next standard size while remaining legible.

**The types of lettering:** single-stroke (the standard for engineering drawings, vertical or inclined at 75°), Gothic, Roman and italic. **Single-stroke vertical capitals** are the norm because they are quick, unambiguous and reproduce well.
