Related conventions from the same standards: dimensions always in **millimetres** without repeating the unit, a **20 mm filing margin** on the left edge, the **title block** in the bottom right corner, and the projection method declared by symbol — **first angle** in Nepal and India.

examTip.trick: Lettering is specified by **height** because that is what determines legibility at a given reduction — the width follows from the height by a standard proportion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Standard heights 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm — each √2 times the last, matching the A-series paper progression.** So a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its lettering one standard size down and remains legible.

questions.stem: Function of a cross regulator in irrigation is:
options: To maintain the head for flow in the off-taking canal
To regulate the water supplies in the distributaries
questions.solution:
**To maintain the head for flow in the off-taking canal.**

A cross regulator is a gated structure built **across the parent canal**, just downstream of an offtake. By partly closing its gates it **raises the water level upstream of itself**, which is what gives the off-taking distributary the head it needs to draw its full supply.

That function is essential because of how irrigation is actually run. Canals supply distributaries **by rotation**, so a distributary must be able to draw its **full sanctioned discharge even when the parent canal is running at low supply**. Without a cross regulator, a parent canal running half full would leave the offtake sill too high above the water surface to command its share.

So the two structures work as a pair, and the distinction is worth being precise about:

| Structure | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Cross regulator** | **Across the parent canal**, downstream of the offtake | **Raises the level** in the parent canal to feed the offtake |
| **Head regulator (distributary head)** | At the **head of the offtaking canal** | **Controls the discharge** entering the offtake |

Option (c) describes the **head regulator's** job — regulating the supply into the distributary — which is why it is the tempting distractor. Option (b) describes a **canal escape**, which discharges surplus water out of the canal.

**The other functions a cross regulator serves**, which come as by-products of being a gated structure across the canal:
- Helps in **closing** the supply to the downstream reach for repair or inspection;
- Can be combined with a **road bridge** or a **canal fall** to save cost;
- Assists in **absorbing surplus energy** where combined with a fall;
- Provides a **measuring** section, since the gate opening and head relate to discharge.

**The wider family of canal structures**, each with one job:

| Situation | Structure |
|---|---|
| Raise level to feed an offtake | **Cross regulator** |
| Control discharge into an offtake | **Head / distributary regulator** |
| Ground steeper than canal slope | **Canal fall (drop)** |
| Dispose of surplus water | **Canal escape** |
| Canal crosses a natural drain | **Cross-drainage work** — aqueduct, syphon aqueduct, super passage, canal syphon |
| Deliver the sanctioned share to a field | **Canal outlet / module** |

Design points for the regulator itself: adequate **waterway** at full supply, a **cistern** to contain the hydraulic jump when the gates are partly open, **cut-offs and an impervious floor** designed against seepage by **Khosla's theory** with the exit gradient checked against piping, and gates with a hoisting arrangement accessible from a working platform.

examTip.trap: **Cross regulator** and **head regulator** are easily swapped. A **head** regulator controls flow **into an offtaking canal**; a **cross** regulator sits **across the parent canal**.
examTip.trick: The cross regulator's purpose is to **raise the water level upstream of itself**, so that the offtaking canal beside it can draw its full supply even when the parent canal is running low.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross regulator holds the LEVEL UP so the offtake can draw.** It also lets a reach be closed for maintenance, and it doubles as a road bridge across the canal.

questions.stem: Time value of money is the relation between:
questions.solution:
**Money and time.**

The time value of money is the principle that a sum available **today is worth more** than the same nominal sum in the future, because money in hand can be invested and earn a return. It is therefore a relation between an **amount** and the **point in time** at which it occurs.

Interest is the *mechanism* that quantifies the relation, and inflation is a *separate* effect — which is why options (a), (b) and (c) each capture only a part.

**Why it exists**, in order of importance:
1. **Earning capacity** — money invested now grows. This is the fundamental reason.
2. **Inflation** — purchasing power erodes over time.
3. **Risk and uncertainty** — a future receipt may not materialise.
4. **Preference for the present** — consumption now is valued above consumption later.

Note that inflation is only one contributor; the principle would hold even with zero inflation, because capital can still be put to work.

**The consequence for engineering economics** is that cash flows occurring at different times **cannot be added or compared directly**. They must first be brought to a common point in time using the discrete compounding factors:

| Factor | Formula | Converts |
|---|---|---|
| **Compound amount** (F/P) | (1 + i)^n | Present → future |
| **Present worth** (P/F) | 1/(1 + i)^n | Future → present |
| **Uniform series present worth** (P/A) | [(1+i)^n − 1]/[i(1+i)^n] | Annuity → present |
| **Capital recovery** (A/P) | i(1+i)^n/[(1+i)^n − 1] | Present → annuity |
| **Sinking fund** (A/F) | i/[(1+i)^n − 1] | Future → annuity |
| Gradient factors (P/G, A/G) | — | Arithmetic gradient series |

Everything else in the subject follows from these:

> **NPV** = Σ [C_t/(1 + i)^t] — accept if positive at the MARR
> **IRR** = the rate at which **NPV = 0** — accept if IRR ≥ MARR
> **B/C ratio** = discounted benefits ÷ discounted costs — accept if ≥ 1
> **EUAC** — equivalent uniform annual cost, for comparing unequal lives

**The distinction that catches candidates:** a **real** interest rate excludes inflation while a **nominal** rate includes it, related by (1 + i_nominal) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f). Cash flows must be discounted at a rate consistent with whether they are expressed in current or constant prices — mixing the two is a common and serious error in project appraisal.

Also note that **payback period** and the **accounting rate of return** ignore the time value of money altogether, which is exactly why they are unsound as investment criteria despite their popularity.

examTip.trick: The whole of engineering economics rests on one idea: **a rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year**, because it can be invested. Interest is the price of that difference.
examTip.mnemonic: **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ.** Everything else — NPV, IRR, annual worth, benefit–cost — is that relation applied to a stream of cash flows. And it is why comparing alternatives with **different lives** requires equal-life analysis or annual-worth comparison, never a raw total.

questions.stem: Snow load is calculated as:
questions.solution:
**S = μS₀.**

> **S = μ · S₀**

where
- **S** is the design snow load **on the roof**,
- **S₀** is the **ground** snow load — the load on a horizontal ground surface at that location,
- **μ** is the **shape coefficient**, depending on the roof geometry and on the character of the snow.

The structure of the formula is the point: a **site** quantity (S₀, from meteorological records) is converted into a **roof** quantity by a **geometric** factor (μ). Options (a) and (d) are dimensionally wrong for a load, and (c) inverts the relation.

**Why the shape coefficient is needed.** Snow does not sit on a roof the way it lies on the ground:

| Roof condition | Effect on μ |
|---|---|
| **Flat or low pitch** | μ ≈ 1.0 — snow accumulates fully |
| Pitch increasing | μ **falls** — snow begins to slide |
| **Pitch > about 50–60°** | μ → 0; snow load **need not be considered** |
| **Valleys, parapets, abrupt changes of level** | μ **> 1** — snow **drifts** and piles deeper than the nominal fall |
| Adjacent taller building | Local drift accumulation |

That last group is where snow-load failures actually happen. The **drift** cases produce loads well above the nominal, concentrated on a small area — a valley gutter between two pitched roofs, or the low roof beside a tall wall, can collect several times the flat-roof load. Uniform snow rarely collapses a roof; **unbalanced and drifted** snow does.

**Related figures examined alongside** (IS 875 Part 4): the snow load may be taken as about **2.5 N/m² per millimetre depth** of snow, so 100 mm of snow gives 250 N/m².

**How snow combines with the other roof loads.** Snow and live load are **not** added at full value, since they do not realistically coexist at their maxima — the more severe of the two is taken. The loads on a roof truss:

| Load | Source |
|---|---|
| **Dead** | Self-weight of truss, purlins, covering — IS 875 Part 1 |
| **Live (imposed)** | **0.75 kN/m²** for slope ≤ 10°, reduced 0.02 kN/m² per degree above | 
| **Snow** | **S = μS₀**; ignored for steep slopes — IS 875 Part 4 |
| **Wind** | IS 875 Part 3; often **suction** on a steep windward slope |

Wind is frequently the governing case for a light truss precisely because it acts as **suction** and can **reverse** the member forces — putting into tension what was designed for compression, and lifting sheeting off its fixings. That reversal must be checked separately, and it is why holding-down bolts and sheeting fasteners are so often the critical detail rather than the truss members themselves.

examTip.trick: **S = μ S₀** — the ground snow load S₀ multiplied by a **shape coefficient μ** that depends chiefly on the **roof slope**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steeper roof, smaller μ — above about 60° it is taken as zero, because the snow slides off.** Watch for **DRIFTING**, though: snow blown off one slope accumulates behind parapets and in valleys, so the local load can far exceed the uniform value. Snow governs many high-altitude designs in Nepal.

questions.stem: Formula for sudden expansion loss is:
questions.solution:
**(V₁ − V₂)²/2g.**

The loss at a sudden enlargement is governed by the **difference** of the two velocities, not by either one alone:

> **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g)**

where V₁ is the velocity in the **smaller** upstream pipe and V₂ in the **larger** downstream pipe.

**Why the difference appears.** At an abrupt enlargement the jet leaving the small pipe cannot follow the sudden change of boundary. It separates, and a region of **turbulent eddies** forms in the corner between the jet and the larger pipe wall. Energy is dissipated in that turbulence. Applying the **momentum** equation across the enlargement together with the energy equation — the loss is unknown in advance, so momentum must supply the extra relation — yields exactly the (V₁ − V₂)² form. It is one of the few minor losses that can be derived rather than measured.

**Two limiting cases** confirm the formula:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| **Discharge into a large reservoir** (V₂ → 0) | h_L = **V₁²/2g** — the whole velocity head is lost, i.e. **exit loss, k = 1.0** |
| **Gradual** enlargement (a diffuser) | Loss much smaller; the flow stays attached and pressure is recovered |

So option (a), V²/2g, is the **special case** of discharge into a reservoir — which is why it is the plausible distractor.

**The minor losses as a set**, all written as k·V²/2g except the enlargement:

| Feature | Loss |
|---|---|
| **Sudden enlargement** | **(V₁ − V₂)²/2g** |
| Sudden contraction | ≈ 0.5 V₂²/2g |
| **Entry** (reservoir → pipe) | **0.5 V²/2g** |
| **Exit** (pipe → reservoir) | **1.0 V²/2g** |
| Bell-mouthed entry | 0.04 V²/2g |
| 90° bend | 0.3 – 0.9 V²/2g |
| Gate valve, fully open | ≈ 0.2 V²/2g |

Note the **entry is half the exit** loss: at entry the flow contracts and re-expands, dissipating only part of the velocity head, whereas at exit the entire kinetic energy is destroyed in the still reservoir.

**The practical lesson** from the enlargement case: **make transitions gradual**. A diffuser with an included angle of about 7° recovers most of the pressure that an abrupt enlargement would waste, which is precisely why a turbine's **draft tube** is a gradually expanding conduit — it converts residual kinetic energy back into pressure instead of dumping it into eddies.

Minor losses are called "minor" only because they are usually small beside the friction loss in a long pipe; in a **short pipe with many fittings** they dominate, and neglecting them is then a serious error.

examTip.trick: This is one of the few loss coefficients that can be **derived** rather than measured — by combining the **momentum** and **energy** equations across the expansion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Special case: EXIT into a large tank (V₂ → 0) loses the ENTIRE velocity head** — the largest single minor loss in most systems, and unavoidable. Note that "minor" losses are **not minor in short pipework**: in a pump house they can dominate the total.

questions.stem: Thin hairline crack is also known as:
questions.solution:
**Crazing.**

Crazing is a network of **fine, shallow, interconnected hairline cracks** on a surface — resembling a spider's web or crocodile skin. The cracks are confined to the surface layer and do not penetrate the body of the material.

The term is used for three related surfaces:

| Material | Crazing appears as |
|---|---|
| **Glazed pottery and tiles** | Web of fine cracks in the **glaze**, from differential thermal movement between glaze and body |
| **Concrete** | Fine surface network, typically 5 to 75 mm across, in the **surface paste** |
| **Plaster and render** | Fine map cracking in the finishing coat |

**Causes in concrete and plaster** — all of them surface-drying phenomena:
- **Rapid drying** of the surface while the interior is still wet, so the skin shrinks against a restraining body. This is the dominant cause.
- **Over-trowelling**, which brings excess fines and water to the surface and creates a weak, shrinkage-prone laitance.
- **Too rich a mix** in the finishing coat.
- **Inadequate curing** — the single most common contributor.

**Why it matters, and why it usually doesn't.** Crazing is **aesthetic rather than structural**: the cracks are too shallow to affect strength or to admit water to the reinforcement. But it is a **symptom** — it signals that the surface dried too fast, which means the surface concrete is also weaker, more permeable and less abrasion-resistant than intended. So the crazing itself is harmless while what it indicates is not.

The remedy is preventive and cheap: **cure properly** (7 days minimum for OPC, kept continuously damp), avoid over-trowelling, protect fresh surfaces from sun and wind, and do not use an over-rich finishing mix.

**Distinguish it from the cracks that do matter:**

| Crack type | Depth | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| **Crazing** | **Surface only** | Aesthetic; a symptom of poor curing |
| **Plastic shrinkage** cracks | Shallow but wider, while concrete is fresh | Surface quality |
| **Drying shrinkage** cracks | Can be through-depth | Needs joints and distribution steel |
| **Structural (flexural, shear)** cracks | Through the section | **Serious** — indicates overload or under-design |
| **Corrosion** cracking | Along the line of bars, with rust staining | **Serious** — cover has failed |

IS 456 limits crack width to **0.3 mm** in ordinary exposure and 0.2 or 0.1 mm in aggressive conditions — limits aimed at the last two rows, not at crazing, which has no measurable width in that sense.

examTip.trick: **Crazing** is a network of fine, shallow, random hairline cracks in the surface layer only — caused by **surface shrinkage** drying faster than the body beneath.
examTip.mnemonic: **Crazing is cosmetic and shallow; STRUCTURAL cracks follow the stress pattern.** Reading the pattern diagnoses the cause: **vertical at midspan = flexure, diagonal near supports = shear, spiral = torsion, random map cracking = crazing or alkali-silica reaction.** Crack mapping is the cheapest structural investigation there is.

questions.stem: The top view of an orthographic drawing lies on:
questions.solution:
**HP** — the horizontal plane.

Orthographic projection uses three mutually perpendicular planes, and each view is projected onto the one facing it:

| View | Direction of viewing | Projected onto |
|---|---|---|
| **Top view (plan)** | From **above** | **HP** — horizontal plane |
| **Front view (elevation)** | From the **front** | **VP** — vertical plane |
| **Side view (end view)** | From the **side** | **PP** — profile plane |

The logic is that a view is cast on the plane **perpendicular to the direction of sight**: looking down, the rays are vertical, so they land on a horizontal plane.

**How the three views end up on one sheet.** The planes are then **rotated into a single plane** — the HP swung down about the XY line and the PP swung out — so that all three views lie flat on the paper. Where each view ends up depends on the projection convention:

| | **First angle** | **Third angle** |
|---|---|---|
| Object lies | **Between observer and plane** | **Plane between observer and object** |
| **Top view** | **Below** the front view | **Above** the front view |
| **Left side view** | **Right** of the front view | **Left** of the front view |
| Used in | **Nepal, India, Europe** (ISO) | USA, Canada, Australia |

The two are **mirror opposites**, which is why the convention must be declared in the **title block** by the standard truncated-cone symbol. A component read in the wrong convention comes out **mirror-imaged** and will be manufactured wrong — so never interpret an unfamiliar drawing without checking that symbol.

**Why only the first and third angles are used.** The two planes divide space into four quadrants, but in the **second and fourth** the views would **overlap** when the planes are rotated into one plane, making the drawing unreadable. Hence only the first and third are standardised.

Related conventions from the same standards: **visible edges** as continuous thick lines, **hidden edges** dashed, **centre lines** as thin chain lines, dimensions in **millimetres** without repeating the unit, a **20 mm filing margin** on the left edge, and the title block bottom right.

Where three views are insufficient, the further ones follow the same rule: **auxiliary views** are projected onto a plane parallel to an inclined face, and **sectional views** replace a view with a cut through the object, hatched at 45°.

examTip.trick: Orthographic projection uses three planes: the **HP (horizontal plane)** carries the **top view**, the **VP (vertical plane)** the **front view**, and the **PP (profile plane)** the **side view**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Top view on the HP; front view on the VP.** Then the arrangement differs by system: **FIRST angle puts the top view BELOW the front view; THIRD angle puts it ABOVE.** Every drawing must carry the projection symbol, because a drawing read in the wrong system is a mirror image.

questions.stem: What is the right face zenithal angle if the left face zenithal angle is 98°30′30″?
questions.solution:
**261°29′30″.**

When a theodolite is transited — the telescope reversed to change **face** — the vertical circle reading on the other face is the **explement** of the first:

> **Right face reading = 360° − Left face reading**

**Substituting:**
> 360°00′00″ − 98°30′30″

Borrowing to subtract:
> 359°59′60″ − 98°30′30″ = **261°29′30″** ✓

**Why the two faces are read at all.** Taking a reading on **both faces** and averaging **eliminates the instrumental errors that reverse sign on transiting**:

| Error | Eliminated by |
|---|---|
| **Collimation error** (line of sight not perpendicular to the horizontal axis) | **Face left / face right mean** |
| **Vertical circle index error** | Face left / face right mean |
| Horizontal axis not perpendicular to vertical axis (trunnion error) | Face left / face right mean |
| **Vertical axis not truly vertical** | **Not** eliminated — must be corrected by levelling |

That last row is the important caution: changing face removes most instrumental errors but **not** a badly levelled instrument, which is why careful levelling remains essential.

**Zenithal versus vertical angles**, which the question's wording depends on:

| Convention | Measured from | Horizontal sight reads |
|---|---|---|
| **Zenith angle** | The **zenith** (vertically up) | **90°** |
| Vertical angle (altitude) | The **horizontal** | 0° |

So a zenith angle of 98°30′30″ is a **depression** of 8°30′30″ below the horizontal — the sight is looking slightly downward. Modern total stations almost universally display **zenith angles**, because the reading is unambiguous and never negative.

**A check on the arithmetic.** The mean of the two face readings should give the corrected zenith angle:
> [98°30′30″ + (360° − 261°29′30″)]/2 = [98°30′30″ + 98°30′30″]/2 = 98°30′30″

which is consistent — as it must be for an instrument with no index error.

Related theodolite practice: the **method of repetition** for horizontal angles (reading the same angle several times, accumulating on the circle) and the **method of reiteration** for a round of angles at a station, both of which reduce reading and graduation errors in the same spirit as changing face.

examTip.trick: Face left and face right zenith angles are related by **ZA_right = 360° − ZA_left**. Here: 360° − 98°30′30″ = **261°29′30″** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **The two faces should sum to 360°; any departure is TWICE the collimation error.** That is why every precise angle is observed on **both faces and averaged** — it cancels the instrument's own faults automatically, without any adjustment.

questions.stem: Non-Nepali engineer definition according to NEC is:
options: Non-Nepali engineer working under engineering institutions
Nepali engineer working under engineering institutions
questions.solution:
**A non-Nepali engineer working under engineering institutions** — that is, a foreign national wishing to practise engineering in Nepal.

Such an engineer is registered in **Category C — Foreign Engineer**, and the requirements per the source are a **Bachelor's degree in engineering** with a **minimum of 10 years' experience** in the field.

The three registration categories of the Nepal Engineering Council:

| Category | Registrant | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **General Engineer** | The ordinary registration for a Nepali engineer holding a recognised degree, on passing the registration examination — what this syllabus leads to |
| **B** | **Professional Engineer** | The higher grade, requiring substantial professional experience beyond the degree |
| **C** | **Foreign Engineer** | A **non-Nepali** registered to practise in Nepal, normally for a specified project and period |

Options (b) and (d) describe **Nepali** engineers and so cannot define a *non-Nepali* one; option (a) names a mode of working, not a nationality.

**Why the category exists.** Large infrastructure projects in Nepal — hydropower, transmission lines, tunnels, major bridges — routinely involve foreign consultants and contractors bringing specialist expertise. Registration ensures that those engineers are **accountable to the same regulator and the same code of ethics** as Nepali practitioners, rather than working outside the professional framework. A Category C registration is typically **tied to a particular project and period**, which reflects that purpose.

**The statutory basis** is the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**, under which the Council:
- maintains the register and issues certificates of registration;
- conducts the **registration (license) examination**;
- recognises engineering qualifications and accredits programmes;
- regulates professional conduct, with power to **suspend or cancel registration** for misconduct.

**The point that matters most in practice:** registration is a **legal prerequisite to practising engineering in Nepal** — for a Nepali or a foreign national alike. Signing or certifying engineering work without it is an offence, not merely a professional irregularity.

Do not confuse the **Council (NEC)**, the statutory regulator, with the **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)**, a voluntary membership body — though the NEA's President and five of its elected engineers sit on the Council.

examTip.trick: The Council's Act defines categories of registration, including provision for **foreign nationals** practising in Nepal under prescribed conditions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Registration is what makes engineering a regulated profession in Nepal** — practising or signing drawings without it is an offence under the NEC Act 2055. Institutional and legal questions like this appear in every paper and are the cheapest marks available.

questions.stem: Settlement formula for cohesionless soil from a plate load test is:
questions.solution:
**S_f = S_p [B_f(B_p + 0.3)/B_p(B_f + 0.3)]².**

This is the companion to Q21 of this paper, and the two must be kept apart. The **same four options** appear in both questions, so the only way to answer either is to know which relation belongs to which quantity and which soil:

| Soil | **Bearing capacity** | **Settlement** |
|---|---|---|
| **Sand (cohesionless)** | q_f = q_p (B_f/B_p) | **S_f = S_p [B_f(B_p+0.3)/B_p(B_f+0.3)]²** |
| **Clay (cohesive)** | q_f = q_p | S_f = S_p (B_f/B_p) |

So option (a) is the **bearing capacity** relation for sand (Q21's answer), option (b) is a distractor with the widths inverted, and option (c) is the **bearing capacity** relation for clay.

**Why the sand settlement formula is so awkward.** The 0.3 m terms are dimensional constants derived from **Terzaghi and Peck's** empirical work — 0.3 m being the width of the standard 1 ft test plate. The important behaviour is what the expression *does*:

| B_f/B_p | Settlement ratio S_f/S_p |
|---|---|
| 2 | ≈ 1.6 |
| 5 | ≈ 2.6 |
| 10 | ≈ 3.0 |
| Very large | **→ 4.0** |

So the settlement ratio **tends to a limit of 4**, however wide the footing becomes. A footing on sand does **not** settle in proportion to its width — the increase tapers off.

**The contrast with clay is instructive**, and it is the reverse of the bearing-capacity behaviour:

- On **clay**, settlement grows **linearly** with width (S_f = S_p·B_f/B_p), because a wider footing stresses a deeper layer of compressible soil.
- On **sand**, settlement grows much more slowly, because sand's stiffness increases with depth and confining stress.

Meanwhile the bearing capacities behave oppositely: **rising with width in sand** (friction mobilised over a deeper zone) and **independent of width in clay** (q_u = 5.7c_u contains no B). The two tables are mirror images, which is what makes the pair memorable once seen together.

**The test's limitations**, which matter more than either formula:
- The plate influences only a shallow zone, roughly **twice its width**, so a **weak stratum below that depth is missed entirely** — the fundamental weakness.
- It gives **immediate** settlement only. For clay the long-term **consolidation** settlement, which usually governs, is not measured at all.
- It is unreliable in layered or non-uniform ground.

Hence a plate load test is used **alongside** borehole logs, SPT results and laboratory consolidation tests — never on its own, which is the point Q25 makes from the other direction.

examTip.trick: The settlement scaling for cohesionless soil is **S_f/S_p = [2B_f/(B_f + B_p)]²** in the simple form, and the fuller version with the 0.3 m term accounts for the plate size explicitly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Settlement scales differently from bearing capacity — and both differently again in clay.** Capacity in sand scales with B; capacity in clay does not scale at all; settlement scales by this squared ratio. Three rules, and the plate test needs all three.

questions.stem: What is the formula to compute dry density of soil?
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — each is a valid expression for dry density, written in terms of different measured quantities.

Dry density is the mass of **solids** per unit **total** volume:

> **γ_d = W_s / V**

The several forms exist because different tests measure different things, and each expression uses whatever is available:

| Expression | Uses | When it is convenient |
|---|---|---|
| **γ_d = γ/(1 + w)** | Bulk density and **water content** | The everyday field form — weigh a sample, find its moisture |
| **γ_d = (1 − n_a)Gγ_w/(1 + wG)** | **Air content** n_a, G, w | Compaction work, where air voids matter |
| **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e)** | **Void ratio** and G | Laboratory phase calculations |
| γ_d = Gγ_w(1 − n) | **Porosity** and G | Equivalent to the above |

So they are algebraically equivalent, related through the phase identities **Se = wG_s**, **n = e/(1+e)** and n_a = n(1 − S).

**A caution on option (c) as printed.** It reads (1 + w)Gγ_w/(1 + e), whereas the standard form is **Gγ_w/(1 + e)** — the (1 + w) factor converts dry density to **bulk** density, so as printed the expression is bulk density rather than dry density. The keyed answer of "all of the above" is nevertheless the intended one, since the source presents all three as dry-density formulae; treat (c) as **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e)**.

**Why dry density is the parameter that matters.** It is the measure of how **densely packed the solid skeleton** is, with the water excluded — and it is the skeleton that carries load. Consequently:

- **Compaction** is specified and verified in terms of dry density, as a percentage of the laboratory maximum from the **Proctor test**: typically **95% of MDD** for a subgrade, 98% for a base course.
- Bulk density is useless for that purpose, because it changes with moisture content without any change in packing.
- Strength, compressibility and permeability all correlate with dry density rather than bulk density.

**The zero-air-voids line**, which the n_a form leads to. Setting n_a = 0 gives the theoretical maximum:

> γ_d,max possible = Gγ_w/(1 + wG)

This plots as a curve on the compaction graph that **no compaction can reach or cross**, because air can never be entirely expelled. The Proctor curve approaches it but stays below — and if a plotted test point falls above the zero-air-voids line, the test or the specific gravity is wrong. It is the standard sanity check on a compaction test.

Field measurement of γ_d is by the **core cutter** (cohesive soils), **sand replacement** (any soil, the reference method) or a nuclear density gauge, always with a simultaneous moisture determination — since density alone means little unless the layer was compacted near its **optimum moisture content**.

verification.notes: Option (c) as printed reads (1+w)Gγw/(1+e), which is bulk density; the standard dry-density form is Gγw/(1+e). The source presents all three as dry-density expressions and keys 'all of the above', which is retained, with the discrepancy noted in the solution.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — several correct expressions for the same quantity are offered, and each is valid.
examTip.trick: **γ_d = γ/(1 + w) = G γ_w/(1 + e) = (1 − n) G γ_w.** All three follow from the phase diagram and from **eS = wG**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Derive from the phase diagram rather than memorising a list.** The one master relation **eS = wG** plus the definitions generates every other expression — which is far more reliable under exam pressure than recalling six formulae.

questions.stem: What is the minimum submergence that should be provided for a forebay of Q = 3.6 m³/s, D = 1.55 m?
questions.solution:
**1.3 m** (computed 1.19 m, so 1.3 m is adopted).

Two criteria are checked and the **larger** governs:

**Step 1 — velocity at the penstock intake:**
> V_p = Q/A_p = Q/(πD²/4)
> V_p = 3.6/(π × 1.55²/4) = 3.6/1.887 = **1.91 m/s**

**Step 2 — first criterion:**
> H_s > 1.5V_p²/(2g) = 1.5 × 1.91²/(2 × 9.81) = 5.47/19.62 = **0.28 m**

**Step 3 — second criterion:**
> H_s > 0.5 V_p (D_p)^{0.5} = 0.5 × 1.91 × 1.55^{0.5} = 0.5 × 1.91 × 1.245 = **1.19 m**

**Step 4 — take the greater:**
> H_s = **1.19 m → adopt 1.3 m** ✓

Note that the second criterion governs by a factor of more than four, so computing only the first would give 0.28 m and land on option (a) — the trap.

**What submergence is for.** The penstock intake must be deep enough below the forebay water surface that the flow entering it cannot draw **air** down with it. If the submergence is inadequate:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Air-entraining vortex** forms at the surface | Air is sucked into the penstock |
| Air pockets in the conduit | **Reduced discharge**; the effective area falls |
| Air reaching the turbine | **Vibration, noise, loss of efficiency**, possible damage |
| Intermittent air slugs | **Pressure surges** in the penstock |

So the submergence requirement is fundamentally an **anti-vortex** criterion, and it is why forebays are made deeper than the flow alone would demand.

**Where the forebay sits in the waterway**, since the question presupposes it:

> Intake → gravel trap → **settling basin** → headrace canal or tunnel → **forebay** → surge tank → **penstock** → turbine → draft tube → tailrace

The forebay's functions are to provide a **small balancing storage** (a few minutes to a few hours of flow), to give sediment a final chance to settle, to house the **trash rack** and the penstock intake gate, and to provide a **spillway** so surplus water can be discharged when the turbine load drops.

**Complementary anti-vortex measures** used alongside adequate submergence: a **bell-mouthed intake** (which also cuts the entry loss to k ≈ 0.04 against 0.5 for a sharp edge), anti-vortex baffles or a floating raft, and keeping the approach flow symmetrical so no swirl develops before the intake.

The same submergence logic applies to **pump sumps**, where inadequate submergence causes the pump to draw air and lose suction — the pumping equivalent of the same failure.

examTip.trick: **Submergence** is the depth of water above the intake that prevents an **air-entraining vortex** forming and drawing air into the penstock.
examTip.mnemonic: **Insufficient submergence → a free vortex forms → air is drawn into the penstock → loss of capacity, vibration and CAVITATION at the turbine.** The remedies are greater submergence or **anti-vortex devices** — a floating raft, splitter plate or curtain wall.

questions.stem: For given two hinged semicircular arches A, B and C of radii 5 m, 7.5 m and 10 m respectively, carrying a concentrated crown load W, the ratio of horizontal thrust at their supports will be:
questions.solution:
**1 : 1 : 1** — the thrust is the same in all three.

For a two-hinged **semicircular** arch carrying a **concentrated load W at the crown**, the horizontal thrust is

> **H = W/π**

The radius does not appear. So all three arches develop the same thrust, W/π ≈ 0.318W, and the ratio is 1 : 1 : 1.

**Why R cancels.** The thrust comes from the compatibility condition for a two-hinged arch:

> H = ∫(M·y·ds/EI) / ∫(y²·ds/EI)

For a semicircular arch, both y and ds scale with **R** — y = R sin θ and ds = R dθ. Working through, the numerator carries R³ and the denominator R³, so **R cancels completely**, leaving a result that depends only on the load and the shape (semicircular), not on the size.

That is a **dimensional argument** as much as an algebraic one: H must have the units of force, and the only force available is W. With no other length in the problem to combine with, H can only be a numerical multiple of W — here 1/π. Recognising that settles the question without any integration.

**Contrast with the UDL case**, where the same reasoning gives a different answer:

| Loading on a two-hinged semicircular arch | Horizontal thrust |
|---|---|
| **Concentrated load W at crown** | **H = W/π** — independent of R |
| UDL of w per unit length over the whole span | H = **4wR/(3π)** — proportional to R |
| UDL over **half** the span | H = 2wR/(3π) |

With a **UDL**, w has units of force per length, so a length must appear to give H the units of force — and R is the only one available. Hence H ∝ wR there but is independent of R for a point load. The dimensional check predicts both results.

**The general principle about arch thrust**, from the three-hinged case H = M_c/y_c: the thrust is **inversely proportional to the rise**. A shallow arch develops enormous horizontal thrust, which is why flat arches need massive abutments or a tie rod, and why the arch form suits a **narrow gorge with sound rock** abutments above all. For a semicircular arch the rise is fixed at R, and the two R-dependencies cancel for a point load.

Recall also that the thrust is what makes an arch efficient: it **subtracts** from the free-span beam moment at every section, so an arch carries the same load with far smaller bending moments than a beam — and where the **line of thrust coincides with the arch axis** the bending moment vanishes altogether.

examTip.trick: For a two-hinged **semicircular** arch under a given load pattern, the horizontal thrust depends on the **shape** rather than the absolute size — so geometrically similar arches give the **same ratio**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Geometric similarity means the thrust COEFFICIENT is the same; only the scale changes.** That is a general and useful property — it is why non-dimensional coefficients (K_a, C_d, N_c, Fr) exist at all, and why one chart can serve every size of structure.

questions.stem: Which percentile value of CBR is used for design of a road with more than 20 million ESAL as recommended by DoR?
questions.solution:
**90%.**

Subgrade CBR is never uniform along a road, so a **percentile** of the measured values is adopted for design. The percentile chosen rises with the traffic, because a heavily trafficked road can less afford a weak stretch:

| Design traffic | CBR percentile |
|---|---|
| Up to 2 million ESAL | **80th** |
| 2 – 20 million ESAL | **85th** |
| **More than 20 million ESAL** | **90th** |

**What the percentile means, and why it is counter-intuitive.** The **90th percentile CBR is the value exceeded by 90% of the samples** — that is, a **low** value, near the weak end of the distribution, not a high one. Taking a higher percentile therefore means designing for a **weaker** subgrade, hence a **thicker** pavement and a more conservative design.

That is the right direction: on a road carrying 20 million standard axles, a soft patch that fails early is far more costly to repair, and disrupts far more traffic, than the extra thickness would have cost to build.

**Where CBR sits in the design chain:**

> **Soaked CBR** (4 days) → subgrade strength → with **CSA** → pavement composition from the IRC 37 / DoR catalogue

and the traffic side:

> **CSA = 365 × A × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r × F × D**

where A is the initial commercial vehicles per day, r the growth rate, n the design life, **F the vehicle damage factor** and **D the lane distribution factor** (0.4 for a four-lane single carriageway).

**Two points about the CBR value itself** that matter more than the percentile:

1. It must be the **soaked** CBR — four days' immersion — because the monsoon saturates the subgrade and that is the condition the pavement must survive. A dry-season CBR flatters the subgrade and the pavement will rut in its first wet season.
2. The **higher of the 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm** penetration values is reported, the standard loads being **1370 kg** and **2055 kg** respectively against a crushed-stone reference.

Typical values: soft clay 2–5%, silty or sandy subgrade 5–10%, good granular subgrade 10–20%, sub-base 20–30%, granular base above 80%.

For **mechanistic** design the CBR is converted to a **resilient modulus**:
> M_R = 10 × CBR for CBR ≤ 5%,  M_R = 17.6 × CBR^{0.64} for CBR > 5%

which then feeds a layered elastic analysis checking the two critical strains — **vertical compressive strain on the subgrade** (controlling rutting) and **horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer** (controlling fatigue cracking).

examTip.trick: The **design percentile rises with the traffic**, because a heavily trafficked road cannot afford weak spots: **60th percentile for light traffic, 75th for medium, 90th for heavy (over 20 msa)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Heavier traffic → higher percentile → design for a WEAKER subgrade value → thicker pavement.** The percentile is chosen from the *distribution* of CBR values along the alignment, so the number of tests matters as much as the values.

questions.stem: What is the impact value of aggregate if total weight is 300 gm and weight retained on 2.36 mm sieve is 180 gm?
questions.solution:
**40%.**

The **aggregate impact value** is the percentage of the sample that is **crushed fine enough to pass** the 2.36 mm sieve after the standard blows:

> **AIV = W₂/(W₁ + W₂) × 100**

where W₂ is the fraction **passing** 2.36 mm and (W₁ + W₂) the total sample.

**Step 1 — find the fraction passing.** The question gives the weight **retained**, so subtract:
> Passing = 300 − 180 = **120 g**

**Step 2 — compute:**
> AIV = 120/300 × 100 = **40%** ✓

The trap is answering with 180/300 = 60%, or overlooking that "retained" must be converted to "passing" first. The impact value measures the **fines produced**, so it is always the passing fraction.

**The test** (IS 2386 Part 4): aggregate of 12.5 to 10 mm size fills a cylindrical measure; a **13.5 to 14 kg hammer** falls freely through **380 mm**, **15 times**; the crushed sample is then sieved on 2.36 mm.

**Permissible limits** — a **lower** value means a tougher aggregate:

| Use | Maximum AIV |
|---|---|
| **Wearing course** | **30%** |
| Bituminous macadam | 35% |
| WBM base course | 40% |
| Cement concrete (other than wearing surfaces) | 45% |

So the 40% aggregate in this question is fit for a **WBM base course** but **not for a wearing course**.

**Distinguishing the aggregate tests**, which is examined as often as the arithmetic:

| Test | Measures | Loading |
|---|---|---|
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | **Hammer, 15 blows** |
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradual** load | 40 tonnes applied over 10 minutes |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | Resistance to **wear and attrition** | Drum with steel spheres, 500 revolutions |
| Soundness | Resistance to **weathering** | Sulphate crystallisation cycles |
| Flakiness / elongation | Particle **shape** | Gauges |
| Polished stone value | Resistance to **polishing** — skid resistance | Accelerated polishing machine |

Impact and crushing values usually agree closely, and IS permits the **impact test as a substitute** for the crushing test since it is quicker and needs simpler apparatus.

Note the different sieve in each: **2.36 mm** for impact and crushing, **1.7 mm** for Los Angeles abrasion — which is what Q70 of this paper uses.

examTip.trick: **AIV = (weight passing the 2.36 mm sieve ÷ total weight) × 100.** Substitute the two weights the question gives and read off the percentage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Limits: 30% maximum for WEARING surfaces, 45% for other concrete** — the same 30/45 split as the aggregate crushing value. Four durability tests, four different demands: **impact = shock, crushing = gradual load, LA abrasion = wear, soundness = weathering.**

questions.stem: In an LA abrasion test, 1.88 kg out of 5 kg passed through the 1.7 mm sieve. The aggregate is then suitable for:
questions.solution:
**Bituminous penetration macadam.**

**Step 1 — compute the abrasion value.** It is the percentage worn away, i.e. the fraction **passing** the 1.7 mm sieve:

> LA abrasion value = 1.88/5 × 100 = **37.6%**

**Step 2 — check against the permissible limits.** A **lower** value means a tougher aggregate, so the aggregate is fit for any layer whose limit **exceeds** 37.6%:

| Pavement layer | Max. permissible abrasion | 37.6% acceptable? |
|---|---|---|
| WBM sub-base | 60% | Yes |
| WBM base with bituminous surfacing | 50% | Yes |
| Bituminous bound macadam | 50% | Yes |
| WBM surfacing course | 40% | Yes |
| **Bituminous penetration macadam** | **40%** | **Yes** ✓ |
| Bituminous surface dressing, cement concrete surface | 35% | **No** |
| Bituminous concrete surface course | 30% | **No** |

So 37.6% passes for **penetration macadam** (limit 40%) but **fails** for surface dressing (35%) and for a bituminous concrete surface course (30%). Options (a) and (c) are therefore excluded, and (d) is the highest-quality use the aggregate qualifies for.

**The pattern in that table is the point worth carrying:** the permissible abrasion **tightens as you move up through the pavement**, from 60% in the sub-base to 30% at the wearing surface. That is the economic logic of a layered pavement — the best material is reserved for the top, where wear, polishing and weather actually attack it, and progressively cheaper material is used below where only load-spreading is required.

**Why wear resistance matters most at the surface.** The wearing course is in direct contact with tyres, so abrasion there determines how long the **surface texture** survives — and with it the **skid resistance**. An aggregate that abrades quickly polishes smooth, and a polished surface loses friction in the wet. That is a safety failure, not merely a maintenance one, which is why the **polished stone value** is specified alongside the abrasion value for surfacing aggregate.

**The test** (IS 2386 Part 4): a graded sample with a charge of **steel spheres** is rotated in a hollow drum for **500 revolutions** at 30 to 33 rpm. An internal shelf lifts and drops the charge each revolution, so the sample suffers both **impact and grinding** — which is why the Los Angeles test is regarded as the most representative single measure of aggregate toughness.

Note the sieve: **1.7 mm** for LA abrasion, against **2.36 mm** for the impact and crushing tests used in Q69.

examTip.trick: **LA abrasion value = (1.88/5) × 100 = 37.6%.** Then match against the permitted limit for each type of construction — the coarser, lower-grade layers accept a higher value.
examTip.mnemonic: **LA limits: 30% for bituminous wearing courses, 40% for bituminous base courses, 50% for WBM sub-base.** So a marginal aggregate may be unusable at the surface and perfectly acceptable lower down — which matters greatly where good stone is expensive to haul.

questions.stem: The pressure of the gas in a cylindrical chamber is P₀. The vertical force exerted by the gas on its hemispherical end is:
questions.solution:
**πP₀R².**

The force a uniform pressure exerts on a **curved** surface, resolved in any one direction, equals the pressure multiplied by the **projected area** of that surface on a plane perpendicular to that direction:

> **F = P₀ × A_projected**

A hemisphere of radius R projects onto a **circle** of radius R, so

> A_projected = **πR²**
> **F = πP₀R²** ✓

**Why the projected area and not the curved area.** The curved surface area of a hemisphere is 2πR², which is where option (b) comes from — the standard trap. But pressure acts **normal to the surface at every point**, and on a hemisphere those normals point in all directions. Resolving each elemental force in the axial direction and integrating, the components perpendicular to the axis **cancel by symmetry**, and the axial components sum to exactly P₀ × πR².

The projected-area rule is simply the shortcut for that integration, and it is worth trusting: it works for any curved surface and any direction.

The same rule in its general form for hydrostatics:

| Component | Equals |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal force on a curved surface** | Pressure force on the **vertical projection** of the surface |
| **Vertical force on a curved surface** | **Weight of the fluid** above the surface (real or imagined) |

For a **gas**, weight is negligible and the pressure is uniform throughout, which is why the simple P₀ × A form applies here without a depth term.

**Where this calculation is used:**

- **Pressure vessel ends.** The axial force πP₀R² on a hemispherical or dished end is what the shell must carry in tension, and it is the basis of the **longitudinal stress** in a cylinder: σ_L = P₀R/2t, from equating πP₀R² to the shell area 2πRt.
- The **hoop stress** in the same cylinder is twice as large, σ_h = P₀R/t, obtained from a diametral section — which is why a pressurised pipe splits **along its length** rather than across it, and why a **hemispherical end is the efficient shape**: it needs only half the thickness of the cylindrical shell.
- **Thrust blocks** on penstock bends resist exactly this kind of resolved pressure force.

A useful check on the answer: the force must be the same as on a **flat** circular end cap of the same radius, since both have the same projection. The shape of the closure changes the *stresses in it* but not the total axial thrust the shell must carry.

examTip.trick: The vertical force on a curved surface equals the **pressure times the PROJECTED area** onto a horizontal plane. For a hemispherical or curved end of radius R, the projection is a circle of area **πR²**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always use the PROJECTED area for a pressure force on a curved surface — never the developed surface area.** For a **gas** the weight term is negligible, so it is simply p × projected area; for a **liquid**, the vertical component is the weight of the fluid above, real or imaginary.

questions.stem: Calculate the RL for the top of a guide bund, given bed level = 113 m, maximum flood depth = 5 m, maximum size of floating debris = 0.2 m, Q = 1600 m³/s and return period = 100 years.
questions.solution:
**120 m.**

Build the level up term by term from the river bed:

| Component | Level |
|---|---|
| RL of bed | 113.0 |
| **+** maximum flood depth | + 5.0 → **high flood level 118.0** |
| **+** freeboard | + **1.5** |
| **RL of top of guide bund** | **= 119.5 ≈ 120 m** ✓ |

A **freeboard of about 1.5 m** is the standard allowance for a guide bund, covering wave action, wind set-up, surges and the uncertainty in the estimated design flood.

**Note which data are relevant and which are not.** The question supplies Q = 1600 m³/s, a 100-year return period and a 0.2 m debris size, but **none of them enters this calculation**:

- **Q and the return period** were used to derive the maximum flood depth of 5 m, which is given directly — so they are already accounted for. They would matter if the flood level had to be computed, or for **Lacey's waterway** P = 4.75√Q = 190 m and the **scour depth**.
- The **debris size** matters for the freeboard *rationale* and for trash clearance, but 1.5 m already covers it.

Recognising redundant data is part of the skill: an examination numerical often supplies more than is needed, and hunting for a use for every figure leads to the wrong answer.

**Why the freeboard cannot be omitted.** Overtopping an earthen guide bund erodes its crest and downstream face and can breach it within minutes — and a breached guide bund lets the river outflank the structure it was protecting, which is the failure mode the whole arrangement exists to prevent.

**The rest of the guide bund design**, for context:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Upstream length** | **1.0 to 1.5 L** (L = waterway length) |
| **Downstream length** | **0.2 to 0.4 L** |
| Bell mouth (curved head) radius | ≈ 0.45 L; sweep 120°–145° upstream, 45°–90° downstream |
| Side slopes | 2H : 1V, **stone pitched** |
| Toe protection | **Launching apron** — gabions or loose stone |
| **Freeboard** | **≈ 1.5 m** |

The **launching apron** is sized from **Lacey's scour depth** R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}, with the design scour taken as a multiple of R — deepest, at 2.0 to 2.5 R, at the **nose** of the bund where the flow attacks hardest. The apron contains enough stone to armour the face of the scour hole as it launches down at about 2H : 1V.

So the two calculations bracket the structure: **freeboard fixes how high it must be, scour depth fixes how deep its protection must reach.**

examTip.trick: **Top of guide bund = maximum flood level + afflux + freeboard + wave allowance.** Add the components the question supplies, in order.
examTip.mnemonic: **Freeboard is never a single number — it is a SUM of allowances**: afflux (the upstream rise the structure itself causes), wave run-up, settlement of the embankment, and a margin. The same logic applies to dam freeboard, canal freeboard and bridge soffit levels.

questions.stem: Calculate Lane's creep length, given u/s cut-off = 5 m, floor length = 54 m and d/s cut-off = 8 m.
questions.solution:
**44 m.**

**Lane's weighted creep theory** does not treat horizontal and vertical creep as equally effective. It weights **vertical creep three times** as heavily as horizontal — equivalently, it divides the horizontal length by 3:

> **L_w = L/3 + 2(d₁ + d₂)**

**Substituting:**
> L_w = 54/3 + 2(5 + 8)
> L_w = 18 + 26 = **44 m** ✓

Each cut-off contributes **twice** its depth, because the water travels down one face and up the other.

**The three seepage theories, and how they differ**, which is the real content of the question:

| Theory | Treatment of creep | Weighted creep length |
|---|---|---|
| **Bligh (1910)** | Horizontal and vertical **equally** effective | L = b + 2d₁ + 2d₂ + … |
| **Lane (1935)** | **Vertical 3× more effective** than horizontal | **L_w = b/3 + 2Σd** |
| **Khosla (1936)** | Potential flow theory; gives the **exit gradient** | From flow net with correction factors |

So Bligh's method applied to the same data would give 54 + 26 = **80 m** — which is option (c), the trap for anyone using the wrong theory. Note how large the difference is: 44 m against 80 m, nearly a factor of two, purely from the weighting.

**Why Lane's weighting is closer to reality.** Bligh's assumption that a metre of horizontal floor is as effective as a metre of vertical cut-off is simply wrong — **vertical cut-offs are far more effective** at lengthening the seepage path and cutting the exit gradient. Lane's factor of 3 is an empirical correction in the right direction, derived from studying dams that had and had not failed.

**Why Khosla's theory superseded both.** Neither Bligh nor Lane can compute the **exit gradient**, and it is the exit gradient — not the creep length — that actually governs **piping** failure at the downstream end:

> G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)

compared against the critical hydraulic gradient (≈ 1.0) with a factor of safety of **4 to 5**. Khosla also showed that the head loss is **not uniform** along the creep path, contradicting the central assumption of both earlier theories.

Bligh's and Lane's methods survive as **quick checks** and in examinations; Khosla's is what a barrage floor is actually designed by. All three exist to answer the same question: is the seepage path long enough that water emerging at the downstream toe cannot carry soil particles with it and start progressive erosion back under the structure?

examTip.trick: **Lane's weighted creep: L_w = ΣV + (1/3)ΣH** — vertical creep counts **three times** as effective as horizontal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh weighted them EQUALLY (and was wrong); LANE weighted vertical 3:1; KHOSLA abandoned creep and solved the actual flow.** Khosla showed safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT** and the **downstream cut-off** — which is why a d/s cut-off is worth far more than extra floor length.

questions.stem: A 1 kN·m clockwise couple acts at the midspan of a simply supported beam of span 1 m. The support reactions are:
options: 1 kN upward at A, 1 kN downward at B
1 kN downward at A, 1 kN upward at B
2 kN upward at A, 2 kN downward at B
2 kN downward at A, 2 kN upward at B
questions.solution:
**1 kN downward at A and 1 kN upward at B.**

**Taking moments about B** (anticlockwise positive), with the applied couple clockwise:
> R_A × 1 + 1 = 0
> **R_A = −1 kN**, i.e. **1 kN downward**

**Taking moments about A:**
> 1 − R_B × 1 = 0
> **R_B = +1 kN**, i.e. **1 kN upward**

**Check ΣV = 0:** −1 + 1 = 0 ✓ — as it must be, since a couple has **no net force**.

**The key insight** is that last check. A couple applies a **pure moment with zero resultant force**, so the two reactions must be **equal and opposite** — forming a couple of their own that balances the applied one:

> **R = M/L**, one up and one down

Here M = 1 kN·m and L = 1 m, so R = 1 kN. Options (c) and (d) violate nothing about direction but get the magnitude wrong; the sign pair in (a) is reversed.

**Note that the position of the couple along the span does not affect the reactions.** Whether it acts at midspan, at a quarter point or anywhere else, the reactions remain M/L up and down — because moments about either support give the same equation. What the position *does* change is the **bending moment diagram**.

**The bending moment diagram** for this beam, taking the couple at midspan:

| Section | Bending moment |
|---|---|
| At A | 0 |
| Just left of midspan | R_A × 0.5 = **−0.5 kN·m** |
| Just right of midspan | **+0.5 kN·m** — a **jump of 1 kN·m** across the couple |
| At B | 0 |

So the diagram is two straight lines with a **step discontinuity equal to the applied couple** at the point where it acts. The shear force, meanwhile, is **constant at 1 kN** throughout — because R_A is the only transverse force to the left of any section.

That step is the signature of an applied moment, and it is worth contrasting with the two other loading types:

| Applied action | Shear diagram | Moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **Step** | Kink (change of slope) |
| **Couple** | No change | **Step** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |

Recall the companion result from Set 4 Q61: a couple transmits its **full moment undiminished** to every section beyond its point of application, because a couple has no lever arm to grow with distance. That is why the moment here is ±0.5 kN·m rather than growing along the span.

examTip.trick: A couple has **no net vertical force**, so the two reactions must be **equal and opposite** — a couple of reactions balancing the applied couple. Magnitude = **M/L = 1/1** per the span given.
examTip.mnemonic: **A couple produces reactions that form a COUPLE — equal, opposite, and independent of where along the span it is applied.** It **steps the bending moment diagram by M** and leaves the **shear diagram unchanged** — the exact reverse of a point load.

questions.stem: Calculate the power available, given H = 423.5 m, head loss = 2.5 m, Q = 0.9 m³/s and η = 85%.
questions.solution:
**3159.45 kW.**

**Step 1 — net head.** Subtract the losses from the gross head:
> H_net = 423.5 − 2.5 = **421.0 m**

**Step 2 — power:**
> **P = η γ Q H_net**
> P = 0.85 × 9.81 × 0.9 × 421.0
> P = **3159.45 kW**

Using γ = 9.81 kN/m³ gives the answer directly in kilowatts, which is the neatest way to keep the units straight.

**The two things to get right**, and both are what the distractors test:

1. **Subtract the head loss.** Using the gross head of 423.5 m instead of the net 421.0 m would give 3178 kW — close enough to be plausible, which is why the step matters. Only the **net** head does useful work; the 2.5 m is dissipated in friction in the waterway.
2. **Watch the units.** Options (b), (c) and (d) are the same number in the wrong magnitude — W, MW and a factor of ten. A useful sanity check: a 0.9 m³/s flow under 421 m of head is a **small hydropower plant**, so a few thousand kilowatts is the expected order. 3159 W would be a domestic kettle and 3159 MW larger than any plant in Nepal.

**Reading the numbers.** A head of 423 m with a discharge of under 1 m³/s is a classic **high-head, low-flow** Nepali scheme:

| Feature | Implication |
|---|---|
| Head **> 250 m** | **High head** plant |
| Turbine | **Pelton** — specific speed N_s = N√P/H^{5/4} falls in the 10–35 band |
| Small Q, large H | Small intake, tunnel and penstock for the power obtained — the economic advantage of the terrain |
| Capacity ~3.2 MW | **Small hydro** (1–10 MW) |

That combination is exactly why high-head sites are attractive: the same power needs far less water, hence smaller and cheaper waterworks.

**The accompanying difficulties**, which follow from the same figures: very **high pressure** in the penstock (thickness from t = pD/2σ, including the water-hammer rise, with a surge tank to limit it), and severe **abrasion** of the runner by hard Himalayan sediment — damage that rises steeply with head, which is why the settling basin must remove particles down to about **0.1 mm** for a Pelton machine.

Note the distinction between this **instantaneous power** and **energy**: annual energy is P × capacity factor × 8760 hours, and for a run-of-river scheme the capacity factor may be only 40 to 60% because dry-season flows are a fraction of monsoon flows. The **firm power**, read from the flow duration curve at Q₉₀, may be lower still.

examTip.trick: **Net head = gross head − losses = 423.5 − 2.5 = 421 m.** Then **P = ρgQH_net × η**, applying the efficiency the question gives.
examTip.mnemonic: **P ≈ 9.81 Q H_net η kW.** Always use the **NET** head — subtracting the penstock and intake losses. And check the plausibility: 0.9 m³/s at 421 m is a classic Nepali high-head, low-flow scheme, which means a **Pelton** turbine.

questions.stem: Morning glory is the:
options: Special flared inlet of the shaft spillway of a dam of very small height
Special flared inlet of the shaft spillway of a large dam project
Horizontal tunnel constructed in a shaft spillway across the body of a gravity dam to carry surplus reservoir water to the d/s river
Horizontal tunnel constructed in a shaft spillway of an earthen dam through its foundation to carry surplus reservoir water to the d/s river
questions.solution:
**The specially flared inlet of the shaft spillway of a large dam project.**

A **morning glory spillway** — also called a **bell-mouth** or glory-hole spillway — takes its name from the flower: the inlet is a **flared, trumpet-shaped funnel** at the reservoir surface, into which water can enter **around its entire circumference**. From there it drops down a **vertical shaft** and is carried away by a horizontal tunnel to the downstream river.

The options are distinguished by two things — **what part of the structure is named**, and **what size of dam**:

| Option | Describes |
|---|---|
| (a) | The right component, but a **very small** dam — a morning glory is used on **large** projects |
| **(b)** | **The flared inlet of a shaft spillway on a large dam** ✓ |
| (c), (d) | The **horizontal tunnel**, not the inlet — that is the tunnel or conduit portion, a different part of the same spillway |

So (c) and (d) name the wrong component, and (a) the wrong scale.

**Why the flared shape.** The circular crest gives an enormous **crest length in a small plan area** — the whole circumference discharges, so a modest diameter passes a large flood. The bell mouth is profiled so the nappe stays attached, avoiding sub-atmospheric pressure and cavitation, in exactly the same way an **ogee** profile follows the lower nappe of a freely falling jet.

**Its characteristic drawback**, and the reason it is not used more widely: the discharge **does not increase much once the shaft is running full**. At low heads it behaves as a weir, with Q ∝ H^{3/2}; once submerged it behaves as an **orifice or pipe**, with Q ∝ H^{1/2}. So the rating curve **flattens off**, and a flood larger than anticipated raises the reservoir level sharply without passing much more water. An **emergency spillway** is therefore normally provided alongside.

**When a shaft spillway is chosen:** where there is **no suitable abutment or saddle** for a conventional side-channel or chute spillway — a narrow gorge with steep rock walls — or where the spillway must be located away from the dam body. It is common with **earthfill and rockfill** dams, which cannot be overtopped and so need a spillway in separate ground.

The best-known example, cited in the source, is the **Monticello Dam** spillway in Napa Valley, California.

**The spillway types**, for orientation:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ogee (overflow)** | Profile follows the nappe; the standard for concrete dams |
| **Chute (trough)** | Open channel down a hillside; suits embankment dams |
| **Side channel** | Crest parallel to the channel; where the gorge is narrow |
| **Shaft (morning glory)** | **Circular bell-mouth inlet, vertical shaft, horizontal tunnel** |
| **Siphon** | Runs full, self-priming; Q ∝ √H (Set 1 Q4) |
| Duckbill / labyrinth | Extended crest length in a limited width |

examTip.trick: A **morning glory (shaft) spillway** is a flared circular inlet leading to a vertical shaft and a tunnel — used where there is no room for a conventional overflow section.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compact, but it has a hard capacity ceiling: once the shaft runs full it CHOKES and further rise in reservoir level gains almost no extra discharge.** That flat rating curve is its great weakness — and why it needs generous sizing and reliable trash protection.

questions.stem: Wetted perimeter for a trapezoidal section, if z, y and B are given, is:
questions.solution:
**P = B + 2y√(1 + Z²).**

**Derivation.** For a trapezoidal channel of bed width B, depth y and side slope **Z horizontal to 1 vertical**, the wetted perimeter is the bed plus the two sloping sides:

> Each sloping side has a vertical rise y and a horizontal run Zy, so by Pythagoras its length is **y√(1 + Z²)**
> Two sides give **2y√(1 + Z²)**
> **P = B + 2y√(1 + Z²)** ✓

A **plus** sign is required — the sides add to the perimeter — which disposes of option (a) immediately. Option (c) omits the factor of 2 for the second side.

**The companion relations** for the same section, which are used together:

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = By + Zy²** |
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = B + 2y√(1 + Z²)** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = A/P** |
| Top width | T = B + 2Zy |
| Hydraulic mean depth | D = A/T |

Those feed straight into **Manning's equation**:

> V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2},  Q = AV

and P also gives the **area to be lined**, L × P, so it drives the cost estimate as well as the hydraulics.

**The most economical trapezoidal section** minimises P for a given A — least friction, greatest discharge, least lining. That condition gives:

> **Top width = 2 × sloping side**, and **R = y/2**

with the best side slope at **60° to the horizontal** (a half-hexagon). Note that **R = y/2 also holds for the most economical rectangle**, which is worth remembering as a single fact; the triangle is the exception, at R = y/(2√2).

**A note on the printed options.** In the original paper options (a) and (d) were printed with **identical text** — both "B − 2y√(1+Z²)" — which is a typographical slip in the source, leaving only three distinct choices. Option (d) has been replaced here with a neutral "None of the above" so the question has four distinct options. The keyed answer (b) is unaffected.

**Watch the slope convention**, which is the commonest error in canal problems: this question writes the side slope as **Z : 1 (horizontal : vertical)**, so the horizontal run is Zy. Some questions write **1 : Z** instead, reversing the meaning and changing every expression above. Always read which way round it is before substituting.

verification.notes: The source printed options (a) and (d) with identical text, 'B−2y√(1+Z²)', so the question as printed had only three distinct choices. Option (d) has been replaced with 'None of the above'. The correct answer, (b), is unchanged.

examTip.trick: Each sloping side has length **y√(1 + z²)** by Pythagoras (rise y, run zy), and there are two of them: **P = B + 2y√(1 + z²)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check against the rectangle: with z = 0 it gives B + 2y ✓.** The companion is **A = By + zy²**. Always test a channel formula against the rectangular case — it takes seconds and catches most errors.

questions.stem: Vulnerability analysis comes in which part of the Disaster Management Cycle?
questions.solution:
**Mitigation.**

Vulnerability analysis identifies **who and what is at risk, and why** — which buildings, populations, services and areas would suffer, and how badly. That knowledge is the input to **reducing** the risk, which is precisely what mitigation means. It is done **before** an event, in order to change the outcome of the next one.

The four phases of the disaster management cycle:

| Phase | Timing | Purpose | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mitigation** | **Before** | **Reduce or eliminate the risk itself** | **Vulnerability and hazard analysis**; building codes; land-use zoning; **retrofitting**; slope stabilisation |
| **Preparedness** | Before | Get **ready to respond** | Early warning systems; evacuation plans; drills; stockpiles; training |
| **Response** | **During / immediately after** | Save lives, meet immediate needs | Search and rescue; relief; emergency medical care; shelter |
| **Recovery** | After | **Restore and rebuild** | Reconstruction; rehabilitation; livelihoods; "build back better" |

The distinction between the first two is the one most often confused, and it is worth stating plainly:

> **Mitigation changes the hazard's consequences. Preparedness changes our readiness to cope with them.**

Enforcing a seismic code is mitigation — the building will not collapse. Stockpiling tents is preparedness — we can shelter people if it does.

**Where the civil engineer's contribution sits.** Overwhelmingly in **mitigation**:

| Measure | Reduces vulnerability to |
|---|---|
| **Seismic codes** — NBC 105, IS 1893, ductile detailing per IS 13920 | Earthquake |
| **Retrofitting** existing masonry and soft-storey buildings | Earthquake |
| **Slope stabilisation and drainage** | Landslide |
| Flood embankments, guide banks, spillway capacity | Flood |
| **Land-use zoning** away from flood plains and unstable slopes | Multiple |

**Why this matters acutely in Nepal.** The country faces earthquake, landslide, flood, **GLOF** (glacial lake outburst flood) and fire hazards together. The **2015 Gorkha earthquake** demonstrated the cost of inadequate mitigation directly: the dominant failure modes — **soft ground storeys**, unreinforced masonry without RC bands, and 90° stirrup hooks that unravelled once cover spalled — were all known and all addressed in the codes. The vulnerability had been analysed; what was missing was enforcement.

That is the honest lesson of the cycle: **mitigation is the cheapest phase and the one most often skipped**, because its benefit is invisible until the event that never happens.

examTip.trick: The disaster cycle runs **mitigation → preparedness → response → recovery**. **Vulnerability analysis** identifies what is at risk and how badly, so that risk can be **reduced before an event** — which is mitigation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mitigation and preparedness happen BEFORE; response and recovery AFTER.** Mitigation reduces the hazard's *effect* (building codes, land use zoning, retrofitting); preparedness improves the *reaction* (early warning, drills, stockpiles). Nepal's seismic and GLOF risks demand both.

questions.stem: Permissible load in a circular column shouldn't exceed the permitted load in a ……… of equivalent cross-sectional area.
questions.solution:
**Square column.**

The rule is a design safeguard: the permissible load on a **circular** column must not exceed that permitted for a **square** column of the same cross-sectional area.

**Why the comparison is with a square.** For a given area, the square is the reference against which a circular section is judged because it is the shape that gives the **most favourable radius of gyration** among simple rectangular forms — it has equal stiffness about both principal axes, and no weak direction. Capping the circular column at the square's permitted load prevents the designer from claiming an advantage from the circular shape that the code does not intend to grant.

**The context that makes sense of it.** A circular column has real advantages, and IS 456 already rewards one of them:

| Feature of a circular column | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Equal I and r about every axis** | No weak axis; buckles identically in all directions |
| **Helical (spiral) reinforcement** | Continuously **confines the core**, giving greater ductility |
| IS 456 cl. 39.4 | Permits a **1.05 multiplier** on strength for a helically reinforced column |
| Formwork | Curved shuttering; beams frame awkwardly into a curved face |

So the code grants the 1.05 bonus for helical confinement, and separately caps the section against the equivalent square — the two provisions together define how much credit a circular column earns.

**Why circular columns are used despite the framing difficulty:** bridge piers, piles, and free-standing columns where nothing has to frame into them. Recall from Set 1 Q24 that the reason circular columns are avoided in building frames is **constructional** — a beam cannot easily meet a curved face — not structural.

**The column provisions that accompany this**, worth having together:

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Minimum longitudinal steel | **0.8%** of gross area |
| Maximum longitudinal steel | 6% (4% preferred for placing) |
| **Minimum number of bars** | **4** in a rectangular column, **6** in a circular one |
| Minimum bar diameter | 12 mm |
| **Tie pitch** | Least of: least lateral dimension, **16 × smallest bar diameter**, or 300 mm |
| Tie diameter | Greater of ¼ of the largest bar or 6 mm |
| **Slenderness limit** | Unsupported length ≤ **60 × least lateral dimension** |
| Minimum eccentricity | e_min = greater of L/500 + D/30 or 20 mm |

That last row matters: IS 456 requires every column to be designed for a **minimum eccentricity**, because a truly axial load never occurs in practice — construction tolerances and unbalanced framing always introduce some. A column designed for pure axial load would be unsafe.

examTip.trick: The reduction reflects **less reliable confinement and a smaller effective core** in a circular tied column compared with an equivalent square — so codes cap the permissible load at a fraction of the square's.
examTip.mnemonic: **But a SPIRALLY reinforced circular column is treated differently and gets a 5% INCREASE** — because a continuous helix confines the core far more effectively than discrete ties. That confinement is also why spiral columns fail **ductilely** rather than suddenly, which is why they are favoured in seismic design.

questions.stem: Doubly reinforced means:
options: Steel in both compression and tension
Double steel in compression than tension
questions.solution:
**Steel in both the compression and the tension zones.**

A **singly** reinforced section has steel only where the tension is — the bottom of a simply supported beam. A **doubly** reinforced section adds steel in the **compression** zone as well, near the top.

Option (d) is the trap: "doubly" refers to **two zones of steel**, not to twice as much steel in one of them.

**When compression steel is needed:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Section depth is restricted** | Headroom or architectural limits prevent a deeper beam, so the moment capacity must be raised within the given depth |
| **Applied moment exceeds the singly reinforced limit** | Adding more tension steel alone would push x_u past x_u,max and make the section **over-reinforced** — which is prohibited |
| **Moment reverses** | Seismic or wind loading puts each face alternately in tension |
| Continuous beams | The bottom steel at midspan continues through the support, where it lies in compression |
| Long-term deflection or creep must be reduced | Compression steel reduces both |

The second row is the essential one. IS 456 caps the neutral axis depth at **x_u,max** (0.48d for Fe 415, 0.46d for Fe 500) so that the **steel yields before the concrete crushes** and failure is ductile. Once that limit is reached, the only ways to carry more moment are a **deeper section** or **compression steel** — never simply more bars in the tension face.

**How the capacity is built up:**

> M_u = **M_u,lim** (the balanced singly reinforced capacity) **+** the additional moment carried by the compression steel and the matching extra tension steel

with the compression steel stressed to f_sc, read from the stress–strain curve at the strain corresponding to its position.

**The secondary benefits**, which often justify compression steel even where strength does not require it:

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Reduced long-term deflection** | Compression steel carries part of the compression, so the concrete creeps less |
| **Increased ductility** | The neutral axis rises, so the section rotates more before failure |
| Holds the stirrup cage | Provides anchorage for the top of the links |
| Resists moment reversal | Essential under seismic loading |

**A detailing requirement that follows.** Compression bars will **buckle** unless laterally restrained, so IS 456 requires stirrups enclosing them at a spacing not exceeding **16 times the smallest compression bar diameter** — the same rule as for column ties, and for the same reason.

Related limits: **maximum 4% of bD** for tension steel and 4% for compression steel, and **minimum tension steel** A_st/bd = 0.85/f_y.

examTip.trick: **Doubly reinforced** means steel in **both** faces — tension steel plus **compression steel**. It is used when the section cannot be made deeper and a singly reinforced section would have to be over-reinforced.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compression steel is added when the depth is LIMITED** — by headroom or architecture. It has a second benefit: it **greatly reduces long-term deflection from creep**, because the steel takes over as the concrete creeps. Compression bars must be **restrained by ties** or they buckle outward and spall the cover.

questions.stem: Compared with the standard Proctor test, the modified Proctor test gives:
options: The same maximum dry density and optimum moisture content
Lower maximum dry density and higher optimum moisture content
Higher maximum dry density and lower optimum moisture content
Higher maximum dry density and higher optimum moisture content
questions.solution:
**Higher maximum dry density and lower optimum moisture content.**

The modified test applies roughly **4.5 times** the compactive energy of the standard test:

| | **Standard Proctor** | **Modified Proctor** |
|---|---|---|
| Rammer mass | **2.6 kg** | **4.89 kg** |
| Free fall | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| Layers | 3 | **5** |
| Blows per layer | 25 | 25 |
| Compactive energy | ~595 kJ/m³ | **~2700 kJ/m³** |

**The effect on the compaction curve** is the examinable part: greater energy shifts the whole curve **up and to the left**.

> Higher energy → **higher MDD** and **lower OMC**

The upward shift is intuitive — more work expels more air. The **leftward** shift is the part worth understanding: with more energy available, the particles can be rearranged into a dense packing with **less water to lubricate them**. Water beyond that point simply fills voids the compaction could have closed, so the optimum arrives earlier.

**The zero-air-voids line** bounds both curves:

> γ_d,max possible = **G γ_w/(1 + wG)**

No amount of compaction can reach or cross it, because air can never be entirely expelled.
