Both Proctor curves approach it and run roughly parallel to it on the wet side — and a test point plotting **above** that line means the test or the assumed specific gravity is wrong. It is the standard sanity check on a compaction result.

**Which test to specify.** The choice should match the compactive effort the site plant will actually deliver:

| Test | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Standard** | Earth fills, embankments, subgrades — ordinary rolling |
| **Modified** | **Pavement base and sub-base**, airfields, heavily loaded fills — heavy modern plant |

Specifying the standard test where heavy plant is used sets a target the contractor will exceed easily; specifying the modified test where only light plant is available sets one that cannot be met. Field compaction is then required as a **percentage of the relevant MDD** — typically **95%** for a subgrade and **98%** for a base course — and verified by the **sand replacement** or core cutter method, always with a simultaneous moisture determination.

**Why the moisture matters as much as the density.** Compacting far from the OMC wastes effort entirely: too dry and the particles will not slip past one another, too wet and the pore water cannot escape fast enough to let them. Note also that compacting **wet of optimum** produces a lower permeability and less swelling potential — which is why an earth dam **core** is deliberately placed slightly wet of optimum even though the density is marginally lower.

examTip.trick: The modified test delivers about **4.5 times** the compactive energy of the standard test, and more energy always shifts the curve **up and to the left**.
examTip.mnemonic: **More energy: HIGHER density at a LOWER optimum moisture content.** Every compaction curve behaves this way, which is why the specified OMC falls as the roller gets heavier — and why field compaction must be matched to the laboratory test actually used.

questions.stem: A combined footing is provided when:
options: The soil is rock and the load is light
Two columns are so close that their individual footings would overlap
A single column carries a very small load
The water table is deep below the foundation level
questions.solution:
**When two columns are so close that their individual footings would overlap.**

A combined footing supports **two or more columns on one base**. The usual triggers:

| Situation | Why a combined footing |
|---|---|
| **Columns close together** | Isolated footings would **overlap**, so one base is simpler and cheaper |
| **Column near a property line** | An isolated footing cannot be centred on it without trespassing, so it is combined with the next column inward |
| Weak soil, large required areas | The footings grow until they merge |
| Columns of very unequal load | Combining lets the base be proportioned so the pressure stays uniform |

**The design principle that governs it.** The footing is proportioned so that the **centroid of the base area coincides with the centroid of the column loads** — because only then is the bearing pressure uniform and the footing free of the tilting that unequal pressure would cause.

With two unequal loads that requirement usually forces a **trapezoidal** shape rather than a rectangle: the wider end goes under the heavier column. Where a rectangle would have to project beyond a property line, a **strap (cantilever) footing** is used instead — two separate bases tied by a stiff beam that transfers the eccentricity, leaving the boundary column's footing concentric.

**The shallow foundation types**, so the choice is clear:

| Type | Carries |
|---|---|
| **Isolated (pad) footing** | One column |
| **Combined footing** | **Two or more columns** — rectangular or trapezoidal |
| **Strap / cantilever footing** | Two columns, bases linked by a beam; used at a boundary |
| **Strip (wall) footing** | A wall, or a row of columns |
| **Raft (mat)** | **All** columns, when isolated footings would cover more than about 50% of the plan area |

So the sequence as soil weakens or loads grow is: isolated → combined → strip → **raft** → and then piles.

**Why the other options are wrong.** Rock with a light load (a) needs the *smallest* possible footing, not a combined one; a single small load (c) is the clearest case for an isolated pad; and the water table depth (d) affects buoyancy, excavation and the choice between shallow and deep foundations, but not whether two columns share a base.

**Structural behaviour worth noting:** a combined footing spans between its columns like an **inverted beam**, carrying upward soil pressure. So it develops **hogging moment between the columns** — tension on the **top** face — which is the reverse of an isolated footing and a detailing point frequently got wrong on site. It must also be checked for **one-way shear** at d from each column face and **two-way punching shear** on the perimeter at d/2, in addition to bending in both directions.

examTip.trick: The trigger is **overlap**: when two columns are so close that separate footings would run into each other, one footing must serve both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shape it so the CENTROID coincides with the RESULTANT of the two loads** — trapezoidal if the loads are unequal and space is tight. The structural surprise: it spans as a beam **loaded upward by the soil**, so the main steel between the columns goes in the **TOP** face, opposite to an isolated footing.

questions.stem: The unit of kinematic viscosity is:
questions.solution:
**m²/s.**

Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density:

> **ν = μ/ρ**

**Checking the units** confirms it, and this is the reliable way to answer rather than memorising:

> ν = (N·s/m²) ÷ (kg/m³) = (kg·m/s² · s/m²) ÷ (kg/m³) = **m²/s** ✓

Note that ν contains **no unit of force or mass** — only length and time. That is exactly why it is called *kinematic*: it describes motion alone, whereas **dynamic** viscosity involves force.

Distinguishing the two, and the distractors:

| Quantity | Symbol | SI unit | CGS unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dynamic (absolute) viscosity** | **μ** | **N·s/m² = Pa·s** (also kg/m·s) | **poise** (1 P = 0.1 Pa·s) |
| **Kinematic viscosity** | **ν** | **m²/s** | **stoke** (1 St = 10⁻⁴ m²/s) |

So option (a), N·s/m², and option (c), kg/m·s, are the **same** quantity — dynamic viscosity — written two ways, and option (d) is a **stress**.

Values for water at 20°C, worth carrying as an anchor:

> μ = **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s**,  ν = **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s**

**Where each one is used**, which is the practical point:

| Use | Which viscosity |
|---|---|
| **Newton's law of viscosity**, τ = μ(du/dy) | **Dynamic**, μ |
| **Reynolds number**, Re = ρVD/μ = **VD/ν** | Either — but ν gives the neater form |
| **Stokes' law** settling velocity | ν (or μ with ρ) |
| Laminar head loss, h_f = 32μVL/γD² | Dynamic |

The Reynolds number is the clearest illustration: written as **VD/ν** it contains only kinematic quantities, which is why ν is the natural viscosity for problems about *flow patterns* while μ suits problems about *forces*.

**How both vary with temperature** — a distinction examined in its own right:

| Fluid | Rising temperature |
|---|---|
| **Liquid** | Viscosity **falls** — cohesion between closely packed molecules weakens |
| **Gas** | Viscosity **rises** — faster molecules transfer more momentum between layers |

Water's viscosity falls by a factor of more than six between 0°C and 100°C, which is not a small correction: since Re = VD/ν, warming a flow **raises** Re and can push it from laminar into turbulent, changing the friction factor and the head loss.

Pressure, by contrast, has almost no effect on the viscosity of a liquid over ordinary ranges — so temperature is the variable that matters.

examTip.trick: **ν = μ/ρ**, so the units are **Pa·s ÷ kg/m³ = m²/s** — the units of a **diffusivity**, because kinematic viscosity IS the diffusivity of momentum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s at 20 °C — the reference value.** Striking comparison: **air is 55× LESS viscous than water in dynamic terms but 15× MORE in kinematic terms**, because its density is 800× lower. Use **μ** for shear force, **ν** for Reynolds number.

questions.stem: The effective length of a column fixed at one end and free at the other is:
questions.solution:
**2L.**

A column **fixed at one end and free at the other** — a cantilever column, or flagpole — is the **weakest** of the standard cases. Its effective length is **twice** its actual length:

> P_cr = π²EI/l_e² = π²EI/(2L)² = **π²EI/(4L²)**

so it carries only a **quarter** of the load of a pinned-pinned column of the same length.

**Why 2L.** The effective length is the distance between successive **points of contraflexure** in the buckled shape — equivalently, the length of an equivalent pinned-pinned column that would buckle at the same load. A cantilever column buckles into a quarter sine wave; extending that curve by its mirror image gives a half sine wave of length 2L, which is the pinned-pinned equivalent.

The standard cases, which must be known cold:

| End conditions | l_e | P_cr | Relative capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Both ends fixed** | **0.5 L** | 4π²EI/L² | **4** |
| One fixed, one hinged | 0.7 L (L/√2) | 2.05π²EI/L² | 2 |
| **Both ends hinged** | **L** | π²EI/L² | **1** |
| **One fixed, one free** | **2 L** | π²EI/(4L²) | **¼** |

So the range across the table is **sixteen to one** — which makes end restraint the most powerful lever available to the designer of a compression member, far more effective than changing the material.

**Two consequences worth holding:**

1. **Buckling depends on stiffness, not strength.** P_cr contains E and I but no yield stress, so specifying a higher grade of steel does **nothing** for a slender strut. What helps is increasing I — making the section hollow, or spreading material away from the axis.
2. **Buckling occurs about the weak axis**, so the slenderness ratio uses the **least** radius of gyration:

> λ = l_e/**k_min**,  with k = √(I/A)

IS 800 caps λ at **180** for a member carrying dead and live load (250 for one resisting wind only), and IS 456 limits an RCC column's unsupported length to **60 times its least lateral dimension**.

**Where Euler's formula stops applying.** It tends to infinity as L → 0, which is absurd — a short column simply crushes. Hence the ranges:

| Column | Slenderness (steel) | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| Short | λ < ~32 | **Crushing** |
| Intermediate | 32 – 120 | Combined — **Rankine's** formula |
| Long | > 120 | **Buckling** — Euler |

**In practice** ideal end conditions never occur. Real effective lengths are found from the **relative stiffness of the members meeting at each joint**, using the charts in IS 800 Annex D and IS 456 Annex E — and a column in a sway frame has a substantially longer effective length than the same column in a braced one.

examTip.trick: A fixed–free column is a **cantilever**: its buckled shape is **half** a sine wave, equivalent to a pin-ended column of **twice** the length.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective lengths: hinged–hinged L, fixed–fixed 0.5L, fixed–hinged 0.7L, fixed–FREE 2L.** Since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, a cantilever column carries only a **QUARTER** of a pinned column's load and a **SIXTEENTH** of a fixed–fixed one's. Effective length is the single most important quantity in compression design.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, when the dead load provides stability against overturning or uplift, the partial safety factor applied to it is:
questions.solution:
**0.9.**

This is the one load factor that is **less than one**, and the reason is the direction in which the load acts.

Usually a larger load is the dangerous case, so IS 456 multiplies it up: **1.5 (DL + LL)**. But where the dead load is **resisting** — holding a retaining wall down against overturning, or a light roof down against wind uplift — the dangerous case is that the dead load turns out to be **smaller** than assumed. Multiplying it up would then be **unsafe**, because it would credit the structure with stabilising weight that might not be there.

So the factor is inverted in effect: **0.9 DL** is used, deliberately under-estimating the weight that is doing the resisting.

The load combinations of IS 456 Table 18 for the limit state of collapse:

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| DL + LL | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| DL + WL / EL | **1.5 DL + 1.5 WL** |
| DL + LL + WL / EL | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL)** |
| **DL opposing** the effect (overturning, sliding, uplift) | **0.9 DL** |

Note also the **1.2** in the three-way combination: when dead, live and wind loads are all counted together, it is unlikely they all peak simultaneously, so the factor is reduced from 1.5.

**Where the 0.9 case actually bites:**

| Structure | Failure it guards against |
|---|---|
| **Retaining wall** | **Overturning** about the toe, and sliding on the base |
| Light roof / canopy | **Wind uplift** tearing it off its supports |
| Cantilever slab or balcony | Overturning of the whole element |
| Basement raft below the water table | **Buoyant uplift** floating the structure |
| Gravity dam | Overturning and sliding, with **uplift pressure** reducing effective weight |

That last row is instructive: a gravity dam resists by its own weight, and **uplift pressure** from seepage beneath the base reduces the effective weight available. The design must therefore both add the uplift as a load *and* refrain from over-estimating the resisting weight.

**The companion material factors**, which are applied alongside the load factors:

> **Concrete γ_m = 1.5** → design strength **0.446 f_ck**
> **Steel γ_m = 1.15** → design strength **0.87 f_y**

Concrete carries the larger factor because it is mixed, placed and cured on site and its strength scatters far more than factory-rolled steel.

For the **serviceability** limit state all partial safety factors on both loads and materials are taken as **1.0**, since the question there is how the structure behaves under the loads it will actually experience — deflection and crack width — not whether it will collapse.

examTip.trick: Where dead load **helps** — resisting overturning, sliding or uplift — factoring it **up** would be unconservative, because the real dead load might be **less** than estimated.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.9 DL when dead load is STABILISING; 1.5 DL when it is destabilising.** This is the load case most often omitted, and omitting it hides overturning and uplift problems entirely — retaining walls, cantilever canopies, empty basements and light structures under wind uplift.

questions.stem: For a given cement and aggregate, the compressive strength of concrete:
options: Increases as the water–cement ratio increases
Is independent of the water–cement ratio
Decreases as the water–cement ratio increases
Depends only on the cement content, not on the water content
questions.solution:
**Decreases as the water–cement ratio increases** — this is **Abrams' law**, the single most important relation in concrete technology.

> **Strength ∝ 1/(w/c ratio)**

**Why.** Cement needs only about **0.23 by weight of water** for complete hydration, plus roughly another 0.15 to fill the gel pores — so about **0.38** in total. Any water beyond that:

1. occupies space in the paste while the concrete is plastic;
2. later evaporates or bleeds away;
3. leaves behind **capillary pores** — permanent voids in the hardened paste.

Strength depends on the **density of the hardened paste**, and every void is a defect. So the excess water does not weaken the concrete chemically; it weakens it by **leaving holes where solid should be**.

The practical figures:

| w/c ratio | Approximate 28-day strength | Character |
|---|---|---|
| 0.35 | Very high | Needs plasticiser and good compaction |
| **0.45 – 0.50** | **M25 – M30** | Ordinary structural concrete |
| 0.55 – 0.60 | M20 | Workable, moderate strength |
| > 0.65 | Low | Porous, poor durability |

**The durability consequence matters as much as strength.** A high w/c ratio gives a **permeable** concrete, and permeability is what admits water, chlorides, sulphates and carbon dioxide to the reinforcement. That is why IS 456 sets **maximum** w/c ratios by exposure condition rather than by strength alone:

| Exposure | Max w/c | Min grade | Min cement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mild | 0.55 | M20 | 300 kg/m³ |
| **Moderate** | **0.50** | **M25** | 300 kg/m³ |
| Severe | 0.45 | M30 | 320 kg/m³ |
| Very severe | 0.45 | M35 | 340 kg/m³ |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | **M40** | 360 kg/m³ |

**The tension this creates, and how it is resolved.** Lower w/c gives strength and durability but poor **workability** — and concrete that cannot be placed and compacted properly will be full of voids anyway, defeating the purpose. The wrong resolution is to add water on site; the right ones are:

- **Plasticisers and superplasticisers**, which raise workability at constant w/c;
- **Better compaction** — a vibrator permits a slump of 25 mm where hand compaction needs 50–100 mm;
- Good aggregate **grading and shape**, which reduce the water demand for a given workability.

Adding water at the mixer to make a stiff mix placeable is the commonest and most damaging site malpractice, because it silently converts a designed M25 into something much weaker and far more permeable. That is why **weigh-batching** and a controlled slump are specified, and why the correction for aggregate moisture — and for **bulking** of damp sand — matters so much in volume batching.

examTip.trick: **Abrams' law**: for a fully compacted concrete, strength depends almost entirely on the **water–cement ratio** — more water means more capillary porosity in the hardened paste, and porosity is what governs strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lower w/c = higher strength AND better durability — the two move together.** The catch: less water means a stiffer mix, so **plasticisers** are used to keep it workable without adding water. The critical caveat is "fully compacted": **5% voids from poor compaction costs about 30% of the strength.**

questions.stem: In a bolted connection, the term 'single shear' means the bolt:
options: Is subjected to shear on two planes
Is subjected to shear on one plane only
questions.solution:
**It is subjected to shear on one plane only.**

The number of shear planes depends on how many pieces of steel the bolt must be cut through for the joint to fail:

| Arrangement | Shear planes | Called |
|---|---|---|
| **Lap joint** — two plates overlapping | **1** | **Single shear** |
| **Butt joint with two cover plates** | **2** | **Double shear** |
| n plies in a multi-plate joint | n − 1 | Multiple shear |

So a bolt in **double shear** has **twice the shear capacity** of the same bolt in single shear, because two cross-sections must fail instead of one. That is the whole practical point: a double-covered butt joint is far more efficient in bolts than a lap joint, and it is also free of the **eccentricity** that makes a lap joint bend.

**The design strength**, from IS 800:

> **V_dsb = (f_ub/√3)(n_n A_nb + n_s A_sb)/γ_mb**,  with **γ_mb = 1.25**

where n_n and n_s are the numbers of shear planes passing through the **threaded** and the **shank** portions respectively, A_nb the net tensile stress area at the threads (about **0.78** of the gross) and A_sb the gross shank area.

That distinction matters: a shear plane falling in the **threads** has only 78% of the area of one falling in the plain shank, so where possible the joint is arranged so the shear planes miss the threads.

**The three failure modes of a bolted joint** — the capacity is the **least** of them, which is the logic behind every riveted or bolted connection calculation:

| Mode | Governed by |
|---|---|
| **Shear** of the bolt | Bolt area × number of shear planes |
| **Bearing** — bolt crushing against the plate | Bolt diameter × plate thickness |
| **Tearing** of the plate through the net section | Plate width less the holes |

Set 1 Q66 works exactly this comparison: given shear, bearing and tearing strengths of 3425, 4575 and 5025 kg, the **rivet value is the minimum, 3425 kg**, and the bolt count follows from it.

**Bolt spacing rules** that accompany the capacity check:

| Requirement | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Minimum pitch** | **2.5 d** |
| Maximum pitch | Lesser of 32 t or 300 mm |
| Minimum edge distance | 1.7 × hole diameter (sheared edge), 1.5 × (rolled edge) |
| Hole diameter | Bolt + 1 mm (≤14 mm), **+2 mm** (16–24 mm), +3 mm (>24 mm) |

Note the contrast with a **friction grip (HSFG)** bolt, which does not work in shear at all: it is pre-tensioned so hard that load transfers by **friction between the plate faces**, which is why it is the right choice where the stress **reverses** — the point of Q49 of this paper.

examTip.trick: Count the **planes the bolt is cut across**. A **lap** joint shears the bolt on **one** plane; a **double-cover butt** joint shears it on **two**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Double shear has TWICE the capacity of single shear** for the same bolt — which is why a double-cover butt joint is preferred for important connections. Also check **bearing** on the plate and **tearing** of the net section: the **rivet/bolt value is the LEAST of the three**.

questions.stem: In load-bearing masonry, the strength of the mortar should generally be:
options: Much greater than that of the masonry unit
As high as possible regardless of the unit strength
Independent of the strength of the masonry unit
Comparable to or slightly less than that of the masonry unit
questions.solution:
**Comparable to, or slightly less than, that of the masonry unit.**

This is one of the genuinely counter-intuitive rules in masonry design: **a stronger mortar does not give a stronger wall**, and beyond a point it makes the wall worse.

**Why a weaker mortar is preferred.** The mortar joint is the **more flexible** and **sacrificial** component of the assembly, and that is deliberate:

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Cracks go through the joints** | A mortar weaker than the unit lets movement be accommodated in many fine joint cracks rather than splitting the bricks. Joint cracks are **repairable by repointing**; cracked bricks are not |
| **Accommodates movement** | Thermal, moisture and settlement movements are absorbed by the flexible joints instead of building up stress |
| **Avoids brittleness** | A very rich mortar is stiff and brittle, so the wall cracks in fewer, wider, more damaging cracks |
| Shrinkage | A rich cement mortar shrinks more, opening the very joints it was meant to seal |

So the aim is a **balanced** assembly. An excessively rich mortar transfers the weak link from the joint to the unit, which is the wrong place for it.

**Mortar mixes and their uses:**

| Mix (cement : sand) | Use |
|---|---|
| **1 : 3** | Very rich — only for special work, damp-proof courses |
| **1 : 4 – 1 : 5** | **Load-bearing masonry**, structural work |
| **1 : 6** | **General brickwork**, the commonest mix |
| 1 : 8 | Lean — partition walls, low stress |
| **Cement–lime–sand**, e.g. 1 : 1 : 6 | **Better workability and water retention**; more flexible than plain cement mortar |

The **cement–lime** mixes deserve note: adding lime improves workability, water retention (so the mortar does not stiffen as the brick sucks water out of it) and — crucially — gives the joint some capacity to **autogenously heal** fine cracks. That is why traditional lime-based mortars have performed so well in old masonry, and why replacing them with a rich cement mortar during repair often **accelerates** damage to historic brickwork.

**How masonry strength is actually determined.** The compressive strength of the assembly depends on the **unit strength, the mortar grade and the slenderness**, and IS 1905 gives it through the **basic compressive stress** modified by:

| Factor | Depends on |
|---|---|
| **Stress reduction factor** | **Slenderness ratio** (effective height ÷ effective thickness), capped at **27** |
| **Shape modification factor** | Height-to-width ratio of the unit |
| Eccentricity allowance | +25% where e/t > 1/24 |

Note the **effective thickness** rule for a cavity wall with both leaves loaded — the **greater** of ⅔(t₁+t₂) and the thicker leaf — which is the provision the circulating key for Set 1 Q38 gets wrong.

The practical hierarchy is worth remembering: **masonry strength is governed by slenderness far more than by mortar richness**, so a wall that is too slender cannot be rescued by a richer mix — it needs a **buttress, cross wall or pilaster** instead.

examTip.trap: "Much stronger than the unit" is the instinctive but wrong answer — a mortar stronger than the brick is actively harmful.
examTip.trick: A **weaker, more flexible mortar** lets small movements be accommodated by **fine distributed cracks in the joints**, which are easily repointed. A **strong, rigid** mortar forces the movement to crack **the units themselves**, which cannot be repaired.
examTip.mnemonic: **The mortar should be the sacrificial element — never stronger than the brick.** This is why over-cemented repointing destroys old masonry, and why lime mortars are specified for conservation work.

questions.stem: The total storage capacity of a service reservoir is usually provided as:
options: The whole of the maximum daily demand
One third of the maximum daily demand
Three times the maximum daily demand
One tenth of the average daily demand
questions.solution:
**About one third of the maximum daily demand.**

That total is made up of three components, each meeting a different contingency:

| Component | Purpose | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **Balancing (equalising) storage** | Evens out the mismatch between **steady pumping** and **fluctuating hourly demand** | The largest part |
| **Breakdown storage** | Maintains supply while a pump, main or treatment unit is out of service | **≤ 25%** of the total; about 1.5–2 hours of maximum daily demand |
| **Fire storage** | Meets the short, heavy draw of firefighting | From a fire-demand formula |

**Why balancing storage is needed at all.** Treatment works and pumps run most economically at a **steady rate**, but consumption peaks morning and evening. The reservoir absorbs the difference — filling overnight when demand is below the pumping rate, and drawing down during the peaks. Without it the whole supply chain would have to be sized for the **peak hourly** demand rather than the daily average, which is roughly **2.7 times** larger.

That is the economic argument in one line: **storage is cheaper than capacity.**

**Why the total is capped rather than made generous.** Storage is expensive, occupies elevated land, and water held too long **loses its chlorine residual and deteriorates in quality**. Beyond about a third of the maximum daily demand the extra security is not worth the cost or the stagnation risk — better to provide **standby pumps and duplicate mains** so that breakdowns are shorter in the first place.

**The demand hierarchy** the reservoir sits within:

| Demand | Multiplier on average daily | Sizes |
|---|---|---|
| Average daily | 1.0 | Source, treatment plant |
| **Maximum daily** | **1.8** | Pumps, transmission main |
| **Peak hourly** | **2.7** | **Distribution mains, service reservoir** |
| Coincident draft | Max daily **+ fire demand** | Mains near hydrants |

**Siting and levels.** A service reservoir is placed so it can deliver by gravity at a residual pressure of about **7 to 17 m** of water at the consumer's tap, which usually means an elevated site or an overhead tank. Its **inlet is controlled by an altitude valve**, which closes automatically when the tank is full to prevent overflow and reopens to let the tank feed the network as demand draws the pressure down.

Related figures: **fire demand** from Kuchling's Q = 3182√P or Buston's Q = 5663√P (P in thousands, Q in L/min), and the **design period** for a reservoir of 15 to 30 years — long, because a tank is expensive and disruptive to extend, unlike a pump.

examTip.trick: Service reservoir storage has three components: **balancing (equalising)** storage, **breakdown (emergency)** reserve, and **fire** reserve.
examTip.mnemonic: **Balancing storage is about one third of the maximum daily demand**, because that is roughly the volume by which peak-hour draw exceeds the steady pumping rate. It exists so the **treatment works and pumps can run at a steady rate** while demand fluctuates — which is far cheaper than sizing them for the peak hour.

questions.stem: A drop manhole in a sewerage system is provided where:
options: Two sewers of the same invert level meet
An incoming sewer is at a considerably higher level than the outgoing sewer
The sewer needs to be flushed
questions.solution:
**Where an incoming sewer is at a considerably higher level than the outgoing sewer.**

A drop manhole takes the vertical fall **inside the chamber** — by a vertical pipe down the side, or a stepped arrangement — instead of letting the sewage cascade freely into the chamber.

**Why the drop must be contained:**

| If the fall is uncontained | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Sewage plunges into the chamber | **Scours** the benching and invert |
| High-velocity impact | Erodes the floor and undermines the structure |
| Splashing and turbulence | **Releases hydrogen sulphide** into the air space, accelerating **crown corrosion** |
| Aerosols and odour | Hazard to anyone entering |

So a drop manhole is as much an **odour and corrosion** control measure as a structural one. That last row matters more than it appears: H₂S released into the air space is oxidised by bacteria on the damp crown into **sulphuric acid**, which destroys concrete sewers from the inside top downward. Turbulence is what drives it out of solution.

**When such a fall arises.** Chiefly in **hilly terrain**, where the ground slopes far more steeply than the sewer's design gradient. The sewer must keep a gentle self-cleansing slope, so the surplus fall has to be surrendered in steps — exactly the same problem, and the same solution, as a **canal fall** on a steep ground slope.

A drop is used where the difference exceeds about **600 mm**.

**The manhole types**, so the distinctions are clear:

| Type | Provided where |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary manhole** | Change of direction, gradient, diameter; junctions; at intervals on straight runs |
| **Drop manhole** | **Large difference in invert levels** |
| **Flushing manhole** | At the **head** of a branch on a flat gradient, to flush deposits |
| **Junction chamber** | Where large sewers meet |
| Lamphole | Inspection only, no entry |

So option (a) describes an ordinary **junction**, (c) an ordinary manhole, and (d) a **flushing** manhole.

**Manhole spacing and classification** examined alongside: about **30 m** for sewers up to 0.3 m diameter, rising to 90 m or more for large sewers; and by depth — **shallow 0.7–0.9 m**, medium 0.9–1.5 m, **deep above 1.5 m**.

**A safety point that always accompanies this topic.** A manhole is a **confined space** containing toxic **H₂S** — which deadens the sense of smell and so gives no warning — and explosive **methane**. Entry requires forced ventilation, gas testing, harness and a standby person at the surface. A drop manhole is worse than most, because the turbulence it contains is precisely what liberates the gas.

examTip.trick: A **drop manhole** brings a high incoming sewer down to the outgoing invert through a **vertical drop pipe** outside the chamber, instead of letting the sewage fall freely inside it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Free-falling sewage splashes, erodes the invert, releases H₂S and makes the manhole unenterable.** The drop pipe contains all of it. Drop manholes are common on **steep hill alignments**, where the ground falls faster than the sewer's design gradient.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant of installed capacity up to 100 kW is classified as:
questions.solution:
**Micro hydro.**

Classification by **installed capacity**:

| Class | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Micro** | **up to 100 kW** |
| Mini | 100 kW – 1 MW |
| Small | 1 – 10 MW |
| Medium | 10 – 300 MW |
| Large | above 300 MW |

This is a **separate** scheme from classification by **head**, and the two must not be confused:

| By head | Head | Turbine |
|---|---|---|
| Low | < 30 m | **Kaplan** (axial) |
| Medium | 30 – 250 m | **Francis** (mixed) |
| High | > 250 m | **Pelton** (impulse) |

A micro hydro plant may operate at **any head at all** — the two classifications are independent.

**Why micro hydro matters particularly in Nepal.** It has been the principal means of electrifying remote hill villages far from the national grid, because:

- the terrain supplies **high head over short distances**, so a small flow yields useful power;
- schemes are built **without a dam** — a small diversion weir, a canal, a forebay and a penstock;
- they can be constructed and maintained by **local labour** with locally manufactured turbines (crossflow and Pelton units are made in Nepal);
- there is **no transmission line** to build, which is usually the dominant cost of connecting a remote settlement.

Several thousand such schemes have been installed, largely through the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre, and they are the standard example of appropriate-technology infrastructure in the syllabus.

**Their limitations** are equally worth knowing: output falls in the dry season with the flow, there is little or no storage so supply follows the river rather than the demand, and load growth quickly outstrips a fixed small capacity — which is why many early micro schemes have since been superseded by grid connection.

**The regulatory position.** Under the Electricity Act 2049, licensing is administered by the **Department of Electricity Development**, and very small schemes are **exempt from licensing** altogether. The environmental study tier also steps up with capacity — **BES, IEE or EIA** — so a micro scheme faces a far lighter approval burden than a large one, which is part of what makes it deployable.

For scale: Nepal's theoretical potential is about **83,000 MW**, of which roughly **42,000 MW** is considered technically and economically feasible.

examTip.trick: Nepal's hydropower classification by installed capacity: **micro up to 100 kW, mini 100 kW – 1 MW, small 1–25 MW, medium 25–100 MW, large above 100 MW.**
examTip.mnemonic: **The classification matters because it determines the LICENSING and approval route** — micro schemes are essentially unregulated and community-built, while anything above 1 MW needs a full survey license, generation license, EIA and power purchase agreement. Micro-hydro is how much of rural Nepal was first electrified.

questions.stem: In a zoned earth dam, the function of the central impervious core is to:
options: Provide the main structural strength of the dam
Reduce seepage through the body of the dam
Protect the upstream slope from wave action
Drain the seepage water to the downstream toe
questions.solution:
**To reduce seepage through the body of the dam.**

A zoned earth dam separates the two jobs an embankment must do, giving each to the material best suited to it:

| Zone | Material | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Central core** | **Impervious** — clay, or clayey silt | **Controls seepage** — the water barrier |
| **Shells (casing)** | **Pervious and strong** — sand, gravel, rockfill | Provide **stability and strength** |
| **Filters / transition zones** | Graded sand and gravel | Prevent **migration of core fines** into the shell |
| **Drainage blanket / rock toe / chimney drain** | Coarse, free-draining | **Intercept seepage** and lead it away safely |
| Riprap / slope pitching | Stone | **Protect the upstream slope** from wave action |

So the options each name a real zone, but only (b) names the **core's** job. Strength comes from the **shells** (a), wave protection from **riprap** (c), and interception of seepage from the **drainage zones** (d).

**Why separate the functions at all.** A clay core is impervious but weak and compressible; a gravel shell is strong and free-draining but would leak. A homogeneous dam of either material alone is a compromise: clay throughout gives poor stability and slow construction, gravel throughout leaks. Zoning lets each material do what it is good at.

**Two design points about the core:**

1. It is deliberately compacted **slightly wet of optimum**. That gives a marginally lower dry density but a **lower permeability** and a more plastic, less crack-prone material — which matters more in a water barrier than the last percent of density.
2. It must be protected by **graded filters** on both sides. Without them, seepage carries fine core particles into the coarse shell, hollowing the core out from within — **internal erosion (suffosion)**, one of the principal failure mechanisms of embankment dams.

**The seepage line the whole arrangement exists to control.** Water seeping through the dam has a free upper surface at atmospheric pressure — the **phreatic line**, closely approximated by Casagrande's base parabola. The governing requirement is that it **must not emerge on the downstream face**. If it does:

| Failure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Sloughing** | Saturated surface layer slips away, progressively eating into the face |
| **Piping** | Internal erosion works a channel backward from the exit point |

Hence the **drainage blanket, rock toe or chimney filter** — they keep the phreatic line inside the dam and discharge the seepage under control. Recall the quantitative reason it matters so much: steady seepage roughly **halves** the factor of safety of a slope, so the **downstream slope under steady seepage** is the critical stability case for an earth dam.

The other loading cases checked in design: end of construction, **steady seepage** with the reservoir full, **rapid drawdown** (which leaves the upstream shell saturated with no water pressure to support it), and seismic.

examTip.trick: A zoned earth dam separates the two functions: the **impervious clay core** stops the water, and the **pervious shells** provide the **stability and strength**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Core for WATERTIGHTNESS, shells for STABILITY, FILTERS between them.** The filters are the critical detail — without a properly graded filter the core material **pipes** into the shell and the dam fails from the inside. Filter criteria: **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4–5 AND D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4–5** — both at once.

questions.stem: In the New Austrian Tunnelling Method (NATM), the primary support is provided by:
options: Shotcrete with rock bolts and wire mesh
questions.solution:
**Shotcrete with rock bolts and wire mesh.**

NATM's central idea is that the **rock mass itself is the principal load-bearing element**, and the support's job is to help it carry its own load rather than to replace it. So the support is applied **immediately** after excavation, is **thin and flexible**, and is adjusted as the ground reveals itself:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **Shotcrete** (sprayed concrete) | Seals the surface at once, preventing loosening and weathering; provides a thin flexible shell |
| **Rock bolts / anchors** | **Knit the rock mass together**, mobilising its own shear strength |
| **Wire mesh or steel fibre** | Gives the shotcrete tensile capacity and holds loose blocks |
| Steel ribs / lattice girders | Added only where the ground demands them |

**The principle that distinguishes it.** Excavation lets the rock deform slightly, and that **controlled deformation** mobilises the ground's own strength — the arching action around the opening. A support that is too stiff prevents this and attracts the whole load onto itself; a support that is too flexible lets the rock loosen and fail. NATM aims for the middle: allow enough deformation to mobilise the arch, then stabilise it.

Because the correct amount of deformation cannot be known in advance, **monitoring is not optional but part of the method**: convergence measurements, extensometers and load cells are read continuously, and the support is thickened or lightened in response. A permanent inner lining is placed later, once movement has stabilised.

**Contrast with the segmental methods** named in the other options:

| Method | Support | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **NATM** | **Shotcrete + rock bolts**, flexible, monitored | **Rock**, and soft ground with modification |
| **Shield tunnelling** | **Cast iron or precast concrete segments**, bolted, stiff and watertight | Soft, water-bearing ground; **subaqueous** tunnels |
| Timber sets and lagging | Timber | **Temporary** support only; largely historical |

So cast iron (a) and precast segments (b) belong to **shield** tunnelling, where a rigid watertight ring is erected inside the shield tail — the right answer for a tunnel under a river, as Set 4 Q41 asks. Timber (c) rots and is temporary.

**Where NATM matters for Nepal.** Nearly every hydropower scheme needs a **headrace tunnel**, and the Himalayan geology is exactly the difficult case: highly variable rock, thrust zones, high in-situ stresses, squeezing ground and water inflows. NATM's ability to **adapt the support as conditions change** is precisely why it is used, since no single pre-designed lining would suit the whole drive.

The accompanying hazards, examined alongside: **squeezing and rock burst** under high cover, **water inrush**, and the gas and ventilation limits — **oxygen not below 19.5%**, CO₂ not above 0.5%, and H₂S in trace only.

examTip.trick: NATM's principle is that **the rock supports itself** if it is allowed to deform slightly and is then supported flexibly and promptly — hence a thin **shotcrete shell with rock bolts and mesh**, not a rigid lining.
examTip.mnemonic: **NATM works WITH the ground, mobilising the rock's own arching capacity; segmental lining works AGAINST it.** So NATM suits **rock that stands up for a time**, and shield tunnelling with segmental lining suits **soft, water-bearing ground** that will not. Monitoring convergence is integral to NATM, not optional.

questions.stem: For maximum efficiency of a Pelton wheel, the bucket speed should be approximately:
options: One quarter of the jet velocity
One half of the jet velocity
questions.solution:
**One half of the jet velocity.**

> **u = V/2**, giving the **speed ratio** u/V ≈ 0.46 in practice

**Why one half.** The work done per second on the buckets is

> P = ρQ(V − u)(1 + k cos θ)·u

The (V − u) term is the **relative velocity** at which the jet strikes, and u is the **speed at which the bucket moves**. The two pull against each other:

| If u is | Then |
|---|---|
| **Zero** | The jet strikes hardest, but the bucket does not move — **no work done** |
| **Equal to V** | The bucket runs away with the jet — no relative velocity, **no work done** |
| **V/2** | **The product (V − u)·u is maximised** — maximum power |

Differentiating u(V − u) with respect to u and setting it to zero gives **u = V/2** directly. It is the same mathematics as maximising the area of a rectangle of fixed perimeter — the optimum is the midpoint.

In practice the ratio is taken as about **0.46** rather than exactly 0.5, to allow for windage, mechanical friction and the fact that the jet is not perfectly deflected.

**The bucket angle.** The theoretical maximum efficiency would occur with the jet turned through **180°**, reversing it completely. That is impossible in practice because the returning water would strike the back of the following bucket, so the deflection angle is limited to about **165°**, and the (1 + k cos θ) term accounts for it. Maximum hydraulic efficiency then works out at around **88 to 92%**.

**The jet velocity itself** comes from the available head:

> **V = C_v √(2gH)**,  with C_v ≈ 0.98

so a Pelton wheel at 400 m head has a jet moving at about 87 m/s and buckets at some 40 m/s — which is why sediment abrasion is so destructive at high heads, and why the settling basin must remove particles down to about **0.1 mm**.

**The other Pelton design ratios**, examined alongside:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Speed ratio** u/√(2gH) | **0.43 – 0.48** |
| **Jet ratio** D/d (wheel to jet diameter) | **11 – 14** |
| Number of buckets | **15 + D/2d**, typically 17–26 |
| Bucket width | 4 – 5 d |
| Bucket depth | 1.2 d |

**Speed control.** Because u must stay near V/2 for efficiency, and the generator requires a constant speed N = 120f/P to hold 50 Hz, the **governor** adjusts the **discharge** rather than the speed — moving the spear (needle) valve in the nozzle, with a **deflector** to throw the jet clear of the buckets for rapid load rejection. The deflector exists precisely because closing the nozzle quickly would cause **water hammer** in the penstock: the jet can be diverted instantly while the valve closes slowly.

examTip.trick: Differentiate the power **P = ρa(V − u)²(1 − cos θ)u** with respect to u and set to zero: the maximum is at **u = V/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **At u = V/2 the water leaves the bucket with almost ZERO absolute velocity** — having given up virtually all its kinetic energy, which is exactly what maximum efficiency means. Buckets deflect through **165°, not 180°**, so the outgoing water misses the incoming jet — costing under 2% of the theoretical maximum.

questions.stem: The width of land acquired along the alignment of a road is called the:
questions.solution:
**Right of way (ROW).**

The cross-section terms nest inside one another, and the question is testing which is the outermost:

| Term | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Carriageway** | The **paved surface** carrying vehicles — 3.75 m single lane, **7.0 m two lane** |
| **Roadway / formation width** | **Carriageway + shoulders** — the full width of the prepared earthwork |
| **Right of way** | **The whole strip of land acquired** — formation plus side drains, side slopes, footpaths, utilities and future widening |

So ROW ⊃ formation ⊃ carriageway. Note that "roadway" and "formation width" are effectively the same thing, which is why both appear as options.

**Why the ROW is made wider than the road needs today.** It must accommodate:

- **side drains and catch drains**, without which the road fails in the monsoon;
- **cut and fill slopes**, which on hill roads can be far wider than the carriageway itself;
- **utilities** — water mains, electricity, telecommunications;
- **footpaths and cycle tracks** where required;
- **future widening**, which is by far the most important. Land is cheap to acquire before development and ruinously expensive afterwards.

That last point is the practical lesson: a ROW acquired generously at the outset makes later widening a construction problem; one acquired narrowly makes it a **land acquisition** problem, which in Nepal typically dominates the cost and the programme of a road upgrade.

**Typical ROW widths** (Nepal Road Standard):

| Road class | ROW |
|---|---|
| **National Highway** | **50 m** (25 m each side of the centre line) |
| Feeder road | 30 m |
| District road | 20 m |
| Urban road | As per the municipal plan |

**Building line and control line**, the related concepts: the **building line** sets a further setback within which construction is prohibited, and the **control line** a wider limit within which building is restricted. Both exist to protect future widening and to preserve sight distance — and both are widely ignored in practice, which is why road widening in Kathmandu has required demolition.

The other cross-section elements, for completeness: **camber** (1.7–2.5% for bituminous surfaces), **superelevation** (max 7% plains, 10% hills), **extra widening** on curves, kerbs, medians and **shoulders** (minimum 2.5 m on a highway). Note that **gradient** is *not* a cross-section element — it belongs to the vertical alignment, which is the point the circulating key for Set 1 Q46 gets wrong.

examTip.trick: **Right of way** is the **total width of land acquired**; the **formation width** is what is actually built (carriageway plus shoulders); the **carriageway** is the paved running surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Right of way > formation width > carriageway.** The extra land is acquired for **future widening, drainage, utilities and services** — which is why acquiring too narrow a right of way is a mistake that cannot be corrected once development lines the road.

questions.stem: The camber provided on a bituminous pavement in a heavy rainfall area is usually:
questions.solution:
**1 in 60 to 1 in 40, that is 1.7% to 2.5%.**

Camber is the **transverse slope** from the crown to the edge of the carriageway, and its sole purpose is to **drain rainwater off the surface** as quickly as possible.

**Why water must be shed quickly.** Water standing on or soaking through the surface is the principal cause of pavement failure:

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Weakened subgrade** | Cohesive soil loses shear strength on wetting, so the foundation softens and the pavement ruts |
| **Stripping** | Water displaces bitumen from the aggregate, leading to ravelling and potholes |
| **Aquaplaning** | A film of water lifts the tyre off the surface — a safety failure |
| Frost damage | Water in the layers freezes and heaves |

**Camber values by surface type** — a rougher surface needs a steeper camber, because water drains less readily across it:

| Surface | Camber |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete, high-quality bituminous** | **1 in 50 to 1 in 60** (1.7 – 2%) |
| **Thin bituminous surface** | **1 in 40 to 1 in 50** (2 – 2.5%) |
| Water bound macadam, gravel | 1 in 33 to 1 in 40 (2.5 – 3%) |
| **Earth road** | **1 in 25** (4%) |

And it is increased in **heavy rainfall** areas within those ranges — which is why the 1.7–2.5% band is the answer for a bituminous pavement in wet conditions.

**The tension that fixes the value.** Camber must be:

| Too flat | Too steep |
|---|---|
| Water **ponds** on the surface | Vehicles **drift** towards the edge |
| Drainage is slow | Uncomfortable; risk of **overturning** for high-sided vehicles |
| Pavement deteriorates | Difficult overtaking; edge wear |

So camber is deliberately kept to the **minimum that drains adequately** — never more.

**Do not confuse camber with superelevation.** Both are transverse slopes, but:

| | **Camber** | **Superelevation** |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | **Drainage** | **Counter centrifugal force** on a curve |
| Where | **Straights** (and everywhere as a minimum) | **Horizontal curves** only |
| Direction | Falls **both ways** from the crown | Falls **inward**, towards the centre of the curve |
| Magnitude | 1.7 – 4% | up to **7% plains, 10% hills** |

On a curve the outer half's camber must be **removed and reversed** to build up the superelevation, which is done progressively along the **transition curve** — the same length over which the extra widening is introduced.

Camber shapes used: **parabolic** (comfortable, sheds water well, favoured for high speeds), **straight-line** (simple to construct), and composite.

examTip.trick: Camber is chosen from the **surface type** (how impermeable it is) and the **rainfall** (how much water must be shed). A rougher, more permeable surface needs more camber.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cement concrete 1 in 60; bituminous 1 in 50 to 1 in 40; WBM 1 in 40 to 1 in 33; earth road 1 in 33 to 1 in 25.** Smoother surface, flatter camber. Too little and water ponds and infiltrates; too much and vehicles drift toward the edge and the road is uncomfortable.

questions.stem: In water bound macadam (WBM) construction, the function of the screening is to:
options: Provide the main load-bearing strength of the layer
Fill the voids in the coarse aggregate
questions.solution:
**To fill the voids in the coarse aggregate.**

WBM is built up from three materials, each with a distinct role:

| Material | Role |
|---|---|
| **Coarse aggregate** | The **load-bearing skeleton**; interlocking stone that carries and spreads the load |
| **Screenings** | Smaller aggregate or **stone dust that fills the voids** between the coarse stones |
| **Binding material** | Fine material (or none, in modern practice) to help bind the surface |
| **Water** | The medium that **washes the screenings into the voids** during rolling |

So the coarse aggregate provides the strength (which is why option (a) is wrong), and the screenings' job is purely to **fill and lock**.

**Why filling the voids matters.** Without screenings the coarse stones bear on one another at a few points only. Under traffic they shift, grind and eventually crush at those contacts, and the layer loses shape. Filling the voids:

- **locks the stones against movement**, achieving mechanical interlock;
- spreads the contact stresses over a much larger area;
- gives a **dense** layer with a smooth, closed surface.

The name explains the method: **water bound** — the layer is bound by washing the screenings into place with water during rolling, not by any binder. The process is deliberately **wet**, and the layer is rolled until a **wave of grout** appears ahead of the roller wheels, which is the sign that the voids have filled.

**The construction sequence:**

1. Prepare the sub-base or previous layer; provide **lateral confinement** (kerbs or shoulders) so the stone cannot spread sideways.
2. Spread the **coarse aggregate** to a uniform camber and thickness (75 mm compacted per layer).
3. **Dry roll** to key the stones together.
4. Apply **screenings** in thin layers, brooming them in, with **dry rolling** between applications.
5. **Sprinkle water and roll** until the grout wave forms.
6. Apply binding material where specified, sprinkle and roll.
7. **Allow to set and dry** overnight before opening to traffic.

**Its place today.** WBM is cheap, uses local stone and needs no plant beyond a roller — which is why it remains common as a **base or sub-base** on Nepali district roads, and as a surfacing on low-volume roads. Its weaknesses are that it is **dusty and permeable when unsurfaced**, and it deteriorates rapidly under heavy traffic or standing water. So it is normally covered by a **bituminous surfacing**, for which the permissible **Los Angeles abrasion** value relaxes from 40% (WBM surfacing) to 50% (WBM base with bituminous surfacing).

The modern alternative is **WMM (wet mix macadam)**, in which graded aggregate and water are mixed in a plant before laying — faster, more uniform and less labour-intensive, and now preferred on major works.

examTip.trick: In WBM the **coarse aggregate carries the load by interlock**, and the **screenings** fill the voids between the stones so the layer becomes dense and stable rather than loose.
examTip.mnemonic: **WBM sequence: coarse aggregate spread → dry rolling → SCREENINGS applied and rolled in → binding material and water → wet rolling.** The water is what carries the fines into the voids — which is why it is *water*-bound macadam, and why the wet rolling stage cannot be skipped.

questions.stem: A project is economically justified on the benefit–cost criterion when the B/C ratio is:
questions.solution:
**Equal to or greater than 1.**

> **B/C = present worth of benefits / present worth of costs**

A ratio of 1 means the discounted benefits exactly equal the discounted costs — the project breaks even in present-value terms. **Above 1** it returns more than it consumes and is justified; **below 1** it is not.

Note that both streams must be **discounted to the same point in time** before the division, because a benefit received in year 20 is not comparable with a cost incurred in year 1. Dividing undiscounted totals is a common and serious error — it was one of the internal inconsistencies in the canal-lining question of Set 1 Q68.

**Where B/C is used, and why it is not simply NPV.** The B/C ratio is the standard criterion for **public** projects — roads, irrigation, water supply, flood control — because such projects produce benefits that accrue to society rather than revenue to the owner. It appears in **economic** analysis, where NPV appears in **financial** analysis:

| | **Financial analysis** | **Economic analysis** |
|---|---|---|
| Viewpoint | The **owner / investor** | **Society as a whole** |
| Prices | Market prices | **Shadow (economic) prices** |
| Includes taxes, subsidies, transfer payments | Yes | **No** — they are transfers, not resource costs |
| Includes externalities | No | **Yes** — environmental and social effects |
| Typical criterion | **NPV, IRR** | **EIRR, B/C ratio** |

**The relationship between the criteria** is worth stating, because they must agree:

> **B/C ≥ 1** ⟺ **NPV ≥ 0** ⟺ **IRR ≥ discount rate**

So the three are equivalent accept/reject tests at the same discount rate. Option (a) confuses the criteria: **MARR** is the hurdle *rate* against which **IRR** is compared, and it is not a value the B/C ratio takes.

**Two cautions on B/C in practice:**

1. It is **sensitive to how items are classified**. A recurring cost can be entered as a cost in the denominator or as a negative benefit in the numerator, and the two give the *same* NPV but **different** B/C ratios. So B/C ratios are only comparable between projects if the conventions match — which is why the **net** B/C ratio, (B − C_operating)/C_capital, is often specified.
2. It **cannot rank** mutually exclusive alternatives reliably, for the same reason IRR cannot: a small project may have a high ratio while leaving most of the available capital idle. Ranking requires **incremental analysis** — ordering by increasing investment and testing each increment.

The other quantities the appraisal reports alongside it: **EIRR**, the **payback period** (which ignores the time value of money and everything after payback, so it is not a sound criterion on its own), and a **sensitivity analysis** showing how the verdict changes if costs overrun or benefits disappoint.

examTip.trick: **B/C ≥ 1** means the discounted benefits at least equal the discounted costs — the project returns more than it consumes.
examTip.mnemonic: **B/C ≥ 1 justifies a project; the HIGHEST B/C does not necessarily choose between mutually exclusive ones** — for that you need **incremental** analysis, comparing the extra benefit against the extra cost of each step up. A small project can show a high ratio and a large one deliver far more net benefit.

questions.stem: The work breakdown structure (WBS) of a project is:
options: A bar chart showing activity durations
A list of the resources required for the project
A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into manageable work packages
The network diagram showing activity dependencies
questions.solution:
**A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into manageable work packages.**

The WBS breaks the project down level by level, each level more detailed than the one above:

> **Project → Deliverables / phases → Sub-deliverables → Work packages → Activities**

The lowest level is the **work package** — a piece of work small enough to be estimated, scheduled, assigned to one responsible party, and monitored as a unit.

**Why it comes first.** The WBS is the **foundation** of every other planning document, and none of them can be built correctly without it:

| Depends on the WBS | How |
|---|---|
| **Cost estimate** | Each work package is estimated, and the estimates roll up |
| **Schedule (CPM / PERT)** | Activities are derived from work packages, then sequenced |
| **Resource plan** | Requirements are assigned package by package |
| **Responsibility matrix** | Each package gets one accountable owner |
| **Progress measurement / earned value** | Progress is measured against packages, not against vague percentages |
| Risk register | Risks are identified per package |

So options (a), (b) and (d) all name documents that are **produced from** the WBS: a bar chart and a network show *when* and *in what order*, and a resource list shows *with what* — but the WBS establishes **what work exists at all**.

**The rule that makes it rigorous** is the **100% rule**: the WBS must include **all** the work of the project and **nothing outside** it. Each level sums exactly to its parent. That is what makes it a control document rather than a wish list, and it is why scope creep is detectable — new work either fits an existing package or requires a change to the WBS.

Two further conventions:
- It is **deliverable-oriented**, describing *outputs* rather than actions — "foundation complete", not "excavate".
- Each element carries a **WBS code** (1.2.3), which becomes the key linking the schedule, the cost account and the progress report. That coding is what allows costs and progress to be aggregated consistently.

**What happens without one**, which is the practical argument: work that nobody estimated, nobody scheduled and nobody owns — discovered late, when it is expensive. Most claims for **extra work** and most disputes about scope trace back to a WBS that was incomplete or never agreed.

The planning sequence it heads:

> **WBS** → activity list → sequencing (network logic) → duration estimates → **CPM / PERT schedule** → resource levelling → **baseline** → monitoring and control

Recall that **resource levelling** treats resources as the constraint and lets the duration extend, while **resource smoothing** holds the completion date and shifts activities within their float — a distinction that only becomes meaningful once the WBS has defined the work being levelled.

examTip.trick: The WBS **decomposes the scope**, not the schedule or the organisation. Each level breaks the work into smaller pieces until the bottom level is a **work package** that can be estimated, assigned and controlled.
examTip.mnemonic: **The WBS defines WHAT; the schedule defines WHEN; the organisation chart defines WHO.** Its cardinal rule is the **100% rule** — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less. Work not in the WBS is not in the project.

questions.stem: A variation order in a construction contract is:
options: A penalty imposed on the contractor for delay
The final account settling the contract
The contractor's claim for additional payment
A written instruction by the employer or engineer altering the scope of the work
questions.solution:
**A written instruction by the employer or the engineer altering the scope of the work.**

A variation order (change order) formally authorises a departure from the contract as originally let — a change in the quantity, quality, dimensions, specification or sequence of the work, or an addition or omission.

Why the other options are different things, and the distinctions matter contractually:

| Instrument | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Variation order** | **The employer's instruction** changing the work |
| **Claim** | The **contractor's** application for additional time or money, which may *arise from* a variation |
| **Liquidated damages** | A pre-agreed sum deducted for **delay** — option (a) |
| **Final account** | The settlement of all payments at completion — option (b) |

So a variation is an **instruction going one way** and a claim is an **application coming back the other**. Conflating them is the root of a great many disputes.

**Why variations are provided for at all.** No construction contract can foresee everything: ground conditions differ from the investigation, the client's requirements evolve, statutory requirements change, and design errors emerge. Without a variation mechanism the only options would be to build something unwanted or to terminate — so the contract builds in a controlled way to change the work.

**The essential requirement is that it be in writing and issued before the work is done.** An oral instruction, or work done first and authorised later, is the classic source of dispute: the contractor claims it was instructed, the employer denies it, and there is no record. Under Nepal's **Public Procurement Act 2063** and the PPMO documents, variations must be **written, within the authorised limits**, and valued by the contract's own rules.

**How a variation is valued**, in order of preference:

| Basis | When used |
|---|---|
| **Contract rates (BOQ rates)** | Work of the **same character** under similar conditions — the normal case |
| **Derived / analogous rates** | Similar work, adjusted from a BOQ rate |
| **Star rate** — newly negotiated | Work of a **different character**, with no comparable rate |
| **Daywork** | Minor or incidental work, paid on time and materials |

**Its consequences**, which follow automatically and are often overlooked:
- **Time**: a variation may justify an **extension of time**, which in turn protects the contractor from liquidated damages.
- **Cost**: adjustment of the contract price.
- **Cumulative limits**: variations beyond a stated percentage of the contract price usually require higher approval, precisely to prevent a contract being transformed into a different one without re-tendering.

That last safeguard is the public-procurement rationale: unlimited variations would let an authority award a small contract competitively and then expand it many times over without competition — which is why the limits exist and why exceeding them is treated as a serious irregularity rather than a technicality.

examTip.trick: A **variation (change order)** is a **formal written instruction** altering the scope. Verbal instructions and site conversations are exactly what cause contractual disputes.
examTip.mnemonic: **In writing, from the authorised person, before the work is done.** A variation triggers **valuation** (using contract rates where applicable, new rates where not) and possibly an **extension of time**. Most construction claims arise from work done on an instruction that was never properly issued or recorded.
